bullets: The new DIB-Bench release tests a gap that behavioral scoring cannot see: whether the deployed runtime has been tampered with while preserving expected evaluation outputs. Across 7,560 examples and six tamper types, its source reports that rule-based and model-based judges accepted 88.6% to 94.1% of tampered outputs. [E024] Why it matters: If you are approving an agent for deployment, a high output score alone cannot establish that the running model, tools, and surrounding software match the tested stack. DIB-Bench adds a concrete reason to evaluate deployment identity and integrity separately from task behavior. [E024] Evidence: E024. Medium confidence.

The new VELD-QA benchmark separates finding evidence from interpreting it in long visual documents. Its 15,000 human-authored question-answer pairs span 5,859 real-world Portable Document Format files, with annotations for supporting pages, charts, tables, and other visual elements. [E001] Why it matters: If you are choosing a system for document analysis, one answer-accuracy score can hide whether failures come from retrieving the wrong page or misunderstanding the right chart or table. VELD-QA makes those two capabilities independently measurable. [E001] Evidence: E001. High confidence.

The new MAI-Gym platform uses one rollout pipeline for graphical user interface agent evaluation, data collection, and online reinforcement learning, where agents learn through interactive rewards. It supports ten established benchmarks across mobile, desktop, and web environments and claims scaling to 20,000 parallel instances. [E002] Why it matters: If you are selecting infrastructure for training interface-using agents, MAI-Gym offers a way to reduce behavior differences caused by using separate training and evaluation systems. Its shared pipeline also makes training throughput and benchmark compatibility part of the same platform decision. [E002] Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.

The new FDE-Gym benchmark evaluates forward-deployed engineering work before requirements become a clean task specification. Its 95 tasks place agents in simulated customer environments where they must question scripted stakeholders, uncover unstated constraints, modify production-like systems, and deliver working solutions. [E008] Why it matters: If you are evaluating agents for customer-facing technical delivery, benchmarks built from complete issue tickets omit requirements discovery and negotiation. FDE-Gym makes those interactions part of the scored workflow rather than assuming that a human has already resolved the ambiguity. [E008] Evidence: E008. High confidence.

The new LIBERO-PeRM benchmark separates successful robotic manipulation from satisfying a household user’s preference. It tests zero-shot preference following, learning from demonstrations, data efficiency, generalization across layouts and tasks, and retention when preferences change. [E004] Why it matters: If you are comparing household robot policies, task completion alone cannot tell whether the robot followed the requested way of completing the task. LIBERO-PeRM adds preference satisfaction and adaptation as distinct selection criteria. [E004] Evidence: E004. High confidence.

The new HPCAgent-Bench evaluates code-optimizing agents across 689 high-performance computing kernels while varying processors, graphics processors, node counts, harnesses, and available skills. A separate judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and measures execution time. [E019] Why it matters: If you are choosing an optimization agent or its software harness, fixed-hardware benchmarks cannot isolate whether gains come from the model, tools, or target platform. HPCAgent-Bench provides a common interface for comparing those components while guarding against fast but incorrect code. [E019] Evidence: E019. High confidence.

The new INFUSE benchmark evaluates indirect prompt injection across complete agent workflows rather than isolated malicious strings. It contains 40 realistic tasks and 56 attack types covering workflows that execute commands, modify code, install dependencies, and interact with remote services. [E018] Why it matters: If you are testing an agent that consumes untrusted external content, a single-step safety test may miss attacks that become effective only after several tools and workflow stages. INFUSE makes exposure across the full execution lifecycle an explicit evaluation target. [E018] Evidence: E018. High confidence.
bullets_zh: 新发布的 DIB-Bench 测试了行为评分无法察觉的一项缺口：已部署的运行时是否遭到篡改，同时仍能保持预期的评测输出。其来源报告称，在 7,560 个样例和六类篡改方式中，基于规则和基于模型的评判器接受了 88.6% 至 94.1% 的篡改输出。[E024] Why it matters: 如果你正在审批某个智能体投入部署，仅凭较高的输出得分无法证明实际运行的模型、工具及周边软件与受测技术栈一致。DIB-Bench 提供了一个具体理由，说明应将部署身份与完整性同任务行为分开评估。[E024] Evidence: E024. Medium confidence.

新发布的 VELD-QA 基准将长篇视觉文档中的证据查找与证据解读区分开来。它包含 15,000 个人工编写的问答对，覆盖 5,859 个真实世界的 Portable Document Format 文件，并标注了作为支撑证据的页面、图表、表格及其他视觉元素。[E001] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择文档分析系统，单一的答案准确率得分可能会掩盖失败究竟源于检索了错误页面，还是误解了正确的图表或表格。VELD-QA 使这两项能力可以分别衡量。[E001] Evidence: E001. High confidence.

新发布的 MAI-Gym 平台使用统一的 rollout 流水线开展图形用户界面智能体评测、数据收集和在线强化学习；在在线强化学习中，智能体通过交互式奖励进行学习。它支持移动端、桌面端和 Web 环境中的十个成熟基准，并声称可扩展至 20,000 个并行实例。[E002] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择用于训练界面操作智能体的基础设施，MAI-Gym 提供了一种方法，可减少因训练系统与评测系统相互分离而导致的行为差异。其共享流水线还使训练吞吐量和基准兼容性成为同一平台决策的一部分。[E002] Evidence: E002. Medium confidence.

新发布的 FDE-Gym 基准在需求尚未形成清晰任务规格之前，评估前线部署工程工作。其 95 项任务将智能体置于模拟客户环境中，要求它们询问由脚本驱动的利益相关方、发现未明确说明的约束、修改类似生产环境的系统，并交付可运行的解决方案。[E008] Why it matters: 如果你正在评估面向客户的技术交付智能体，基于完整问题工单构建的基准会遗漏需求发现与协商。FDE-Gym 将这些交互纳入计分工作流，而不是假设人类已经消除了歧义。[E008] Evidence: E008. High confidence.

新发布的 LIBERO-PeRM 基准将机器人成功完成操作与满足家庭用户偏好区分开来。它测试零样本偏好遵循、从示范中学习、数据效率、跨布局和任务的泛化能力，以及偏好发生变化时的保持能力。[E004] Why it matters: 如果你正在比较家用机器人策略，仅凭任务完成情况无法判断机器人是否按照用户要求的方式完成了任务。LIBERO-PeRM 将偏好满足和适应能力作为彼此独立的选择标准。[E004] Evidence: E004. High confidence.

新发布的 HPCAgent-Bench 在改变处理器、图形处理器、节点数量、测试框架和可用技能的情况下，对代码优化智能体进行评估，涵盖 689 个高性能计算内核。一个独立评判器会基于隐藏的模糊测试输入检查正确性，并测量执行时间。[E019] Why it matters: 如果你正在选择优化智能体或其软件测试框架，采用固定硬件的基准无法区分性能提升究竟来自模型、工具还是目标平台。HPCAgent-Bench 提供了一个用于比较这些组件的通用接口，同时防范速度快但不正确的代码。[E019] Evidence: E019. High confidence.

新发布的 INFUSE 基准针对完整的智能体工作流评估间接提示词注入，而不是评估孤立的恶意字符串。它包含 40 项现实任务和 56 种攻击类型，覆盖执行命令、修改代码、安装依赖项以及与远程服务交互的工作流。[E018] Why it matters: 如果你正在测试会处理不受信任外部内容的智能体，单步骤安全测试可能会漏掉只有经过多个工具和工作流阶段后才会生效的攻击。INFUSE 将整个执行生命周期中的暴露风险明确设为评测目标。[E018] Evidence: E018. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Existing long-document QA benchmarks rarely combine large-scale human-authored questions with detailed visual evidence annotations, limiting diagnosis of evidence localization and interpretation failures. We present VELD-QA, a large-scale benchmark for Visual Evidence grounding and question answering in Long Documents. It contains 15,000 fully human-authored question-answer pairs across 5,859 real-world PDFs totaling 372,445 pages, balancing chart, table, and complex-layout tasks. Human annotations identify supporting pages and evidence elements and describe cited visual content, enabling separate retrieval and interpretation evaluation. We evaluate nine vision-language models under four evidence settings and seven retrieval-augmented and agentic systems. Our analysis identifies bottlenecks in evidence localization and interpretation. Retrieval-based methods substantially underperform the oracle setting with ground-truth supporting pages; full-document access does not close the gap. Localization alone is insufficient: oracle accuracy peaks at 81.7%, highlighting persistent visual interpretation and reasoning challenges. Enriching inputs with our visual-element annotations narrows the performance gap by 17-24%, demonstrating value beyond evaluation and motivating data enrichment for multimodal document QA. Our code is available at https://github.com/oracle-samples/veld-qa.
evidence_items.title: VELD-QA: A Large-Scale Dataset for Visual Evidence Grounding and Question Answering in Long Documents

evidence_items.summary: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.
evidence_items.title: MAI-Gym: An Open All-in-One Platform for GUI Agent Evaluation and RL Training across Mobile and Computer Environments

evidence_items.summary: Abstract. Flash floods develop within minutes to hours, occur mainly in small to medium-sized watersheds, and are documented through scattered sources such as news reports, social media, stream gauges, operational storm events databases, and post-flood field surveys. Such fragmentation historically limits flash flood research advances and model evaluation or intercomparisons. We present TORRENT (the Traceable, Observation-constrained, Rapid-Response, Episode–gauge–watershed Network of Testbeds), a benchmark-ready community dataset of flash-flood hydrological response in the contiguous United States (CONUS). Each testbed links one reported NOAA/NCEI flash-flood episode, one U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) stream gauge, and the gauge’s contributing watershed, combining the observed discharge hydrograph—the primary benchmark target—with watershed boundaries, temporally screened in-basin high-water marks, and quality-control metadata; full packages additionally provide Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) precipitation forcing and auxiliary gridded products. TORRENT follows a three-level structure distinguishing what was reported, what observations are available, and what can be evaluated reproducibly: a national inventory of 42,466 reported episodes for 1996–2025; observation-availability documentation for 5,424 recent CONUS episodes during 2021–2025, including episodes without usable external observations; and 806 episode–gauge–watershed evaluation packages representing 160 episodes and 208 gauges. Each Level-3 package has a retrievable watershed, at least one in-basin high-water mark meeting the stated temporal-screening criterion, and a detected discharge response. Flash-flood-response screening, deduplication, in-basin NCEI corroboration, station-relative severity screening, and post-selection curation yield a conservative primary benchmark of 21 testbeds representing 14 episodes and 21 gauges.
evidence_items.title: TORRENT: An observation-constrained and benchmark-ready community shared dataset in the contiguous United States for flash-flood research and model intercomparison

evidence_items.summary: Personalization is essential for general-purpose robots to transition into household environments and achieve true practicality. While general robotic manipulation has been extensively studied, personalized robotic manipulation (PeRM) lacks a controlled benchmark for separating task completion from preference satisfaction. We introduce LIBERO-PeRM, a benchmark for preference learning in embodied agents. LIBERO-PeRM studies five questions: 1) how policies follow preferences in zero-shot settings; 2) how they learn single preferences from demonstrations; 3) how efficiently they acquire preferences as demonstrations increase; 4) how learned preferences generalize across layouts and tasks; and 5) how policies compose preferences and behave under conflicts. We propose a controlled formulation and taxonomy of observable preferences in simulation, covering motion, skill, and user-profile choices. This formulation is restricted to language-expressible preferences that can be instantiated in LIBERO without changing the task goal, evaluated automatically, and reused across tasks. Building on LIBERO, our procedural pipeline generates paired demonstrations with and without preferences. We create five task suites (312 tasks) with high-quality demonstrations, rich metadata, and preference-satisfaction metrics. Experiments show that current VLA policies struggle with zero-shot personalization, while SFT makes preferences learnable. Mixed training achieves better no-preference retention than sequential adaptation and improves performance with contextual prompts compared with preference-only training, but can weaken motion-preference learning; preference generalization, decomposition, and conflict handling remain difficult. The code, datasets, and demos can be found on the project website: https://libero-perm.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: LIBERO-PeRM: Benchmarking Personalized Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.
evidence_items.title: 3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning models for tabular prediction typically assume that training data are representative of the population on which they will be deployed. In practice, however, data are often collected based on convenience, availability, or cost, resulting in systematic sampling biases that can distort feature--target relationships and undermine real-world generalization. Existing tabular distribution-shift benchmarks primarily construct out-of-distribution (OOD) settings by partitioning observations across naturally occurring domains. While such partitions may induce changes in P(Y | X), the resulting shifts are neither explicitly controlled nor isolated, and the evaluation distributions themselves are often not representative of the broader target population. We introduce INCONVENIENT, a benchmark designed to study robustness to convenience-sample bias. Rather than relying on naturally occurring domain partitions, INCONVENIENT directly perturbs feature--target relationships in the training distribution while preserving the original population distribution as the deployment environment. This setting more closely reflects real-world scenarios in which models are developed from unrepresentative samples and subsequently deployed on a broader population. The distinction is particularly relevant for large language models (LLMs), whose pretraining may encode population-level knowledge that extends beyond the relationships observed in a biased training dataset. Unlike existing distribution-shift benchmarks, INCONVENIENT provides explicit control over both the direction and severity of relationship shifts, enabling a systematic assessment of robustness to convenience sampling. The benchmark comprises 200 tabular classification and regression datasets spanning diverse application domains and generates around 15,500 shifted training distributions which lead to substantial downstream degradation.
evidence_items.title: INCONVENIENT: A Benchmark to Assess LLM Generalization Capabilities from Convenience Samples

evidence_items.summary: Existing agent benchmarks typically evaluate agents on well-specified tasks defined by issue reports, specifications, or task tickets. Real-world customer delivery is different: forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and uncover unstated constraints. We introduce FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks from 20 customer scenarios across 18 sectors, each adapted by industry experts from real-world delivery projects. In simulated customer environments with scripted stakeholders and modifiable customer systems, agents interact with stakeholders and operate on production-like systems to deliver working solutions. FDE-Gym scores a delivery by how much it improves the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder interactions (messages, trial runs, and waiting time). An online platform lets humans practice FDE skills under the same grading criteria. We evaluate 13 model configurations from seven providers. In the realistic setting, where unstated constraints must be discovered, the best configuration achieves a mean FDE-Gym score of 0.56 and resolves only 14 of the 95 tasks (a score of at least 0.8 with no incident). Discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck: performance drops sharply when models must uncover them without explicit guidance. Yet information discovery alone does not account for the gap: even on the 23 tasks where the best configuration obtains every key fact from stakeholders, it reaches a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10. These results reveal a substantial gap between solving well-specified tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers.
evidence_items.title: FDE-Gym: The Last Mile of AI Delivery

evidence_items.summary: The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control. While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized optimization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability. We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures. X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient training, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and interpretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near-RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement. To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics. We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments. X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance.
evidence_items.title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in Omni Language Models (OLMs) provide a unified solution for audiovisual video captioning. Nevertheless, existing approaches predominantly treat captioning as an unstructured text generation process, neglecting the inherent semantic structure of videos and leading to suboptimal fine-grained audiovisual alignment. To bridge this gap, we propose EVA-Cap, a novel framework that decomposes captions into atomic audiovisual events and transforms unstructured text supervision into event-centric alignment. We train EVA-Cap via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a self-curated dataset, EVA-Data, which is built with event-centric quality control. During the GRPO phase, the model is explicitly optimized against three event-centric alignment targets: global event completeness, intra-event attribution, and inter-event synchronization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EVA-Cap significantly outperforms existing methods in event-centric evaluation (e.g., +9.0% average gain on ChronusAV), while achieving competitive performance on general audiovisual captioning benchmarks (e.g., +3.3% on WorldSense).
evidence_items.title: EVA-Cap: Optimizing Audiovisual Video Captioning via Event-Centric Alignment

evidence_items.summary: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.
evidence_items.title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning (ML) for analog IC design is constrained by limited open data and the absence of standardized evaluation: results reported in different papers are typically obtained on bespoke, often closed, datasets and with ad-hoc metrics, leaving comparisons across methods unreliable. We address both gaps with a large opensource dataset and a suite of standardized benchmarks. The dataset contains more than 100 operational amplifier (opamp) topologies (1-, 2-, and 3-stage) in the SkyWater130 PDK, each shipped with structural and functional annotations, topology-specific sizing constraints (symmetry and sizing rules), an Ngspice testbench, and a multi-objective NSGA-II sizing run producing around 103 Pareto-optimal and 106 intermediate sizing-performance pairs per topology. On top of this data we define six benchmark tasks with precise protocols: inverse sizing, topology selection, sub-circuit classification, structural circuit generation, Pareto-membership prediction, and multi-objective optimization. Thus, the data presented here constitutes the most comprehensive dataset for ML development in over four decades of analog IC design automation. The dataset, ground-truth annotations, and reference implementations of the metric-defining routines are released under an open license, enabling reproducible and directly comparable evaluation across heterogeneous analog design automation methods.
evidence_items.title: LOADBench: A Large Open Analog Dataset and Benchmark for Machine Learning in IC Design

evidence_items.summary: Existing deepfake detection models are built upon manipu- lated images that are tampered with either exclusively fully swapped or fully synthesised faces, which leads us to an open question: Can off-the-shelf deepfake models detect manipulation effectively while tampering is confined to a local facial sub-region? To fill this gap, we introduce RLDF (Region-Level Deepfake), the first dataset for region-level deepfake evaluation. Employing the proposed region-aware partial swap synthesis model, we generate over 2M par- tial face-swap images by using eight face-swapping meth- ods. Altogether, we considered seven face regions, among which there are four discrete regions (eye, nose, mouth and eyebrow) and four composite facial regions (eye and nose; eye, nose and mouth; eye, nose, mouth and eye- brow; and full face). In addition, we define three evalu- ation protocols and benchmark 12 state-of-the-art detectors across the five popular standard cross-dataset evaluations, DF40, and the proposed RLDF, providing a comprehen- sive audit of where and why existing detectors underper- formed. Our evaluation reveals that existing detectors fail to generalize consistently across partial facial regions, re- sulting in an overall drop of 10.5% AUC and 10% accu- racy under region-level evaluation. Further, we propose a mask-guided cross-attention model as a baseline approach that can effectively detect region-level manipulation. The proposed dataset, code, and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RLDF-Dataset/RLDF.
evidence_items.title: RLDF: A Region-Level Deepfake Dataset and Benchmark for Partial-Face Manipulation Detection

evidence_items.summary: Current value alignment evaluations for large language models (LLMs) heavily rely on output compliance, overlooking whether LLMs maintain value consistency when alternating between generator and evaluator roles. Such consistency is increasingly important because modern LLM agents and alignment pipelines often rely on the same LLM to both generate actions and evaluate their acceptability. To mitigate this limitation, we propose VALCON, a role-driven data construction framework that operationalizes value consistency into three benchmark suites (VAB-Consistency, VAB-Boundary, VAB-Challenge) via dual-role variation. By systematically pairing an LLM's generative behavior with its evaluative judgments under identical principles, VALCON synthesizes target evaluation data that exposes hidden value discrepancies. Experiments on 28 LLMs reveal pervasive cross-role inconsistency: models with highly compliant outputs frequently fail to align their judgments with their own generations. To understand and address this gap, we perform mechanistic probing that uncovers a role-dependent representational decoupling associated with this behavioral asymmetry. Guided by these insights, we propose a representation-directed intervention that effectively mitigates consistency failures. Our work establishes value consistency as a distinct alignment dimension and provides a complete evaluation-analysis-mitigation pipeline. Code and data are available at https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/VALCON.
evidence_items.title: VALCON: Benchmarking and Enhancing Value Consistency in Large Language Models via Dual-Role Variation

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale multi-agent ecosystems require mechanisms for discovering suitable agents without exposing entire registries to a large language model (LLM) orchestrator. The challenge is not only to retrieve relevant Agent Cards from a growing registry, but also to maintain a compact candidate context, since each additional candidate increases prompt size, inference cost, latency, and the risk of exceeding the model context window. We formulate this problem as candidate-context scalability and propose the Structural Signal Retriever (SSR), our deterministic and training-free retrieval method designed for Agent Card discovery. SSR derives structural lexical signals from capability-bearing Agent Card fields, weights them using inverse document frequency (IDF), and uses an Inverted Signal Index (ISI) for selective candidate scoring. We evaluate SSR using a synthetic agent benchmark, a public MS MARCO adaptation, and end-to-end LLM orchestration. At 1,000 agents, SSR reduces LLM input by 98.8% and orchestration latency by 70.9% relative to full-catalog orchestration. On MS MARCO, IDF improves retrieval effectiveness within the structural representation, while the ISI preserves retrieval effectiveness and reduces explicitly scored passages by 96.8%. End-to-end experiments show that candidate pre-selection maintains a compact candidate context as registry size grows and avoids the operational failures observed with full-catalog orchestration. These results support SSR as an Agent-Card-native, traceable retrieval mechanism for candidate-context scalability.
evidence_items.title: SSR: Structural Signal Retriever for Scalable Agent Discovery in LLM-Orchestrated Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_items.summary: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.
evidence_items.title: Kolab: Benchmarking Human-Agent Collaboration in Long-Horizon Workflows

evidence_items.summary: Computational biologists increasingly delegate substantial analyses to AI agents in long-horizon, multi-turn sessions, yet most benchmarks of agents' bioinformatics capabilities pose a single short task with a single-shot prompt. We present OmicsBench, a long-horizon, multi-turn bioinformatics benchmark for AI agents. Each of its 97 tasks links dependent subtasks into a directed acyclic graph, for 662 underlying subtasks in all. Each subtask is posed as one user turn and graded deterministically against an answer key, with optional in-context feedback on incorrect answers. Across 12 models on three harnesses, the slowest agent averages 3.6 hours per task, and no combination comes near saturating the benchmark, with mean scores of 0.43 to 0.57 out of a possible 1 without in-context feedback and 0.54 to 0.67 with it. Multi-turn evaluation also uncovers behavior that single-shot prompts cannot, as agents score lower on subtasks that depend on earlier subtasks, and in-context feedback helps agents recover some of that loss. Because deterministic scoring gives no qualitative account of how an agent failed, we also introduce an unsupervised failure mode discovery pipeline that describes, embeds, and clusters agents' failed attempts to surface emergent failure modes. Applied to OmicsBench, this pipeline exposes qualitative shortcomings in how agents carry out bioinformatics analyses, ranging from agents applying their own statistical filters in place of the specified ones to agents writing whole answers from memory.
evidence_items.title: OmicsBench: a long-horizon multi-turn benchmark of AI agents on research-study-scale bioinformatics

evidence_items.summary: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.
evidence_items.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly used to optimize code, but existing benchmarks fix one accelerator, programming model or harness, so they cannot isolate what each component contributes or show whether added skills and tools repay their cost. We present HPCAgent-Bench with 689 kernels in three tracks: loop-level optimization challenges, kernels extracted from HPC codes, and machine-learning models. The framework specifies each kernel once in NumPy, derives C and Fortran references, accepts submissions through a common C ABI or Python interface, and runs them on CPUs or GPUs, on one or multiple nodes. An external judge checks correctness on hidden fuzzed inputs and times each submission, closing paths agents use to exploit the testing system. We introduce two metrics for reporting results: \textit{intervention efficacy} measures an intervention, such as adding a tool, through paired runs on speedup, success rate and cost, and \textit{weighted token cost} reports input, cached-input and output tokens under explicit weights. Agents reach up to $4.2\times$ speedup over automatic parallelizers, and their optimizations transfer to another machine: $93$--$99\%$ of answers without device-specific code remain correct, and per-kernel speedups keep a rank correlation of $r_s\ge0.84$. Across 40 matched setups, interventions significantly change speedup only twice but token cost by up to $3.0\times$. Because token weighting decides whether a saving is significant, we state the weights and release every token count as a standard for cost reporting. We provide the first comprehensive, broad and hardened benchmark for the sound evaluation of agentic optimization, with transparent cost metrics.
evidence_items.title: HPCAgent-Bench: A Framework for Sound Benchmarking of Code-Optimizing Agents, Harnesses, and Skills

evidence_items.summary: Trustworthy biomedical AI requires reliable action selection when evidence is missing, stale, conflicting, or late, not only accurate answers on static inputs. We instantiate an episode-level evaluation protocol as 400 synthetic healthcare workflow episodes: 40 hand-authored semantic seeds across four task classes, two surface parameterizations, and five controlled variants, scored on ANSWER/ASK CLARIFICATION/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE under a pre-declared 5:1 missed-versus-unnecessary escalation cost. Reference actions are single-author study-policy labels, not clinician-adjudicated ground truth. Across five open-weight configurations (1.7B--9.7B), clean decision accuracy reaches 0.97, yet uncertainty-prompted models miss 32--97% of required escalations. The stronger 9.7B configuration narrows but does not remove the gap, falling from 0.97 clean accuracy to 0.78 under conflict. Verbalized confidence is inconsistent (ECE 0.10--0.54; failure AUROC 0.48--0.77), and a development-tuned confidence-only policy yields no utility gain. A transparent workflow-aware controller improves 5:1 utility for every model and reduces missed escalations to 0.12--0.24, at specificity 0.83--0.93. However, a 30-concept lexical stress test reduces each rule detector's recall from 1.00 on trigger phrases to 0.00 on unseen paraphrases, limiting the controller claim to this benchmark. Seed-clustered statistics, ablations, cross-task transfer, raw outputs, and manifests are packaged for audit. The results motivate explicit workflow-state evaluation while showing that apparently effective routing controls need their own generalization tests.
evidence_items.title: Auditing Escalation Reliability in Healthcare LLM Agents: A Perturbation-Controlled Benchmark of Workflow-State Failures

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Quantum image processing methods that rely on amplitude encoding are sensitive to channel-induced noise, yet reusable benchmarks for evaluating these effects under controlled conditions remain limited. We present QN-AEI, a simulation-based benchmark constructed from 200 images in the BSDS500 training subset. Each image is resized to 64 × 64 pixels and normalized to a 4096-dimensional amplitude vector representing a 12-qubit quantum state, then subjected to three noise channels (amplitude damping, Pauli-Z dephasing, and depolarizing noise) at four levels, η ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7}, with 200 stochastic trajectory realizations per image–channel–noise condition. This yields 2,400 conditions, 480,000 noisy realizations, and 1,966,080,000 normalized perturbation samples in total. Each record pairs the clean image and amplitude vector with its noisy statevectors, raw and normalized perturbations, and condition-level metadata; the release also includes source-image provenance, a dataset manifest, validation outputs, summary statistics, documentation, and the MATLAB generation and validation code. QN-AEI supports reproducible benchmarking of quantum-noise characterization, denoising, uncertainty and reliability analysis, and bounded-domain perturbation modeling.
evidence_items.title: A benchmark dataset for quantum noise effects in amplitude-encoded images

organizations: Georgia Southern University , , , ,
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate segmentation of protein secondary structures in cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) maps is crucial for protein tracing and atomic model building, yet remains challenging at intermediate resolutions. Although deep learning architectures have recently been applied to this task, there remains a lack of standardized evaluation protocols and systematic resolution-stratified analyses. Consequently, it remains unclear how segmentation performance varies across finer resolution ranges within the intermediate-resolution regime and how different volumetric segmentation architectures compare under controlled experimental conditions. To address these gaps, we present a nonredundant, resolution-stratified benchmark dataset and a controlled evaluation framework for protein secondary-structure segmentation in intermediate-resolution cryo-EM maps. The dataset comprises 972 nonredundant protein-chain samples from 495 cryo-EM protein structures resolved at 4.5–8.0 Å, with voxel-level annotations for helices, sheets, and non-periodic secondary-structure (NPSS) regions. The dataset is stratified into three resolution ranges─4.5–5.5, 5.5–6.5, and 6.5–8.0 Å─to enable systematic analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance. Using this benchmark, we evaluate five representative convolutional and transformer-based volumetric segmentation architectures─U-Net, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, and Swin-UNETR─under standardized preprocessing, training, and evaluation protocols. Residual U-Net achieves the highest macro-averaged foreground (Macro-FG) F1 score in all three resolution bins, while helices are segmented more accurately than sheets and NPSS regions. All five architectures achieve their highest Macro-FG F1 scores in the highest-resolution bin, whereas performance varies between the two lower-resolution bins across architectures and secondary-structure classes.
evidence_items.title:
Deep Learning for
Protein Secondary-Structure Segmentation
in Intermediate-Resolution Cryo-EM Maps: A Resolution-Stratified Benchmark
Dataset and Controlled Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Static benchmarks for large language model (LLM) agents face saturation and data contamination risks, motivating continual updates to evaluation tasks. However, aggregate scores and success rates offer limited insight into specific problem-solving bottlenecks and provide limited guidance for subsequent task design. We propose EvoProbe, an evaluation-driven benchmark evolution framework that integrates task generation, diagnostic evaluation, and feedback-driven regeneration into a closed loop. It combines verifiable subtask outcome scoring with evidence-supported multi-judge trajectory evaluation and distills phase-level bottlenecks, success patterns, and failure patterns into diagnostic feedback for generating new executable tasks. Across two rounds of cybersecurity experiments, evaluations of eight models on 66 tasks reveal phase-level performance differences and common failure patterns beyond aggregate scores. In a cross-round comparison with the Examiner model set and solver configuration held fixed, all eight models achieve lower Outcome scores on the updated tasks, with relative decreases of 11.8\% in mean Outcome and 40.0\% in mean Pass\textasciicircum{}3. These results support using fine-grained diagnostics to guide iterative task updates and probe agents' current capabilities and limitations.
evidence_items.title: EvoProbe: Evaluation-Driven Benchmark Evolution for LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal objects can require different partitions under different instructions, as when products in an e-commerce catalog are grouped by color, material, or both. Retrieval-oriented embeddings may not recover these partitions, while generative clustering often relies on intermediate descriptions or iterative decisions. This paper presents CIM-Embed, a framework for learning instruction-conditioned multimodal embeddings for clustering. Supervised contrastive learning uses same-group positives and negatives from other groups, optionally including other tasks; heterogeneous structured batches accommodate tasks with different group counts. At inference, the model maps each object's image, text, and instruction directly to an embedding; HDBSCAN then forms a partition without the ground-truth cluster count. We construct ProductMIC from product metadata in Amazon Reviews 2023, comprising training data and an evaluation benchmark for instruction-conditioned clustering. The benchmark contains 5,373 products and 449 single-attribute and compositional grouping tasks spanning 50 leaf categories excluded from our training. With full-dimensional embeddings and HDBSCAN, direct within-task SupCon training achieves a mean per-task V-measure of 95.01, compared with 53.06 for WeMM 9B, the strongest general-purpose embedding baseline evaluated. Frozen product-trained encoders also improve out-of-domain conditional grouping, while controlled transfer experiments distinguish partition transfer from instruction response. We will release the code and dataset upon acceptance.
evidence_items.title: CIM-Embed: Learning Instruction-Conditioned Multimodal Embeddings for Clustering

evidence_items.summary: LLM-agent evaluation reports behavioral scores but leaves the identity of the deployed runtime stack unreported. A tampered deployment that preserves evaluated outputs passes every output-only evaluator. We introduce DIB-Bench, a benchmark that measures this deployment-integrity blindness across 7,560 scored examples, six tamper types, and an evaluator ladder from regex scorers through LLM judges to GPT-5-nano. Stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs: mean acceptance rises from 88.6% (rule-based) to 94.1% (GPT-5-nano), and a trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48-100% harmful outputs, rising with model capability. A PAC-style bound shows that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size; a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples. Behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers one of six stack components. We also propose a graded deployment-identity descriptor for evaluation reports.
evidence_items.title: Stronger Judges Do Not See More: Deployment-Integrity Blindness in LLM Evaluation

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in multimodal retrieval have improved the ability to retrieve information from visually rich documents such as PDFs and reports. However, existing benchmarks remain largely centered on English and provide limited coverage of Korean visual documents with complex structures. Furthermore, most existing Korean resources primarily evaluate single-page retrieval, failing to capture realistic scenarios that require evidence aggregation across multiple pages. To address these gaps, we introduce KoViDoRe, a benchmark for Korean visual document retrieval. The dataset is constructed from publicly available Korean documents with diverse layouts, including tables, figures, and multi-column structures. We develop a multi-stage data curation pipeline consisting of structured document parsing, synthetic query generation using both summary-based and context-based strategies, and relevance mapping with human verification. Using KoViDoRe, we evaluate a wide range of multimodal retrieval models and observe that current models struggle to effectively handle Korean visual document retrieval, particularly in settings involving structured content and diverse query types. Motivated by this finding, we further curate a large-scale training dataset, Ko-VDR Train Public, to support the development of retrieval models tailored to Korean visual documents. Together, KoViDoRe and Ko-VDR Train Public provide a unified benchmark and training resource for Korean visual document retrieval.
evidence_items.title: KoViDoRe: A Benchmark for Korean Visual Document Retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have exhibited significant enhancements in performance across various tasks. However, the complexity of their evaluation increases as these models generate more fluent and coherent content. Current multilingual benchmarks often use translated English versions, which may incorporate Western cultural biases that do not accurately assess other languages and cultures. To address this research gap, we introduce KULTURE Bench, an evaluation framework specifically designed for Korean culture that features datasets of cultural news, idioms, and poetry. It is designed to assess language models' cultural comprehension and reasoning capabilities at the word, sentence, and paragraph levels. Using the KULTURE Bench, we assessed the capabilities of models trained with different language corpora and analyzed the results comprehensively. The results show that there is still significant room for improvement in the models' understanding of texts related to the deeper aspects of Korean culture.
evidence_items.title: KULTURE Bench: A Benchmark for Assessing Language Model in Korean Cultural Context

organizations: Universidade Estadual de Goiás
evidence_items.summary: Research Data and Analysis Code for Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene This repository provides the archived molecular dynamics data, analysis scripts, processed datasets, and supplementary computational materials associated with the study entitled "Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene," submitted to Theoretical Chemistry Accounts. The study investigates the reconstruction and coarse-graining of electronic-state kinetic networks from a finite ensemble of 19 nonadiabatic surface-hopping trajectories of phosgene (COCl₂). The original simulations were performed using a TDDFT/TDA-PBE-based trajectory surface-hopping implementation within the Car–Parrinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) framework. The analysis reconstructs the complete 13-state singlet kinetic network from the observed electronic-state transitions and accumulated residence times. The original trajectory histories are subsequently mapped onto reduced kinetic representations, with effective rate constants re-estimated directly from the remapped trajectories. The repository consolidates the original computational archives and supporting analysis materials, including: Archived electronic-state histories and molecular-coordinate records from the phosgene surface-hopping simulations. Python scripts for kinetic-network reconstruction, population propagation, coarse-graining, and statistical validation. Computational workflows for grouped cross-validation, leave-one-trajectory-out analysis, bootstrap resampling, rare-channel sensitivity, and structural uncertainty assessment. Scripts and supporting materials for electronic-structure benchmarking, basis-set sensitivity analysis, and EOM-CCSD data extraction. Residence-time analysis and complementary kinetic and temporal diagnostics.
evidence_items.title: **Research Data and Analysis Code for Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene**  This repository provides the archived molecular dynamics data, analysis scripts, processed datasets, and supplementary computational materials associated with the study entitled "Trajectory-Based Coarse-Graining of Nonadiabatic Excited-State Dynamics: A Four-State Kinetic Representation of Phosgene," submitted to *Theoretical Chemistry Accounts*.  The study investigates the reconstruction and coarse-graining of electronic-state kinetic networks from a finite ensemble of 19 nonadiabatic surface-hopping trajectories of phosgene (COCl₂). The original simulations were performed using a TDDFT/TDA-PBE-based trajectory surface-hopping implementation within the Car–Parrinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) framework.  The analysis reconstructs the complete 13-state singlet kinetic network from the observed electronic-state transitions and accumulated residence times. The original trajectory histories are subsequently mapped onto reduced kinetic representations, with effective rate constants re-estimated directly from the remapped trajectories.  The repository consolidates the original computational archives and supporting analysis materials, including:  * Archived electronic-state histories and molecular-coordinate records from the phosgene surface-hopping simulations. * Python scripts for kinetic-network reconstruction, population propagation, coarse-graining, and statistical validation. * Computational workflows for grouped cross-validation, leave-one-trajectory-out analysis, bootstrap resampling, rare-channel sensitivity, and structural uncertainty assessment. * Scripts and supporting materials for electronic-structure benchmarking, basis-set sensitivity analysis, and EOM-CCSD data extraction. * Residence-time analysis and complementary kinetic and temporal diagnostics. * Structural and geometric analyses of the archived molecular trajectories, including periodic-image proximity assessments. * Selected processed datasets, numerical outputs, supplementary figures, source-package inventories, and SHA-256 checksums.  The original computational packages are preserved in their archived form, while the extracted analysis scripts and selected processed data are organized into a consolidated directory structure to facilitate inspection and reuse.  **Scope and limitations**  The deposited materials document the computational data and analysis procedures associated with the available 19-trajectory ensemble. The resulting kinetic parameters and reduced-state representations are conditional on the original electronic-structure model, trajectory sampling, and periodic simulation conditions.  The repository does not establish convergence of the original molecular dynamics ensemble, independent physical validation of the simulated S₁/S₀ transfer, or transferability of the inferred kinetic parameters to other molecular systems.  This consolidated workspace preserves the available source packages and supporting computational materials. Complete end-to-end reproduction of every result in the final revised manuscript has not yet been independently certified. Users should consult the included README, source-package documentation, and release-audit notes for information on individual workflows, input requirements, and known limitations.  The dataset is intended to support scientific transparency, methodological evaluation, and further research on kinetic reconstruction and coarse-graining of nonadiabatic molecular dynamics trajectories.

evidence_items.summary: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.
evidence_items.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: Task completion alone does not determine whether a stateful agent satisfied its obligations, and a recorded judgment does not guarantee that its supporting evidence remains valid. We present AgentEval, a system that carries a contract-bound assessment record through tool execution, state and event capture, report qualification, and case maintenance. It separates what the agent did, what the evidence establishes, and whether the conclusion is supported for present use. On 32 tool-world administrations, independent checks agree on all 30 complete episodes, distinguishing satisfied, violated, and unresolved obligations; two interrupted administrations are retained. Controlled interventions on 48 evidence views expose 36 binding faults missed by hash-only checks without changing agent behavior. Scenario Studio connects reviewed cases to 12 two-turn reports with 24 independently checked answers. A separate public-benchmark study on 192 held-out executions reveals ten completed return subgoals within broader task failures and isolates the effect of missing evidence. These studies show how an executable assessment record makes scope, evidential support, and report reuse inspectable across an agent evaluation workflow.
evidence_items.title: AgentEval: Evidence-Bounded Assessment of Stateful Agents

evidence_items.summary: As coding agents increasingly undertake real-world work autonomously, judging whether their risk treatments are warranted has become important. Existing work evaluates related agent behaviors from separate perspectives, but lacks a systematic framework for unifying these behaviors. To bridge this gap, we introduce ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents. Grounded in the well-established Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance framework in software engineering risk management, ParanoiaEval operationalizes its 4 fundamental treatments for coding-agent settings and contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs, each differing only in treatment-defining evidence. We further introduce dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness, using a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation. Large-scale experiments on 8 representative models and a post-hoc human study reveal that (I) unnecessary risk treatment occurs in 11.2%-58.7% of runs despite explicit evidence, with substantial variation across agent configurations; (II) stronger task capability does not ensure more appropriate risk treatment, while treatment violations substantially harm developers' experience, establishing risk treatment as an independent capability dimension; and (III) agents exhibit systematic patterns consistent with established risk-management findings, suggesting that knowledge from human practice can guide the diagnosis and improvement of this capability.
evidence_items.title: ParanoiaEval: Benchmarking Unnecessary Defensive Work in Agentic Coding

evidence_items.summary: Memory has emerged as a cornerstone of modern LLM-based agents, supporting their evolution from single-turn assistants to long-term collaborators. However, memory is not always beneficial: retrieved memories often induce a critical issue of sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with the user at the cost of factual accuracy or objective reasoning. Despite this emerging risk, existing memory benchmarks primarily evaluate whether memories are correctly stored, retrieved, or updated, while overlooking how retrieved memories influence downstream reasoning and decision-making. To bridge this gap, we propose MemSyco-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating memory-induced sycophancy in agent systems. MemSyco-Bench measures when memory should influence a decision and how valid memory should be used. Specifically, it covers five tasks that assess whether agents can reject memory as factual evidence, respect its applicable scope, resolve conflicts between memory and objective evidence, track memory updates, and use valid memory for personalization. All related resources are collected for the community at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/MemSyco-Bench.
evidence_items.title: MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory

evidence_items.summary: In recent advancements within speech processing, converting read speech to conversational speech has gained significant attention. The primary challenge in this domain is maintaining naturalness and intelligibility while minimizing computational overhead for real-time applications. Traditional read speech often lacks the nuanced prosodic variation essential for natural conversational interactions, posing challenges for applications in virtual assistants, customer service, and language learning tools. This paper introduces a novel approach, Prosodic Adjustment with Conversational Context (PACC), aimed at converting read speech into natural conversational speech used in various modern applications. PACC utilizes advanced deep neural networks to analyze and modify prosodic features such as intonation, stress, and rhythm. Unlike conventional methods, our approach uses High-Fidelity Generative Adversarial Networks (HiFi-GAN) for speech synthesis. Our experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in speech conversion, enhancing naturalness and achieving better model accuracy with additional training on speech datasets. This research establishes new benchmarks in speech conversion tasks and Mean Opinion Score (MOS) evaluation for testing model accuracy, and we show that our approach can be successfully extended to other speech conversion applications.
evidence_items.title: Bridging the Gap: Converting Read Text to Conversational Dialogue

evidence_items.summary: TORRENT (the Traceable, Observation-constrained, Rapid-Response, Episode–gauge–watershed Network of Testbeds) converts reported flash floods in the contiguous United States into traceable episode–gauge–watershed testbeds for reproducible hydrological-response analysis and model intercomparison. The dataset is organised in three levels. Level 1 preserves the national inventory of 42,466 NOAA/NCEI flash-flood episodes for 1996–2025 (110,251 event records; 342,238 location records), retained without hydrological screening. Level 2 documents observation availability for 5,424 recent CONUS episodes (2021–2025), annotating USGS stream-gauge and USGS/FEMA Short-Term Network high-water-mark (HWM) availability for the full population rather than pre-selecting cases; 4,599 of those episodes have discharge availability at a queried nearby gauge. Level 3 provides 806 episode–gauge–watershed evaluation packages (160 episodes, 208 gauges), each requiring a retrievable NLDI contributing watershed, at least one temporally confirmed in-basin high-water mark, and a detected discharge response. Successive screening on Level 3 yields 175 strict flash-flood testbeds, 115 after deduplication, 54 with in-basin NCEI corroboration, and 31 with a Log-Pearson III return period of at least 2 years. Two documented post-selection reviews — direct flood-control influence and recent-wildfire applicability — remove ten further testbeds and define a conservative primary benchmark of 21 testbeds representing 14 episodes and 21 gauges. Every removed testbed remains in Level 3 with the reason recorded as a flag, so users can widen or narrow the sample themselves. The full 13,315-pair screening audit trail ships as data/L3/l3 candidate pairs.csv, so the entire funnel can be re-derived from the archive alone.
evidence_items.title: TORRENT: a benchmark-ready flash-flood dataset for the contiguous United States

organizations: Newcastle University
evidence_items.summary: © 2026 Elsevier B.V.Background: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)-only radiotherapy (RT) is increasingly adopted, but still lacks standardized commissioning procedures. This variability limits consistent clinical implementation: the Multicenter Evaluation of commercial Synthetic-Computed tomography ALgorithms (MESCAL) project aims to establish a benchmark dataset, provide commissioning guidelines, and define tolerance levels to support safe and reproducible MRI-only photon-beam RT adoption. Methods: Data from 32 patients (16 brain, 16 pelvis) were retrospectively collected from two centers. Four sCT solutions licensed for clinical use were evaluated: MRI Planner (Spectronic), SyngoAI (Siemens), MR Box (Therapanacea), and MRCAT (Philips). For each patient, multiple sCTs were generated and compared with the planning CT. Image quality was assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and three additional indicators. Dose accuracy was evaluated by recalculating treatment plans on sCTs and performing dose–volume histogram (DVH) analysis. Position–verification accuracy was quantified by comparing CBCT–to–sCT versus CBCT–to–CT registrations. Plans meeting acceptability criteria (DVH differences < 2%, gamma-passing rate 95% at 2%/2 mm) were used to derive tolerance intervals. Results: Three to four sCTs were generated per case. Brain cases showed higher inter–software variability than pelvic cases, particularly in MAE within body (pelvis: 30–70 HU; brain: 40–130 HU). DVH differences remained within 3% (pelvis) and 4% (brain). Position–verification accuracy was higher in the brain (89% within 1 mm/1°) than in the pelvis (74%). Acceptability criteria were met by 37/43 pelvic and 30/39 brain plans: tolerance values were derived from these cases. Conclusion: MESCAL provides a commissioning framework, benchmark dataset, and tolerance levels to guide local sCT commissioning and promote standardized MRI-only photon-beam RT implementation.
evidence_items.title: Standardizing MRI-only radiotherapy commissioning: Benchmark dataset and acceptance levels from the MESCAL initiative

evidence_items.summary: RCA-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) select appropriate levels of autonomy when responding to organizational requests. It uses a two-gate decision framework distinguishing human-reserved substantive decisions from execution authorization, with three possible autonomy outcomes: ACT, CONFIRM, and ESCALATE. The benchmark contains 60 expert-validated organizational scenarios across six domains. The accompanying experimental dataset comprises 1,440 valid responses from four LLMs evaluated under Baseline and Agent Delegation Policy (ADP)-guided prompting conditions, with three repetitions per scenario. The repository includes benchmark scenarios, expert-established reference labels, experimental responses, prompting procedures, execution configurations, reproducibility scripts, statistical analysis, and supporting audit documentation. The overall classification accuracy was 87.92%. Although ADP-guided prompting produced a descriptive improvement, the scenario-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals did not establish a statistically conclusive improvement. The package is intended to support transparent evaluation, independent verification, and future research on risk-calibrated autonomy, human oversight, and authorization-aware AI agents. The included documentation specifies the scope of the licenses, known reproducibility limitations, and considerations concerning third-party model outputs.

evidence_items.summary: A pre-registered, falsifiable benchmark comparing three AI-agent architectures on a regulated-style (GxP) deviation-triage task that is deliberately seeded to trigger four known context-failure modes: poisoning, distraction, confusion, and clash. The three arms are: (A) a monolithic single agent holding everything in one growing context window; (B) a multi-agent orchestration sharing a growing scratchpad; and (C) a single-agent, one-event-one-record design that assembles a bounded context, exposes only scoped tools, applies a deterministic evidence-presence and source-validation gate before committing any conclusion, prunes superseded documents, and emits one ALCOA+ record per action. Primary endpoints are citation faithfulness and silent-error rate, graded deterministically via hidden passage identifiers (no LLM judge). The hypothesis is that architecture C preserves traceability and lowers failure incidence relative to A and B; honest-negative and kill criteria are pre-specified. All data are synthetic; no proprietary or employer content is used.
evidence_items.title: Single-Agent, One-Record vs the Four Context Failures: A Pre-Registered Benchmark of Agent Architectures on a GxP Deviation-Triage Task

evidence_items.summary: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone's native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33--34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.
evidence_items.title: Intern-Decision: Efficient Multimodal Decision Making with Autoregressive Masked Language Modeling

evidence_items.summary: Natural language messages often contain quasi-identifiers that are weak in isolation but can jointly reveal an individual's private attributes. We call such a jointly revealing set of cues a quasi-evidence group. Existing privacy benchmarks focus on explicit identifiers, attribute inference, or task-driven disclosures, leaving inference from quasi-evidence groups largely unmeasured. In practice, whether exposing such a quasi-evidence group violates privacy also depends on sender-specified disclosure policies. We introduce QuasiLeak-Bench, a benchmark for policy-conditioned quasi-evidence group recovery, which evaluates whether detectors recover complete quasi-evidence groups and flag the disclosures the given policy prohibits. To obtain reliable ground truth at scale, a reverse-construction pipeline first selects weak quasi-identifiers, composes them into quasi-evidence groups verified to jointly reveal a target attribute, and generates documents around this evidence, followed by automated quality control. Experiments show that existing privacy detectors transfer poorly to QuasiLeak-Bench, and locally deployable LLM-based detectors fall far behind proprietary models, mainly because they miss most quasi-evidence groups altogether. However, a 4B model fine-tuned on our training split surpasses the strongest prompted model on held-out documents, showing that the task is learnable.
evidence_items.title: QuasiLeak-Bench: Evaluating LLM-Based Privacy Detectors on Policy-Conditioned Quasi-Evidence Group Recovery

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly used in social interactions, where appropriate responses require recognizing implicit cues, inferring mental states, identifying conflicts, and considering potential consequences. However, existing benchmarks often focus on specific social abilities, constrained task formats, or particular interaction settings, offering limited coverage of social awareness across diverse contexts. To address this gap, we introduce APRiL, an open-ended benchmark for Chinese social awareness with instance-specific rubrics. APRiL contains 2,196 Social Awareness Evaluation Instances across six categories and two complementary tasks: Social Scenario Analysis evaluates models' understanding of social cues, mental states, and conflict structures, while Socially Aware Response assesses whether they can translate this understanding into appropriate, natural responses. Experiments on 12 models from six families reveal a consistent understanding-to-response gap. Higher-quality scenario analyses improve responses, while weak analyses may reduce response quality. APRiL provides a systematic resource for advancing socially aware language models in Chinese contexts. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/APRiL-05DE/.
evidence_items.title: APRiL: An Open-ended Benchmark for Chinese Social Awareness in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This dataset preserves the accepted R6.5.4.5 controlled paired local HTTP/3 experiment for NGI541. The experiment compares two server-side cryptographic execution paths under the same application protocol, workload objects, network path, and measurement rules. Baseline configuration.NGINX QUIC/HTTP/3 with the standard OpenSSL-based server-side cryptographic path. In the internal experiment labeling, this variant is named stock. Candidate configuration.The same NGINX QUIC/HTTP/3 server, configured so that the supported QUIC AES-GCM packet-protection operations and AES-based QUIC header-protection operations are executed through NGI541. In the internal experiment labeling, this variant is named ngi541-direct. TLS 1.3 handshake processing, certificate validation, and the surrounding QUIC/HTTP/3 protocol logic remain under NGINX/OpenSSL in both variants. The comparison is therefore scoped to a controlled substitution in the server-side cryptographic execution path rather than to a full protocol-stack replacement. The archived material contains the accepted publication bundle, frozen execution provenance, paired result summary, methods, per-condition measurements, integrity information, and supporting visualizations. The scientific workload inputs are deterministic object profiles representing three data-movement styles: CLAS12 event-stream style objects LCLS detector-frame style objects HACC multifile-dataset style objects These are deterministic benchmark object models for controlled experimentation and are not original collaboration datasets.
evidence_items.title: NGI541: Controlled Paired HTTP/3 Cryptographic Execution Benchmark Dataset (R6.5.4.5)

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.
evidence_items.title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation
