evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real-world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain-specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule-reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. To address this gap, this paper introduces RuleTrek, a multi-domain benchmark for agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Its rule-grounded construction pipeline extracts structured rule graphs, generates and incrementally composes rule-specific sub-scenarios while ensuring consistency and solvability. To systematically evaluate agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios, RuleTrek assesses three capabilities in interactive workspaces: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End-to-End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs show that the highest RI and RD scores are only 62.47\% and 60.43\%, respectively, while E2E scores range from 26.97\% to 55.29\%. These results demonstrate that current LLM agents face substantial challenges in rule reasoning over complex scenarios. We make our code and dataset publicly available at https://github.com/yuan247/RuleTrek{RuleTrek}.
evidence_items.title: RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine-learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens and reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
evidence_items.title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Automatic humor detection, the computational task of identifying humorous content, is increasingly critical as Large Language Models (LLMs) integrate into communication platforms such as chatbots and virtual assistants. However, humor poses challenges for AI due to its reliance on context, cultural nuances, linguistic ambiguity, and multimodal cues. Current research is fragmented across humor types, languages, modalities, and evaluation benchmarks, particularly regarding modern LLM capabilities and limitations. This survey synthesizes the automatic humor detection field, tracing its evolution from foundational psychological and linguistic theories through classical machine learning, deep learning, and transformer-based LLMs. We organize and analyze computational methods, feature engineering techniques, benchmark datasets (text-only, multimodal, multilingual), and evaluation metrics. We examine LLM adaptation strategies, including fine-tuning, parameter-efficient methods (PEFT), prompt engineering, and multi-task learning, alongside multimodal and cross-lingual humor understanding developments. Our analysis reveals that while LLMs show improved performance in capturing surface humor patterns, gaps persist in pragmatic reasoning, cultural grounding, multimodal integration, and explainability. We identify open challenges, including data scarcity, evaluation inconsistencies, the humor–offensiveness boundary, and the need for culturally aware and interpretable models. By consolidating progress and pinpointing limitations, this survey guides future interdisciplinary research toward developing socially intelligent AI systems capable of understanding humor.
evidence_items.title: A Survey of Automatic Humor Detection: From Theoretical Foundations to Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Comparing paired signals and trajectories is commonly framed as distance or alignment estimation, whereas controlled diagnostics may require identifying concurrent transformations. We formulate the supervised prediction of 19 applied-transformation labels, which need not all produce observable changes, and evaluate 5 1D and fifteen axis-wise 2D scenario profiles. Each profile uses 12,000 pairs of length-256 sequences per seed across five seeds (42, 142, 242, 342, and 442). A classifier using the full feature set is compared with a classifier using nine established similarity/alignment measures, and four raw-pair deep models are evaluated in two 2D X+Y scenarios. Across the 20 profiles, the unweighted mean Macro-F1 values for full and similarity-only features were, respectively, 0.8193 and 0.5677 on validation, 0.8102 and 0.5589 on test samples from training-represented families, and 0.7381 versus 0.4566 on the specified held-out synthetic families—pulse and trend mix in 1D, and spiral alone in 2D. In 1D, the held-out-family Macro-F1 for full features decreased from 0.9317 for one transformation to 0.6536 for four. ResNet1D had the highest mean held-out-family Macro-F1 among the four evaluated deep models, reaching 0.7779 and 0.4961 in the single-transformation and mixed zero-to-four-transformation X+Y scenarios, respectively, compared with 0.8542 and 0.7026 for full features. A separate subject-disjoint, twelve-label evaluation used injected transformations on observational base trajectories from the 2014 white stork dataset; seed-42 test Macro-F1 scores were 0.7285, 0.7234 and 0.7267 for X-only, Y-only and axis-wise X+Y, respectively, on 255 windows from 17 white storks excluded from training and validation. These controlled labels do not establish natural-label field performance.
evidence_items.title: A Controlled Synthetic Benchmark for Multi-Label Transformation Detection in Signal and Trajectory Pairs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Drilling operations require engineers to make sequential, safety-critical decisions under partial observability, physical constraints, and noisy sensor data, yet most existing machine learning approaches treat drilling intelligence as isolated prediction tasks and fail to capture the multi-stage reasoning process used in practice. We introduce DrillBench, a sequential decision-making benchmark that formalizes drilling operation understanding as a structured multi-stage reasoning problem, constructed from 2,155 validated operational episodes derived from a full geothermal drilling campaign and explicitly modeling hypothesis formation, interactive evidence acquisition, physics-aware assessment, control recommendation, and cross-stage dependency. To address the challenges posed by this benchmark, we propose a DrillBench Agent that integrates physics-informed reasoning with an explicit cross-stage feedback mechanism, enabling revision of incorrect early hypotheses when later evidence contradicts prior beliefs. Extensive experiments across strong Large Language Models (LLMs) show that the proposed agent consistently outperforms single-pass and non-feedback baselines, particularly in ambiguous operational regimes where early errors would otherwise propagate, while targeted ablation studies confirm that sequential dependency, interactivity, physics grounding, and feedback are all critical to robust decision-making. Together, DrillBench and the proposed agent framework provide a principled foundation for evaluating and developing AI systems capable of reliable sequential reasoning in real-world drilling operations.
evidence_items.title: DrillBench: A Sequential Decision-Making Benchmark for Drilling Operations with Cross-Stage Agent Feedback

organizations: Tsinghua University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract While deep learning has significantly advanced image reconstruction of electrical capacitance tomography (ECT), most public datasets retain only capacitance vectors and permittivity distributions and do not expose the excitation-wise electric potential field, a physical intermediate in the forward mapping. To address this, we present an electric-potential-augmented ECT benchmark dataset generated via a COMSOL--MATLAB pipeline for a fixed eight-electrode sensor. The dataset comprises 20,000 randomized samples across four typical flow-pattern families. Alongside conventional capacitance vectors and permittivity images, each sample preserves eight spatially registered full-field potential maps. Governing equations and field-perturbation visualizations characterize the relation between potential and dielectric structure. As an initial use of this physical information, we introduce potential-field intermediate supervision to guide representation learning in simple forward and inverse models. Under sample-disjoint independent and identically distributed (IID) and fully held-out two-bar out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation, potential supervision reduces forward capacitance-prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 56.8\% and 74.6\%, respectively, relative to a structure- and capacity-aligned control. In an exploratory forward experiment, a low-weight partial differential equation (PDE) residual yields 5.3--8.3\% lower mean potential-prediction MSE. For inverse reconstruction, the simple model reduces mean MSE by 14.3\% and 3.0\% on IID and OOD data, respectively, relative to the same control. The more modest inverse gains are consistent with the difficulty of recovering dense potential maps from limited capacitance measurements. These results provide initial controlled evidence for the value of potential-field supervision.
evidence_items.title: An electric-potential-augmented benchmark dataset for electrical capacitance tomography: Electric-potential supervision for future physics-guided learning

organizations: University of Missouri-Columbia

evidence_items.summary: TrialCalibre1 is an agentic system that connects clinical evidence, study design, and executable analyses. It supports reference-trial replication, direct target-trial emulation, and BenchExCal, which combines benchmarking, extension, and cal ibration sensitivity analysis. We evaluated an ASCET-based benchmark and an extension comparing clopidogrel with aspirin among adults aged 81-90 years us ing synthetic PCORnet-style claims. Two reviewers assessed benchmark extrac tion, protocol decisions, and implementation. After discussion, 53/62 and 50/62 assessable SQL checks were rated met; both reviewers rated 12/13 assessable R checks met. Protocol and proxy disagreements remained. A separate ten-question routing development set yielded 10/10 route matches and 7/7 applicable reference trial matches. The agent benchmark and extension included 6,069 and 1,602 pa tients. The extension risk ratio was 0.848 (95% CI 0.569-1.184), with a calibrated sensitivity estimate of 1.274 (0.439-3.700). The human implementation provided descriptive comparisons, not same-data validation. Dose proxies, unpopulated co variates, residual imbalance, implementation deviations, and ignored cross-cohort covariance limited interpretation. This case demonstrates a connected workflow whose protocols, code, and results can be reviewed.
evidence_items.title: TrialCalibre1: An Agentic System for Trial Emulation, Benchmarking, and Calibration

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence marks a shift from static prediction toward systems that perceive, reason, act, verify, and adapt through closed-loop interaction with external environments. Although large multimodal models provide the representational substrate for this shift, practical agency emerges only when model inference is embedded within memory, planning, tool use, environment interfaces, verification, and oversight mechanisms. We formalize the notion of an agentic AI system, distinguish it from single-turn assistants, scripted workflows, retrieval-augmented generation, and classical embodied controllers, and propose a taxonomy covering model substrates, observation spaces, memory, planning, action interfaces, multi-agent coordination, evaluation, and autonomy constraints. We then synthesize learning and optimization paradigms for agents, including supervised trajectory tuning, tool-use adaptation, preference optimization, reinforcement learning, process rewards, verifier-guided search, test-time scaling, memory-driven adaptation, and distillation. Across domains such as web search, software engineering, multimodal reasoning, embodied control, scientific discovery, and enterprise automation, we analyze the factors shaping agent performance and reliability. We further examine benchmarks, evaluation protocols, safety considerations, governance challenges, and open research problems in long-horizon reasoning, memory management, multimodal grounding, and trustworthy deployment. A companion repository tracking developments in agentic AI is available at https://github.com/Tajamul21/awesome-agentic-ai.
evidence_items.title: From Models to Agents: A Closer Look into Agentic AI Systems

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Patients with multiple myeloma accumulate hundreds of clinical documents over years of sequential therapy, and every treatment decision depends on synthesis across that history. Whether large language model–based systems can match expert agreement on this task, and where they fail, has not been established. On longitudinal records of 811 patients treated over 25 years (44,962 documents and 1,334,677 laboratory values), an agentic reasoning system guided by an indexed clinical skill library was compared against single-pass retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), iterative RAG, iterative RAG augmented with the same skill library, and full-context input on 469 expert-adjudicated patient-question pairs, with an exploratory cross-dataset evaluation on MIMIC-IV. The skill-guided agent exceeded the ceiling at which iterative RAG (75.7%) and full-context input (75.8%) converged, reaching 80.1% concordance, with its advantage widening on the most complex tasks (+11.2 percentage points) and longest records. Providing the same skill library to iterative RAG matched the agent in aggregate (79.0%) and on shorter records, whereas the agent retained a significant advantage on the longest records (+10.3 percentage points in the top decile, p = 0.017) and a numerical, non-significant advantage on the most complex questions (+5.4 percentage points). The aggregate error rate (12.2%) was comparable to expert disagreement (13.6%), but a higher proportion of system errors were clinically significant (57.8 versus 18.8%).
evidence_items.title: Skill-guided agentic reasoning enables longitudinal synthesis of myeloma records at expert-level concordance

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for long-horizon research and engineering, yet evaluating these capabilities remains expensive, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on human expertise. This motivates a natural question: can LLM agents themselves construct efficient benchmarks that preserve the conclusions of costly reference evaluations? We study this capability by formulating automatic benchmark development as a meta-evaluation problem, where an agent is given a task and an expensive reference benchmark and requested to construct a lower-cost proxy benchmark that faithfully distinguishes among candidate models and solutions. Based on this formulation, we introduce EvalBuilder, a framework for evaluating such benchmark-generation capabilities along three key dimensions: fidelity, efficiency, and robustness. Specifically, we assess whether generated benchmarks preserve model rankings, generalize to held-out models and freshly collected responses, and provide well-calibrated and discriminative scores while substantially reducing evaluation cost. We further provide an iterative environment in which agents can refine their benchmarks under a fixed time budget. Our framework provides a systematic testbed and benchmark for understanding when current LLM agents can develop useful evaluators and how benchmark construction itself can be increasingly automated.
evidence_items.title: EvalBuilder: Can LLMs Build Efficient Benchmarks?

evidence_items.summary: We introduce SEA-HELM Audio, a Southeast Asian (SEA) multilingual evaluation framework that extends the text-based SEA-HELM benchmark to assess performance degradation in cascaded automatic speech recognition and large language model (ASR-LLM) pipelines. Using synthesized speech, we compare speech-input and text-input performance across five languages (Chinese, English, Malay, Indonesian, and Tamil) on multiple-choice reasoning and instruction-following tasks. We evaluate open-weight and commercial ASR-LLM systems using identical verifiers and quantify the speech gap as the difference between text and speech accuracy. Results show substantial degradation, with accuracy drops of 9.00 to 18.50 percentage points for multiple-choice reasoning and 20.00 to 42.86 points for instruction following. Tamil exhibits the largest degradation, exceeding 40 percentage points. Our findings highlight the limitations of text-only benchmarks in predicting voice-agent reliability and demonstrate the value of SEA-HELM Audio for evaluating multilingual voice-agent systems.
evidence_items.title: SEA-HELM Audio: Evaluating Multilingual ASR-LLM Pipeline Performance Across SEA-HELM Subsets

evidence_items.summary: Large language model agents increasingly improve by distilling experience into reusable skills, but errors in that experience can persist in learned rules and affect later tasks. Existing evaluations largely examine clean learning or perturbations encountered after skills are frozen, leaving robustness during self-evolution insufficiently understood. We introduce RSE-Bench, to our knowledge the first benchmark for evaluating skill self-evolution under ordinary, non-adversarial noise. It spans four domains and six benchmarks, with controlled perturbations to instructions, environmental evidence, execution records, and outcome--record pairings that preserve the underlying tasks and native scoring rules. The protocol separates noise during learning from input-side noise at evaluation, testing frozen skill stores on held-out tasks. We also introduce \textsc{RSEClaw}, a method-agnostic framework supporting consistent noise injection and process diagnostics of actual exposure and skill updates. Across three methods and two backbones, noisy learning retains only $25.5\%$--$42.1\%$ of the aggregate gain achieved by clean self-evolution, depending on the noise type. Perturbations confined to execution records and outcome--record pairings cause average losses comparable to input-side noise, despite leaving the original executions and evaluations intact. Diagnostics further identify differences in candidate skill text that coexist with small changes in mean held-out performance.
evidence_items.title: When Non-Adversarial Noise Hurts Learning: Benchmarking Skill Self-Evolution in Agents

evidence_items.summary: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.
evidence_items.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary:
RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES
Automated semantic classification of radiology reports can enhance clinical workflows and research, but often relies on language- and task-specific models, limiting scalability. This study aims to evaluate and improve the 0-shot baseline performance of open-weight large language models (LLMs) in the semantic classification of free-text magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reports.


MATERIALS AND METHODS
A corpus of 1385 reports from a single neuroradiology center was used to assess four LLMs (GPT-OSS-20B, Magistral-Small-2509, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) of comparable scale (∼20-35B parameters). The brain MRI reports were labeled as Pathological or Non-Pathological, with the Pathological ones further classified into five diagnostic categories (Neoformation, Vascular, Inflammation/Infection, Neurodegenerative, Other). The LLMs were evaluated using zero- and few-shot prompting with majority-vote aggregation. Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) fine-tuning was then applied to the best-performing model across multiple configurations. Performance was assessed using Macro F1, Micro F1, Precision, Recall, and Exact Match Accuracy.


RESULTS
The binary classification task achieved a Macro F1 score of 0.84 on the best-performing Qwen3.5-35B-A3B model, while multilabel classification reached 0.81. Majority voting (MV) outperformed individual-set predictions. QLoRA fine-tuning yielded a Macro F1 score of 0.83 on the multilabel task; the improvement over the 0-shot baseline was statistically supported for Macro F1, Micro F1, Macro Precision, and Exact Match, whose bootstrap 95% confidence intervals excluded zero, but not for Macro Recall. Fine-tuning and few-shot prompting strategies are complementary, with neither consistently outperforming the other. Error analysis showed that the models struggled with borderline annotation cases and often missed secondary labels.


CONCLUSION
Open-weight LLMs demonstrate strong capability for neuroradiology report classification without extensive task-specific training. Fine-tuning further improves performance, supporting integration into scalable semantic radiology data pipelines. However, the present evidence comes from a single Italian center without external validation, and the fine-tuning gain was estimated on a small held-out test set, for which the Macro F1 improvement, though statistically significant, has a confidence interval with a lower bound close to zero. In this light, the approach is best positioned as an internal indexing and semantic-retrieval tool, supporting faster report retrieval, structured cohort identification, internal audit, and scalable phenotyping for neuroradiology research and data warehousing, as well as efficient active-learning strategies, with broader generalizability requiring additional external multicentre validation before clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Open-Weight Large Language Models for Pathological Brain MRI Reports Classification: From Prompts to a Fine-Tuned Model.

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.
evidence_items.title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents

evidence_items.summary: Advances in generative AI have made it possible to produce music that is nearly indistinguishable from human compositions, raising the question of whether such works can be reliably distinguished from human compositions. We present MUSEBENCH, a large-scale benchmark for AI-generated music detection and artifact analysis, comprising over 361K tracks. The dataset includes human compositions, stylistically matched music generated by ten state-of-the-art open-source and commercial models, such as Suno and Udio, as well as human-AI co-creations and variants processed with adversarial perturbations, compression, and acoustic post-processing. Using MUSEBENCH, we benchmark 11 automated detectors and evaluate their accuracy, generalization, and robustness, under default, out-of-domain, and transformed-variant experiment settings. We further conduct a comprehensive artifact analysis through acoustic feature inspection, identifying recurring signatures such as non-idiomatic harmonic progressions, upsampling induced spectral periodicities, and violations of physical performance constraints. Our findings reveal key strengths and vulnerabilities of existing detectors and provide practical insights for building more reliable AI music detection systems.
evidence_items.title: MUSEBENCH: A Benchmark for AI-Generated Music Detection and Artifact Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Reasoning over infinitely long documents is becoming a reality with recurrent memory agents. However, increasing context length exacerbates the trade-off between reasoning performance and inference efficiency. Inspired by Kahneman's account of fast and slow thinking, we propose MemDuet, a dual-process memory framework that learns to coordinate a small language model for fast, parallel evidence selection from raw context chunks (System 1) with a large language model for memory-update verification and memory updates in document order (System 2). We train MemDuet in three stages: supervised fine-tuning of System 1 for evidence selection, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) of System 2 for verification and memory rewriting, and joint optimization of both policies to coordinate selection and updating for long-context reasoning. Experiments on diverse long-context reasoning benchmarks (RULER-HQA, LongBench v2, and 2WikiMultiHopQA) demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off as context length grows. Averaged across evaluation settings on the three datasets, MemDuet achieves an end-to-end inference speedup of 9.74x and an output-token reduction of 73.91% relative to RL-MemAgent.
evidence_items.title: MemDuet: Learning Dual-Process Memory for Long-Context Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Language-model (LM) agents are increasingly evaluated on repository-level software engineering (SWE) benchmarks derived from GitHub issues and pull requests. Although these benchmarks cover a broad range of development tasks, they provide limited insight into a common yet technically distinct challenge: migrating an existing implementation from one operating system (OS) to another while preserving behavior on both. We introduce OS-Bench, an executable benchmark for cross-OS code migration between Linux and Windows. Motivated by case studies showing that cross-platform features are frequently implemented on one OS before support is added for another, OS-Bench identifies migration opportunities by comparing execution coverage collected from the same repository on both systems. Platform-specific regions are then verified, organized into five migration scenarios, and transformed into repository-level tasks with target-platform tests and source-platform regression tests. The resulting benchmark contains 140 validated tasks from 111 repositories across C, C++, C#, Go, and Rust, comprising 91 Windows-to-Linux and 49 Linux-to-Windows migrations. We evaluate six models with SWE-agent, Claude Code, OpenHands, and Win-agent. The best configurations achieve only 26.4% success on Linux-target tasks and 20.4% on Windows-target tasks while preserving correctness across both systems. These results indicate that cross-OS migration is a challenging and underexplored capability, and OS-Bench is a testbed for improving platform-aware SWE agents.
evidence_items.title: OS-Bench: Evaluating SWE Agents on Cross-OS Code Migration

evidence_items.summary: Social psychology has long described how people can be persuaded to interpret a harmful act as moral. Recent research suggests that Large Language Models (LLMs) echo aspects of human psychology, from cognitive biases to social conformity. This raises a question with direct safety implications: can LLMs be moralized to bypass safety guardrails? We answer this question with a multi-agent framework grounded in Moral Foundations Theory (MFT). Given a harmful request that is initially refused, our agents diagnose which moral foundation (MF) the prompt is violating, identify a justifiable foundation under which the same request appears virtuous, rewrite the prompt accordingly, and reinforce it with generated precedents of comparable moral reframing. We evaluate our framework on harmful prompts from three well-known jailbreak datasets across five open-source and proprietary models. Our analysis reveals that models are highly susceptible to moralization, exhibiting high single-trial jailbreak rates with success increasing further under repeated attempts. We also find that safety benchmarks are imbalanced in the MFs they violate, concentrating on foundations toward which models already exhibit biases.
evidence_items.title: Moral Combat: Exploiting Moral Foundations Theory to Jailbreak LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD
evidence_items.title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation

evidence_items.summary: Latent reasoning replaces natural-language chains of thought with compact continuous"soft-token"representations, reducing the number of intermediate tokens that must be decoded autoregressively. We use a small external encoder to induce latent reasoning in a frozen backbone model. The encoder iteratively maps the backbone's hidden states to new latent blocks, constructing a latent reasoning prefix, after which the frozen model writes its remaining reasoning and its answer as text. Our method, INTACT, trains this encoder through distillation to reproduce the effect of written reasoning steps while keeping the model's behavior close to that of the frozen backbone, and then reinforces it on answer correctness. Across four frozen backbones from 1B to 8B, INTACT improves both GSM8K and average out-of-domain accuracy, including GSM8K gains from 75.8% to 79.3% on Llama-3.2-3B and from 77.6% to 79.7% on Qwen2.5-3B. It also reduces end-to-end latency per problem by 19% on Llama-3.2-3B and outperforms the evaluated latent-reasoning baselines at the 3B and 8B scales. Beyond the mathematics setting, the same recipe trained on a multi-domain corpus improves the frozen backbone on twelve evaluation benchmarks spanning mathematics, science, and commonsense, without task-specific adaptation.
evidence_items.title: INTACT: Inducing Latent Reasoning on a Frozen Backbone

evidence_items.summary: In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs. It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.
evidence_items.title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_items.summary: Historical code changes provide convenient task boundaries, but do not identify which production functions selected tests exercise or support composing validated behaviors beyond a single change. We present SWE-Nexus, a fully automated pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks from test execution. Four construction agents select tests, adapt tracing and evaluation protocols to each repository, and generate behavioral specifications. For each selected test file, tracing records an observed execution footprint of production function bodies. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced bodies causes at least one failure or error. Compatible scopes are composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. The benchmark contains 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, including 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks. We evaluate 12 models under three agent scaffolds. The best configuration resolves 37.8% of tasks in one attempt, and scope-weighted scoring measures partial recovery. SWE-Nexus enables task construction from validated behavior beyond individual historical changes.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Nexus: Automated Composition of Software Engineering Tasks from Test Execution

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. Attack-class precision, recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) further provide complementary insights into classifier performance beyond overall accuracy. The results provide an empirical comparison of commonly used classical machine learning models under consistent experimental settings and offer insights into how preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology influence reported performance.
evidence_items.title: Empirical Evaluation of Machine Learning for Cloud Cryptojacking Detection: Effects of Preprocessing and Evaluation Protocols

evidence_items.summary: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.
evidence_items.title: Holi-Spatial 360: Generative Reconstruction from Sparse Panoramas for Spatial Rendering and Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Real-time water quality monitoring is essential for protecting aquatic ecosystems and public health; however, existing intelligent monitoring systems typically address either anomaly detection or Water Quality Index (WQI) prediction independently, limiting their effectiveness for continuous environmental surveillance. This study proposes a unified Artificial Intelligence–Internet of Things (AI-IoT) framework that integrates a Long Short-Term Memory Autoencoder (LSTM-AE) for unsupervised temporal anomaly detection with a Random Forest regressor for WQI prediction within a coordinated decision-support architecture. The novelty of the proposed framework lies in the architectural integration of complementary learning models to simultaneously detect abnormal water quality conditions and estimate WQI in real time, rather than introducing new machine learning algorithms. A synthetic multivariate IoT water quality dataset comprising 10,000 observations was developed to emulate realistic environmental monitoring conditions, including temporal dependencies, sensor noise, drift, seasonal variations, and contamination events. Experimental evaluation demonstrated that the proposed LSTM Autoencoder achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.9763, outperforming Isolation Forest (0.8914) and One-Class SVM (0.8732) for anomaly detection. For WQI prediction, the Random Forest regressor achieved the lowest prediction error with an MSE of 2.3573, surpassing Gradient Boosting (2.6841), Sequence-to-One Recurrent Neural Network (2.9137), and Support Vector Regression (3.1048). These results demonstrate that integrating temporal anomaly detection with ensemble-based regression provides a robust and scalable solution for intelligent water quality monitoring. Although validated using a reproducible synthetic benchmark, the framework establishes a practical foundation for AI-enabled environmental monitoring, with future work focusing on validation using real-world IoT water quality datasets.
evidence_items.title: A unified LSTM autoencoder–random forest AI-IoT framework for real-time water quality monitoring, anomaly detection, and water quality index prediction

evidence_items.summary: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.
evidence_items.title: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research

evidence_items.summary: Datasets The main evaluation uses a real, open dataset. Goodbooks-10k (Zajac, 2017) contains about six million ratings, on a scale of 1 to 5, of the ten thousand most-rated books, with book metadata (title, authors, ISBN) and reader shelf tags; its identifiers and metadata derive from Goodreads. We retrieved the current version on 12 October 2026 from https://github.com/zygmuntz/goodbooks-10k (see also http://fastml.com/goodbooks-10k ). The dataset is distributed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license ( https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ ), and the derived sample released with this paper carries the same license. Because the pipeline targets small libraries, a sample matching the synthetic format was drawn: 50 books and 10 readers. Books were eligible if they were in English and had a valid ISBN-13, a title, authors and at least three subject terms; 7,935 of the 10,000 books qualified. Ten readers were drawn at random (seed 42; the first draw meeting the conditions below used seed 142) from the 27,624 readers with 100 to 400 ratings of eligible books, and the 50 eligible books rated by most of them were kept. A draw was accepted only if every reader had at least 15 ratings in the sample and every book at least two raters. Source fields were mapped to the library schema of Table 1: surrogate accession numbers (ACC plus the source book number) and enrollment numbers (GBU plus the source reader number), titles as catalogued, authors separated by semicolons, ISBN-13, and up to five subject terms. The terms were derived from Goodreads shelf tags: only genre shelves were retained and mapped to canonical terms (for example, sci-fi and science-fiction became science fiction). They therefore form a folksonomy rather than a controlled vocabulary such as the Library of Congress Subject Headings. Two faults in the source files were repaired.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Book Recommendation for Libraries with Sparse Interaction Data: A Reproducible Pipeline Study with Nested Tuning

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Systematic reviews are the gold standard for evidence synthesis, but the manual title and abstract screening of thousands of references creates a severe bottleneck. Existing automated tools have historically struggled to achieve the near-perfect recall (sensitivity) required for reliable reviews. We developed MechaScreener as a ‘zero-shot’ automated screening tool that utilises a large language model to rank article relevance. The tool requires no initial training data or manual pre-screening, as MechaScreener directly applies user-provided question elements (PICO) or inclusion/exclusion criteria to assign an ordinal relevance score (1–5) to each reference. We evaluated the tool in two phases: a development phase using five reference libraries to optimise prompts, and an independent evaluation phase using 10 diverse Cochrane review libraries (comprising both randomised controlled trials [RCTs] and non-RCTs) containing over 58,000 references. In the evaluation dataset, MechaScreener achieved a perfect recall of 1.00 (100%) in all 10 reviews, ensuring that no relevant articles were missed (pooled record-level 95% CI: 0.98–1.00). Concurrently, it achieved an overall macro-average specificity of 0.61 (61%, cluster bootstrap 95% CI: 0.46–0.75; pooled record-level specificity 0.59, 95% CI: 0.59–0.60). Specificity varied from 0.21 in broad public health topics to 0.91 in precise pharmacological interventions, reflecting the tool’s built-in conservatism when evaluating ambiguous abstracts. By safely eliminating over 60% of irrelevant literature during the initial screening phase without compromising recall, MechaScreener functions as a highly reliable but low-effort ‘first-pass’ filter, allowing researchers to substantially reduce manual workloads and reallocate resources towards full-text review and data extraction.
evidence_items.title: MechaScreener: Large language model-based automated screening for systematic reviews and research

evidence_items.summary: Access to safe drinking water remains a global challenge, with approximately 2.1 billion people lacking safely managed water services. Continuous, low-cost monitoring of heavy metal contamination is limited because conventional techniques such as atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) are accurate but require centralized laboratories and high operational costs. Although machine learning has shown promise for water quality prediction, existing models are generally trained on empirical datasets and lack the physical constraints governing sensor behavior. This study addresses this limitation by developing a physics-informed machine learning framework based on a physically consistent synthetic dataset of 300 samples generated from Ohm's law, Kohlrausch's law of molar conductivity, and metal-hydrolysis pH chemistry. The dataset was utilized to predict heavy metal concentration from voltage, current, conductivity, temperature and pH. The Random Forest (RF) and Multi-Layer Perceptron Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models were benchmarked against linear regression using cross-validation of 5-folds and 10-folds. The ANN was optimized with L2 regularization and early stopping. During 5-fold cross-validation, the accuracy of RF was found to have R² of 0.38 ± 0.13 (RMSE = 0.049 ± 0.004 mg/L; MAE = 0.039 ± 0.003 mg/L), while ANN optimization was improved from R² = −0.05 till 0.22. Linear regression produced the best performance (R² = 0.47 ± 0.16), consistent with the predominantly linear physics underlying the dataset. Conductivity was identified as the dominant predictor, accounting for approximately 87% of RF feature importance and remaining robust under simulated sensor noise of up to 10%.
evidence_items.title: Physics Informed Machine Learning for Electrical Sensing and Prediction of Heavy Metal Contamination in Water

evidence_items.summary: Deep research agents are increasingly deployed to retrieve precise information from large corpora, yet multi-hop, long-horizon tasks remain challenging. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a scalable solution, with existing pipelines typically expanding seed tasks to increase their apparent depth and breadth. However, this expansion does not reliably translate into necessary reasoning: newly introduced evidence may be only weakly coupled to the answer, creating a mismatch between intended and empirical difficulty. To address this problem, we introduce GRADS, a graph-guided agentic data synthesis framework with explicit difficulty control. GRADS runs a closed loop of seed selection, evidence expansion, question--answer construction, and verification while maintaining a graph of the evidence and inference dependencies required to derive each answer. At each step, it conditions generation on a relevant subgraph, preserving indispensable inference without accumulating irrelevant context. Experiments across security, software-engineering, and scientific-document domains show that GRADS consistently generates verified tasks with empirically separated difficulty distributions, as measured by independent solvers. Moreover, under matched training budgets, post-training on this data delivers consistent gains at every level: SFT raises the solution-termination rate to over 95% while cutting tool calls and turns by up to 75%, RL trims tool use by up to a further 19.5%, and on our held-out, domain-specific benchmarks, the resulting 4B model matches Sonnet~4 on software engineering and surpasses it on the scientific and security domains.
evidence_items.title: GRADS: Graph-Regulated Agentic Data Synthesis with Controllable Difficulty

evidence_items.summary: Python workflows for geological-boundary estimation from 3D spatial data using linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) classification and orthogonal least-squares regression (LSR). The scripts estimate boundary-plane orientation and position, evaluate model or fitting results, and provide reproducible outputs and 3D visualisation. The SVM workflow estimates a separating plane from points assigned to two adjacent geological domains. It performs linear SVM classification, model evaluation, calculation of the decision-plane orientation, identification of support vectors, point-to-plane distance analysis, and visualisation of the results. The LSR workflow fits a best-fit plane to points interpreted to lie directly on a geological boundary. It calculates point-to-plane residuals and structural orientation, applies a median absolute deviation-based filter to identify potential outliers, and refits the plane using the filtered dataset. The two approaches are intended for complementary geological applications. The SVM workflow constrains a boundary from the spatial distribution of adjacent mapped geological domains, whereas the LSR workflow estimates a plane directly from mapped boundary observations. Both workflows report the resulting plane geometry, including dip and dip direction, and export numerical results and visualisations for further geological interpretation. These scripts were developed to support reproducible geological-boundary analysis from three-dimensional digital outcrop and spatial mapping data.
evidence_items.title: SVM-Based-Geological-Boundary-Estimation-from-3D-DOMs

evidence_items.summary: Abstract: The contemporary biomedical and epidemiological reliance on large-scale observational databases and massive biobanks has fostered an uncritical confidence in statistical power, culminating in a critical vulnerability: asymptotic inflation. While massive sample sizes are assumed to guarantee inferential robustness, applying standard asymptotic estimators (such as Wald-based approximations and Cox proportional hazards models) to inherently sparse, skewed, and rare clinical events may create an unwarranted impression of inferential certainty. In fact, by assuming continuous and symmetric distributions, these asymptotic tools may produce misleadingly precise inference and inadequate confidence-interval coverage, when event counts are sparse, potentially exaggerating the apparent strength of statistical evidence. Consequently, numerous published findings across several clinical disciplines may be sensitive to the inferential framework adopted. To resolve this vulnerability, we contrast asymptotic frameworks with exact distribution-based methods rooted in the Poisson distribution and Garwood's framework. Moving beyond traditional p-value reliance, we introduce a conservative internal stability stress test index which completely decouples from the massive population denominator, thus permitting the evaluation of empirical inferential stability. Synthesizing four distinct clinical case studies, we show how apparent dose-response relationships and highly significant risk differentials may attenuate structural stability when evaluated under Poisson based finite-count constraints. We conclude by suggesting a broader adoption of robustness assessments and exact methods where appropriate for methodological refinement, advocating for distribution auditing, integration of exact confidence intervals, and careful stress testing in observational science.
evidence_items.title: Overcoming Asymptotic Inflation in Massive Healthcare Datasets: The Finite-Count Stress Test Index

evidence_items.summary: his deliverable presents the design, implementation and evaluation of the Reliability Trust Function (TF) within the SAFE-6G cognitive trustworthiness framework. The Reliability TF ensures predictable, stable and user-aligned service behaviour across the edge-cloud continuum, with particular emphasis on QoE-critical applications such as real-time video streaming and immersive media. The work carried out in this deliverable focuses on identifying reliability threats, analysing performance-degradation causes, and developing AI-driven mechanisms for proactive reliability assurance. The Reliability TF leverages a multi-layer monitoring framework that collects telemetry from physical servers, virtualisation layers and application components. This telemetry enables the TF to detect anomalies, anticipate reliability degradation and enforce corrective actions aligned with user-centric trust requirements. A range of Artificial Intelligence (AI)/ Machine Learning (ML) models has been developed and evaluated, including lightweight classifiers, deep neural networks and transformer-based approaches. These models support QoE prediction, multi-layer anomaly detection and out-of-distribution (OOD) attack identification. Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Federated Learning (FL) were initially explored as potential techniques for distributed reliability optimisation; however, analysis of SAFE-6G requirements and experimental findings indicated that these methods are not optimal for low-latency inference and multi-layer telemetry fusion. As a result, the Reliability TF adopts alternative AI approaches that better satisfy the project’s objectives. The scientific work conducted in Task 4.6 has led to six peer-reviewed publications  and the creation of two openly accessible multi-layer datasets , which support proactive scaling, reliability inference and transformer-assisted attack detection.
evidence_items.title: Deliverable D4.7: User-centric Reliability Function

evidence_items.summary: Background As the focus shifts towards Industry 5.0, successful implementation requires an understanding of how workers and teams perceive key ELSA dimensions, such as cybersecurity, privacy, trust, and fairness. Despite the centrality of these factors, there is limited systematic baseline data on how these dimensions interact and support AI adoption. The Horizon Europe SEISMEC project aims to co-design and pilot Industry 5.0 technologies in the workplace. Establishing a baseline for this project is essential for examining the efficacy of the co-design process, and for supporting innovation within SEISMEC.    Research Approach This study aims to determine a baseline for worker perceptions on factors which may impact AI adoption. We have developed a survey, utilising standardised instruments, which is being administered to the organisations participating in SEISMEC. Respondents are asked to answer either with reference to (a) the technologies they currently use in their work, or (b) the SEISMEC technology that will be implemented in the future. The survey includes measures covering cybersecurity and privacy perceptions and practices, trust and understanding, perceived fairness, organisational learning opportunities, and existing co-design practices. It also incorporates items on the SEISMEC CAPS factors which include productivity, collaboration, automation and autonomy, and physical and psychological safety.    Findings Data collection is currently underway. This contribution focuses on the survey design, conceptual rationale, and preliminary findings. The presentation will focus on the baseline measures for the concepts and the CAPS empowerment factors, distinguishing between current and anticipated technologies implemented by the pilot organisations.    Conclusion This work provides a methodological foundation for evaluating Industry 5.0 implementation across diverse pilot contexts.
evidence_items.title: Mapping Baseline Perceptions of Industry 5.0 Technology: A Survey Design for Pilot Organisations

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can keep scientific experiments running for months with little human supervision, but reliable autonomous research also requires scientific judgment. Evaluating scientific judgment is difficult because research decisions are open-ended and depend on project context. We construct Sci$Π$vot, a 248-case benchmark of scientific judgment based on human corrections. The benchmark draws on records from six months of research in which senior researchers ran LLM agents on 26 projects across six scientific fields and repeatedly intervened to correct the agents' research judgments. In each case, an agent chooses between the original LLM plan and the human-corrected alternative, using only the project record available before the correction as context. We compare LLM and human performance and examine the effects of reasoning effort, access to the project record, and reconsideration. At medium reasoning effort with the project record, models systematically prefer the original LLM plan over the human-corrected alternative. Four of five frontier models perform below chance on the selected cases. The highest accuracy in the project condition across the tested models and reasoning effort settings is 63.5%, compared with 73.4% for fresh researchers. At medium effort, every model achieves lower accuracy with the project record than without it, and reconsideration does not consistently improve overall accuracy. Even with a human-corrected alternative available, frontier models struggle with the selected research decisions, while Sci$Π$vot supports systematic evaluation of scientific judgment for LLM agents.
evidence_items.title: Sci$Π$vot: Benchmarking Principal-Investigator Judgment at Pivotal Moments of Scientific AutoResearch Agents

evidence_items.summary: Background Large language models are increasingly used for informal mental health support, yet their safety during escalating suicide-risk conversations may depend on how prior information is presented. Native multi-turn conversations and reconstructed cumulative prompts differ not only in the presence of prior model responses but also in prompt reconstruction, information concentration, message positioning, explicit integration cues, and conversation-state processing. Objective This study compared suicide-risk recognition, direct safety inquiry, response urgency, and timely real-world intervention across isolated current-turn prompts, reconstructed cumulative user-only prompts, and native continuous multi-turn conversations. Methods We conducted a controlled repeated-measures evaluation of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao using 12 standardized five-turn trajectories: 4 direct suicide-risk trajectories, 4 implicit or internally inconsistent risk trajectories, and 4 non-suicidal high-distress controls. Each trajectory was evaluated under three context-presentation formats. The 24 model-trajectory combinations were treated as matched repeated-measures units nested within 8 independent risk-trajectory blocks. Primary contrasts were estimated using exact trajectory-level sign-flip tests and trajectory-block bootstrap confidence intervals. Turn-level outcomes were analyzed using multilevel mixed-effects models. Exploratory condition-by-model heterogeneity was assessed using a trajectory-blocked exact permutation sensitivity analysis, with a trajectory-clustered interaction model used only as a secondary asymptotic check. Results Timely appropriate intervention occurred in 10/24 isolated current-turn observations (41.7%), 21/24 reconstructed cumulative observations (87.5%), and 12/24 native continuous observations (50.0%).
evidence_items.title: Context presentation and native conversation structure in large language model responses to escalating suicide risk: a controlled multimodel evaluation

organizations: Banco de la República
evidence_items.summary: This paper develops and applies a standardized framework for forecasting year-on-year inflation in Colombia using large language models (LLMs). We conduct six sequential experiments in which the information set available to the models is progressively expanded by incorporating historical macroeconomic data, contextual indicators, explicit economic structure, and contemporaneous information retrieved through web search. Each configuration is executed daily and generates 24-month inflation forecasts in real time rather than retrospectively, together with qualitative explanations of the forecasts and, in the more advanced configurations, assessments of the shocks affecting inflation. This real-time design mitigates look-ahead bias and produces genuine forecast vintages. The framework is implemented as a programmatic pipeline in Python that queries the OpenAI and Google APIs, executes predefined experiment-specific prompts, and automatically processes and stores the model responses, while applying forecast validation and revision procedures in the more advanced configurations. The results show that richer information environments produce less monotonic inflation paths that remain above the 3% target over the forecast horizon and are more consistent with the contemporaneous domestic and external shocks affecting inflation. The qualitative analysis also enables the identification of key inflation drivers and the interactions among them. These richer forecast paths are broadly consistent with the pattern observed in survey-based inflation expectations. A formal evaluation of forecast accuracy will be conducted as additional real-time forecast vintages become available.
evidence_items.title: Experimenting with Large Language Models for Inflation Forecasting in Colombia

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference is an increasing component of AI energy demand, while the energy effects of weight quantization depend on workload phase and implementation. We benchmarked four LLM families—Gemma 4 E4B IT, Qwen3.5 4B, Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, and Ministral 3 3B Instruct—across Q4 K M, Q6 K, Q8 0, and BF16 weight representations on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 using llama.cpp/CUDA. Five workloads separated prefill from autoregressive generation, and GPU energy was estimated from NVML telemetry. In PP-512, no statistically significant differences were detected under the employed measurement protocol; in PP-1024, precision affected total energy and mean GPU power. In all generation scenarios, model family, precision, and their interaction significantly affected the primary endpoints. Relative to BF16, Q4 K M reduced dynamic energy per token by 63.6–85.7% and increased generation throughput by 85.2–160.2% across all four model families. Ministral 3 3B Instruct–Q4 K M ranked first in TOPSIS, whereas Nemotron 3 Nano 4B–Q4 K M required less GPU memory. Findings are limited to single-request execution on one RTX 4090/llama.cpp-CUDA stack; output quality was not assessed, and 50 ms NVML sampling limits interpretation of short prefill measurements.
evidence_items.title: Does Lower Precision Always Save Energy? Benchmarking Energy–Performance Trade-Offs in Weight-Quantized Large Language Model Inference on a GPU

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Legal decision makers may remember information without using it to update a legal judgment, and may respond differently to the same recommendation depending on its attributed source. LEAD separates these processes into memory-entry, judgment-incorporation, and authority-deference gates. Methods We reanalyzed three public, de-identified datasets: one jury-deliberation misinformation study and two preregistered judge-versus-artificial-intelligence sentencing studies. We compared gate-specific estimates while retaining study-specific outcomes and raw units. Results In Study 1, pro-prosecution misinformation crossed the memory-entry gate more clearly than the judgment-incorporation gate. In Studies 2 and 3, mitigating case facts produced larger judgment-incorporation effects than authority-source assignment. The authority-source effect was equivalent to zero within a prespecified small-effect bound in Study 2 (source Experiment 1), but remained inconclusive in Study 3 (source Experiment 2). Discussion LEAD identifies which process changed and supports cross-gate magnitude comparisons without treating unlike outcomes as identical. This secondary analysis does not estimate behavior in real courts, but it provides a transparent framework for forensic and legal psychology.
evidence_items.title: Legal Evidence–Authority Dissociation in juror judgment: a multistudy reanalysis of memory contamination and AI advice

evidence_items.summary: Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. HM3D-M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation-assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL. We further contribute two baselines. HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis. Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16--27% SR, while our baselines reach 38--41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes. Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team. Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/
evidence_items.title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation

evidence_items.summary: LLMs have achieved strong performance on chemical prediction benchmarks. However, existing evaluation methods typically provide target entity identity information directly, making it difficult to determine whether model predictions arise from transferable structure-property reasoning capabilities or rely on target-related contextual information or memory retrieval. We propose the Identity-Blinded Reasoning Diagnostic framework to evaluate chemical prediction models when target entity identity information is hidden. In this framework, the target is no longer directly defined by its entity identity, but instead by a known source entity and an explicit structural edit operation. This setting preserves the information required to determine the target while reducing the opportunity for models to access target identity cues. We evaluate this framework across six tasks spanning odor prediction, molecular property prediction, retrosynthesis, and reaction yield prediction. The results show that models generally achieve better prediction performance when source and target entity properties are consistent. Providing explicit source entity labels further strengthens this dependence. Moreover, while keeping the target entity, structural change, and ground-truth label unchanged, replacing only the source entity label causes some model predictions to systematically shift toward the substituted source labels. These results indicate that high benchmark accuracy in chemical prediction tasks does not necessarily imply that LLMs possess reliable structure-property reasoning capabilities. Our diagnostic framework provides a controlled evaluation approach for testing whether models can genuinely update predictions according to entity changes. The framework can be extended to other AI for Science tasks, particularly those where targets can be defined through transformations of known entities.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Benchmark Accuracy: A Diagnostic Test for LLM Chemical Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) constitutes over 90% of oral cancers globally and poses a major health burden, particularly in India due to lifestyle-related risk factors such as tobacco and betel-quid use. The tumor biology of OSCC involves regulatory genes such as anti-apoptotic genes like BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL-1 and tumor suppressor genes like PTEN, TP53, NOTCH1 and FAT1 whose dysregulation influences carcinogenesis and tumor progression. Objectives: To evaluate the immunohistochemical expression of BCL-2 and PTEN in OSCC and correlate their expression with different histological grades. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted over one year, in a tertiary care centre of Bundelkhand region in the Department of Pathology, Maharani Laxmi Bai Medical College, Jhansi. It included 100 histologically confirmed OSCC cases. BCL-2 and PTEN expressions were analyzed on paraffin-embedded tissue sections using the VENTANA BenchMark GX system. BCL-2 was scored using the H-score (0–300) and PTEN with the Immunoreactivity Score (0–12). Tumor grading was done according to the Broder’s histological classification. Statistical correlations were evaluated using the chi-square test (p<0.05 considered significant). Results: BCL-2 expression was strong in 49.1% of well-differentiated cases and weak in 31.6% of moderately differentiated cases (p=0.002). PTEN showed strong expression in 60.6% of well-differentiated cases, but only 5.3% of moderately differentiated tumors (p=0.001). Loss or downregulation of PTEN and loss of BCL-2 were associated with  poor differentiation. Conclusion: BCL-2 and PTEN expressions are significantly associated with OSCC histological grades. Inter-relationship between immunohistochemical expression of BCL-2 and PTEN in different grades of tumor did not show significant correlation  (p value 0.74).
evidence_items.title: Histomorphological Significance of BCL-2 and PTEN Expression in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Cross-Sectional Immunohistochemical Study

evidence_items.summary: Multi-object tracking in sports broadcasts is hard for two reasons: athletes move fast and change direction abruptly, and the camera pans and zooms at the same time. We present ARC-SORT (Adaptive, Robust, Compensated SORT), a tracking-by-detection tracker that trains nothing and runs in real time. Its design rule: the tracker measures its own uncertainty, and that measurement decides how it acts. An Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) Kalman filter gives every track a predictive covariance, and we turn it into a per-track search region: the less reliable the motion prediction, the larger the region in which a detection may match (uncertainty-adaptive Expansion IoU, EIoU). On identical inputs, this continuous coupling is what matters: the same covariance used as a hard Mahalanobis gate hurts at every threshold we swept, and richer covariance summaries add nothing measurable. When two tracks cross, the assignment cost itself reports whether the decision was close. ARC-SORT keeps such pairs under review and applies at most one corrective identity swap once post-crossing appearance evidence shows the first decision was wrong; this adds +1.0 HOTA (higher order tracking accuracy) on both the SportsMOT and DanceTrack test sets at under a millisecond per frame. For players who leave the frame for seconds, motion extrapolation carries no information, so our offline re-identification drops the usual motion gate and links tracklets by appearance alone. ARC-SORT reaches 81.82 HOTA on the SportsMOT test set with the fewest identity switches of the 69 leaderboard entries as of August 2026 and tied-third multi-object tracking accuracy (MOTA, 97.09), and 62.1 HOTA on DanceTrack test with the same association settings. On Deep-EIoU's public detections and embeddings it reaches 80.31 HOTA, +3.1 over Deep-EIoU. It runs at about 50 frames per second on a laptop RTX 3060 GPU. Code will be released.
evidence_items.title: ARC-SORT: Adaptive, Robust, Compensated Multi-Object Tracking with Interacting Multiple Models
