evidence_items.summary: Long-horizon agentic RL is constrained by the futures visited by the current policy. When rollouts fail to reach useful behaviors, improved credit assignment cannot provide supervision for states and actions that were never encountered. On-policy distillation (OPD) introduces teacher guidance on policy-induced states, and recent multi-turn variants improve how this guidance is scheduled, replayed, refined, or validated. However, they do not directly use the oracle-controlled future itself as the training trajectory. We introduce State-Rooted Executable Rollout Optimization (SERO), which augments on-policy agentic RL with executable oracle continuations. SERO restores a state actually reached by the current policy and lets a training-only oracle continue interacting with the real environment, making the downstream observations and oracle actions themselves available for learning. It then applies policy-reachability weighting, which weights each oracle step by the frozen behavior policy's compatibility with the preceding oracle actions. This allows deeper supervision to become effective as the policy becomes more compatible with the oracle branch. The oracle loss is optimized separately from the base RL estimator and no oracle is used at inference time. We evaluate SERO on two challenging interactive-agent benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. On ALFWorld, learning the full executable continuation is substantially more effective than supervising only the root oracle action, while policy-reachability weighting further improves out-of-distribution performance.
evidence_items.title: SERO: Learning from Executable Oracle Continuations for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: We present CommerceGen-Studio, an end-to-end framework for generating commercial-grade main images for e-commerce Stock Keeping Units (SKUs). Our framework is organized along a three-stage pipeline of information extraction, semantic rewriting, and multi-condition generation: Prompt-Eval-Refine-Loop Agent (PERL-Agent) distills heterogeneous SKU metadata into concise selling-point text lists through an iterative closed loop of VLM and LLM roles scored by a reference-free rubric. Layout Thinker Optimization (LTO) aligns the rewriter with both caption and rendered-image quality via alternating domain-specific policy optimization. SKU-DiT, trained under Reinforce-Distill-Reinforce (RDR) progressive training, conditions jointly on the white-background product image, the trademark crop, and the structured layout to hold subject fidelity, trademark integrity, and character-level text accuracy together. The framework runs in production at a scale of millions of main images per day with a latency of a few seconds per image, which we believe makes it among the first systems of this kind to operate at commercial scale. We also release CommerceGen-Bench, a benchmark of hard cases collected from live traffic across all product categories. On it, our framework achieves the highest overall scores among the evaluated open-source baselines on both editing tracks, with and without prompt enhancement. It also matches much larger closed-source models, and beats several of them at Instruction Following and Product Integration - the two properties that determine whether an image can be published.
evidence_items.title: CommerceGen-Studio: An End-to-End Framework for Commercial-Grade Main-Image Generation

evidence_items.summary: Video generators serve as interactive worlds for exploration and simulation, yet realistic and visually appealing frames do not necessarily depict a consistent 3D world. Existing benchmarks assess selected geometric properties or use vision-language models to judge memory and consistency, leaving systematic 3D evaluation underexplored. We introduce Orbia, the first benchmark dedicated to a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of 3D consistency in interactive world models. Through controlled exploration and revisit, we organize the evaluation into three dimensions: input preservation, generated-content persistence, and 3D self-consistency. For input preservation, registered RGB-D references and annotated anchors support appearance, geometry, and spatial stability measurements. For generated-content persistence, we compare revisits to regions absent from the input image with their first generated observations to test whether models preserve what they create. For 3D self-consistency, cross-view depth and feature correspondence, regional scale agreement, and held-out Gaussian rendering test whether generated views describe the same 3D scene. Minute-long exploration and revisits further test long-term consistency. Our construction and annotation pipeline brings together public datasets, self-captured scenes, and simulation, yielding 720 instances across indoor and outdoor environments and six exploration-and-revisit protocols. Evaluation spans 27 text-, action-, and camera-conditioned models through native-interface adapters. Our Orbia benchmark provides a systematic basis for diagnosing 3D inconsistency and developing more persistent video world models.
evidence_items.title: Orbia: Do Generated Videos Form a Consistent 3D World?

evidence_items.summary: Cowork agents navigate dependencies across tools and files while adapting to changing user requirements and edits to shared workspaces. Scaling such environments requires maintaining consistency among task objectives, executable resources, user behavior, and success criteria. We introduce Cowork-Gym, a framework that synthesizes Cowork environments through a build-execute-revise loop that uses execution evidence and review feedback to validate and repair generated environments. To capture realistic Cowork dynamics, a stateful user simulator responds to the agent's actions through dialogue and direct edits to the shared workspace. We synthesize 64.9K environments across 14 application scenarios and use them to post-train 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B Qwen models with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation. Averaged across six agentic benchmarks, these models outperform their corresponding base checkpoints by 8.7, 6.4, and 4.1 points, respectively. Ours-27B ranks second overall among the evaluated models and achieves the highest average scores on PawBench and ClawEval, outperforming models with over 100B total parameters on both benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Cowork-Gym: Synthesizing Interactive Work Environments at Scale

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.
evidence_items.title: CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline

evidence_items.summary: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number of seed runs N compared to traditional benchmarking setups. Evaluating across 5 games and 10 LLMs, we show a model's strategic competence varies significantly depending on the game setup and the opponent faced. Building on this, we implement a suite of selector methods and find that approaches that rely on query embeddings or LLM self-reflection do not consistently capture the underlying strategic signal. A lightweight multi-armed bandit algorithm performs more reliably across games, though it still falls short of the best fixed model. Finally, we show that simple non-stationary and adversarial bandit variants fail to outperform a stationary bandit baseline, pointing to a gap in how current methods handle a shifting opponent in strategic settings.
evidence_items.title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions

evidence_items.summary: We study environment scaling as a way to increase agent-benchmark difficulty while holding core task objectives fixed. Our framework, Recursive Environment Scaling (RES), transforms existing benchmark environments while preserving their objectives and completion requirements. A proposer changes information access, resource relations, and execution dependencies; execution-grounded checks validate the resulting candidate, and accepted changes are inherited across rounds. This produces related environments for paired evaluation and training-trajectory collection. Experiments on 294 initial tasks from three benchmarks show lower task success for all six evaluation models, with decreases of 57.14--77.14 percentage points on Claw-Eval-Live. With equal trajectory counts and identical optimization settings, fine-tuning on RES trajectories outperforms original-trajectory SFT in all nine model--benchmark comparisons by 7.00--14.61 percentage points. Ablations identify recursive inheritance and dependency composition as important contributors to increased difficulty. Together, these results support environment scaling for both agent evaluation and training.
evidence_items.title: Recursive Environment Scaling for General Long-Horizon Agents

evidence_items.summary: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.
evidence_items.title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Professional agents increasingly work through command-line interfaces and multiple tools over shared workspaces containing files, messages, and business applications. These environments create safety risks that are difficult to capture with attacks placed at a single, known read location. We introduce APEX-Harm, a benchmark for evaluating prompt and script injection against long-horizon agents performing finance, consulting, and legal tasks in large workspaces. Each task contains 115 to 328 files, together with email, calendar, chat, document, spreadsheet, PDF, and code-execution tools exposed through MCP servers. The benchmark includes six attack categories covering static and dynamic injections, task-specific script replacement, and attacker-provided generic scripts, and evaluates attack success, exposure, and task performance. We evaluate 12 frontier models on 180 task instances per model. Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 have the lowest overall attack success rates (8% and 20%), while task-specific script replacement and attacker-provided generic script attacks remain substantially more effective, averaging 81-84% and 73% attack success, respectively. Gemini 3.8 Flash achieves the highest mean task score (0.877) while still exhibiting a 33% attack success rate. These results show that completing the requested task is not sufficient evidence of safe behavior: an agent can produce a correct deliverable while also performing an unauthorized action in the workspace.
evidence_items.title: APEX-Harm: Evaluating Agent Safety in Shared Professional Workspaces

evidence_items.summary: Open-source web agents are now strong enough to execute realistic browser tasks, but training them with reinforcement learning still depends on weak supervision: binary task success is too sparse for credit assignment, while frontier-language-model judges are too expensive to call at every step and cannot be assumed available at deployment. We introduce CLIFT, a training and test-time scaling method built around conformal self-verification. During training, the agent answers natural-language verification questions about its own rollouts; a Compositional Conformal Certifier keeps only question signals whose URL-conditional evidence agrees with a training-time judge, assigns signed trust weights through polarity-aware lift, and blends the resulting verifier score into per-step rewards in a way that never subtracts from the judge baseline. At test time, the same certified bank is frozen and reused as structured evidence for Conformal Trajectory Selection (CTS): the agent samples a greedy rollout and one or more diverse retries, the self-verifier summarises each URL trace, and a conservative majority-vote rule chooses whether to swap away from the current incumbent without calling any external judge. This single mechanism supports three settings. On WebArena Infinity, CLIFT achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source web agents. On VisualWebArena, a bank trained with the open model transfers to GPT-5.5 at test time and reaches state-of-the-art performance under the canonical harness. On Online Mind2Web, without training an agent on the benchmark, translating the certified question bank improves a live-web agent in zero-shot evaluation. Together these results position conformal self-verification as a way to turn costly judge feedback into a reusable training signal and a judge-free test-time scaling signal.
evidence_items.title: CLIFT: Conformal Self-Verification for Web Agent Training and Test-Time Scaling

The equilibrated trajectory file (17 DPPE 349K 100to200ns.xtc) covers the last 100 ns of the 200-ns trajectory, with coordinates saved every 15 ps.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Sanskrit morphology provides a setting for comparing explicit suffix rules and language-model predictions under changes in word order. This exploratory study evaluates a Python suffix classifier and supplied Gemini prediction files for 100 Bhagavad Gita entries representing 98 distinct verse identifiers. The corpus contains 614 split-token occurrences and 280 selective reference annotations. Natural and scrambled inputs preserve the same token multisets. A scoring audit identified repeated matching and unconditional credit for ambiguous outputs in the original symbolic evaluator. Using one-to-one annotation matching and candidate-set membership, the unchanged symbolic classifier achieved compatibility on 228/280 annotations (81.43%) in each order. The supplied natural and scrambled Gemini CSVs each achieved 242/280 compatible predictions (86.43%), after resolving one scrambled-token transcription mismatch by its input position. Only two of 614 paired Gemini classifications changed; neither affected the annotated score. The comparison shows no decrease in compatibility under scrambling and documents stable compatibility in this recorded comparison, alongside limitations from selective annotations, candidate ambiguity, and incomplete model metadata. The results describe robustness of these outputs under the supplied permutations rather than general word-order invariance or full morphological parsing accuracy.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Analysis of Rule Based Symbolic Logic and a Large Language Model in Sanskrit Morphological Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate plausible responses without using the relevant evidence or meeting task constraints. We separate the Modality Gap in cross-modal correspondence and evidence use from the Intent Gap in behavior relative to specified constraints, goals, and human expectations. Six dimensions organize the review: architecture, objective functions, data construction, training, evaluation, and applications. The first four control evidence access, optimization targets, supervision, and updates. Comparing mechanisms and supervision assumptions shows what interface compatibility, target imitation, preference learning, and verifiable rewards can each demonstrate about alignment. Evaluation at the representation, task, and behavior levels tests these choices through controlled input changes and reward-model validation, and we interpret each gain together with its model, task, and evaluation setup instead of comparing scores across conditions. Studies in robotics, safety, healthcare, recommendation, and climate decision support share three requirements: traceable evidence, valid supervision, and constraint-sensitive decisions. Stronger representations or higher benchmark scores can leave the claimed alignment mechanism unresolved, which motivates four research directions: evidence-consistent alignment across modalities, verified self-correction and test-time alignment, targeted repair from failure diagnosis, and reliable transfer to underrepresented settings.
evidence_items.title: Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Survey

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Hip osteoarthritis (OA) is a highly prevalent musculoskeletal disorder associated with substantial functional impairment and healthcare burden. Although evidence-based clinical practice guidelines exist, including the 2021 guideline of the German Society for Orthopaedics and Trauma Surgery (DGOU), their implementation in routine practice remains incomplete. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly consulted for guideline-related information, but the concordance of their answers with guideline recommendations is uncertain. This benchmark study evaluated the guideline concordance, comprehensiveness and length of answers generated by five widely used LLMs to questions derived from the 2021 German S3 guideline on evidence- and consensus-based indication criteria for total hip arthroplasty in hip OA (EKIT-Hip; AWMF register no. 187-001; lead society DGOU). It did not evaluate the effectiveness or safety of clinical decision support. Methods: In a cross-sectional, single-run benchmark study, 26 structured, context-free questions covering five of the six thematic complexes of the guideline (diagnosis and imaging; assessment of the level of suffering; evaluation of alternative therapeutic options; contraindications; optimisation of modifiable risk factors) were derived from the guideline recommendations and submitted between 9 November 2024 and 25 February 2025 through the consumer web interfaces of five LLM-based systems (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Gemini Advanced and Consensus Premium), yielding 130 responses (one per system–question pair, each in a newly initiated chat session). Responses were evaluated by three board-certified orthopaedic surgeons blinded to model identity, using a four-point accuracy scale and a five-point comprehensiveness scale. Only a single consensus score per response was recorded, so inter-rater reliability could not be assessed.
evidence_items.title: Guideline-Concordant Answer Quality of Five Large Language Models on Indication Criteria for Total Hip Arthroplasty in Hip Osteoarthritis: A Single-Run Benchmark Against the 2021 German S3 Guideline (EKIT-Hip)

evidence_items.summary: The integration of natural language understanding into conversational commerce requires robustly extracting structured intents from idiomatic text. While cloud-based models are highly capable, their latency, privacy risks, and operational costs necessitate efficient local alternatives. To address this, we empirically evaluate locally deployed, open-weights Large Language Models (LLMs) on parsing multi-intent shopping cart commands into deterministic JSON schemas. We benchmark multiple models across minimal, extended, and few-shot prompting paradigms, utilizing a dual-axis framework to simultaneously measure extraction quality (operation F1-score, exact match, schema validity) and hardware performance (latency, GPU power consumption). Our evaluation highlights a fundamental trade-off between schema compliance and computational overhead, demonstrating how advanced prompting techniques improve parsing accuracy while measurably impacting inference latency and power draw. Ultimately, this comprehensive profiling identifies optimal model configurations for resource-constrained environments: a well-chosen 3-8B parameter model (specifically Granite4 3B) paired with few-shot prompting recovers over 95% of the quality of the largest evaluated model at a coarse indicative estimate of 40× lower operational energy per command, establishing a practical baseline for deploying cost-effective LLMs as efficiency candidates in resource-constrained environments.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Local Large Language Models for Structured Knowledge Extraction in Conversational Commerce

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising backbone for time-series forecasting, yet most existing LLM-based forecasters are still optimized with purely supervised objectives such as MSE or MAE. Such point-wise training is often misaligned with the sequence-level properties that matter in real deployments, including waveform fidelity, trend consistency, and robustness under distribution shift. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a natural candidate for sequence-level optimization, but directly transplanting RL recipes from natural language processing to time series is difficult because forecasting involves continuous outputs, long-horizon credit assignment, multi-objective rewards, and unstable policy updates. To address these issues, we propose TSLLM-BO , a two-stage framework that first learns a strong supervised forecaster and then performs structure-aware behavioral alignment through reinforcement learning. The framework combines three key ideas: 1) a time--text alignment architecture that links temporal patches with semantic prompts in a frozen LLM backbone; 2) a differentiable composite reward that jointly optimizes point accuracy, waveform consistency, and trend alignment; and 3) Dynamic Policy Clipping (DPC) , which adapts the PPO trust region over training to stabilize long-horizon optimization. Extensive experiments on standard long-horizon forecasting benchmarks show that TSLLM-BO consistently outperforms strong LLM-based and deep forecasting baselines, especially under long prediction horizons, cross-dataset transfer, and noise/missingness perturbations. These results suggest that behavioral alignment, rather than supervised fitting alone, is a practical route for endowing LLM-based forecasters with stronger temporal structure awareness and deployment robustness.
evidence_items.title: Structure-Aware Behavioral Alignment of Large Language Models for Robust Time Series Forecasting

evidence_items.summary: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational settings creates pedagogical opportunities while raising environmental concerns regarding data center energy consumption and physical infrastructure footprint. This systematic review synthesizes scientific evidence on the algorithmic carbon footprint of AI tools implemented in environmental education programs. Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement and an adapted PICoS framework (Population: educational stakeholders; Phenomenon of interest: AI carbon/energy auditing; Context: environmental/sustainability education; Study design: empirical and theoretical studies), systematic searches were conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ERIC up to 6 August 2026. Seven studies met the eligibility criteria: 5 empirical, 1 scoping review, and 1 theoretical-conceptual synthesis. Quality appraisal utilized MMAT (2018 version) for primary empirical studies and an adapted SANRA (2019 version) for non-empirical documents, followed by qualitative narrative synthesis. Results indicate that, within the reviewed corpus (n = 7), studies predominantly examine conversational agents and large language models (LLMs) applied to sustainability education, while highlighting a critical measurement gap regarding the empirical auditing of energy consumption and physical infrastructure during model training and inference. Conceptual frameworks synthesized across non-empirical literature hypothesize a potential misalignment between educational content promoting planetary conservation and the environmental opacity of underlying technological deployments. Key limitations include inferential fragility due to a small, methodologically heterogeneous evidence base restricted to higher education settings.
evidence_items.title: Evaluation of Algorithmic Carbon Footprint and Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in Environmental Education Programs: Systematic Review

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, is reshaping cardiovascular imaging and electrocardiography (ECG) by enabling automated acquisition support, quantification, disease detection, and risk prediction. Yet, high retrospective accuracy does not by itself establish transportability or clinical benefit. This narrative review first outlines the AI development lifecycle, with emphasis on data and label quality, architecture selection, patient-level data partitioning, calibration, external validation, and prospective evaluation. It then critically examines representative advances in ECG, echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), cardiac computed tomography (CT), and nuclear cardiology. Particular attention is given to three rapidly evolving areas: AI-enhanced ECG, video- and vision-language echocardiography, and volumetric CT and CMR analysis. We compare convolutional, transformer-based, hybrid, and generative approaches; summarize explainable-AI methods, including gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), integrated gradients, and occlusion testing; and analyze failure modes arising from label, sampling, demographic, device, and temporal bias. Quantitative examples show that performance can deteriorate across institutions, demographic groups, and acquisition settings despite apparently strong internal validation. Future progress will depend on prospective workflow-based trials, multimodal foundation models with transparent benchmarks, lifecycle governance and regulation, and continuous post-deployment surveillance.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in cardiovascular imaging and electrocardiography

evidence_items.summary: As digital self-triage becomes more widely used, quality assurance requires evaluation of both emergency recognition and overall agreement with clinical judgement, including how these outcomes differ across generations of large language models. The Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST) project intends to provide a framework to compare systems for digital self-triage against a medical 'gold standard' in Germany. In a first step developing the method and demonstrating its potential we developed a representative set of patient vignettes and compared two regulated medical-device triage systems, SmED and Infermedica, with five structured OpenAI configurations spanning multiple model generations: gpt-4.1, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol, and gpt-6-astra. An LLM-based patient actor covered 480 physician-curated vignettes derived from German routine triage data. A pool of seven physicians provided preliminary reference classifications and consensus for 480 vignettes. Recommendations were mapped to three urgency categories 'emergency', 'acute', and 'not urgent' and evaluated using winsorised weights derived from routine triage frequencies. Weighted emergency sensitivity ranged from 51.3% (95% CI 35.5-66.3%) for gpt-4.1 to 99.9% (99.7-100.0%) for gpt-6-astra. Weighted exact three-category agreement (accuracy) ranged from 54.4% to 68.8%; gpt-4.1 achieved the highest agreement despite the lowest emergency sensitivity. No system performed best across all urgency categories. The later-generation OpenAI configurations showed a more precautionary triage profile resembling SmED, with higher sensitivity for emergency cases; gpt-6-astra showed the strongest shift. This cross-sectional comparison across model generations suggests a shift towards more precautionary triage behaviour, without establishing a longitudinal improvement in accuracy. These findings highlight the limitations of overall agreement for evaluating self-triage and support category-specific assessment.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark Self-Triage (BeST): Comparing Self-Triage Systems and Multiple Generations of OpenAI Models Against Preliminary Expert Consensus

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The integration of AI into fact-checking has significantly enhanced the speed and scale of misinformation detection across digital platforms. AI-driven fact-checking systems can now access information in real-time, leveraging machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. However, the same AI systems that enhance speed and scalability in verification also introduce new ethical and technical concerns. Biases embedded in training data, opaque algorithmic decision-making, and inconsistencies in human oversight can undermine fairness, accuracy, and accountability. Without robust safeguards, AI fact-checking may unintentionally propagate misinformation, exacerbate societal biases, and erode public trust in automated verification. This chapter examines the epistemic challenges AI fact-checking faces, namely bias, fairness, and accountability, against the backdrop of accelerating misinformation. It traces the evolution of verification technologies, evaluates the risks of static governance models, and proposes adaptive, participatory epistemic infrastructures as essential to sustaining public trust. It calls for a shift from technical optimization toward democratic and ethically anchored verification ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Fact-Checking
Real-world evaluation of a multilingual agentic retrieval-augmented clinical AI framework for evidence-grounded medical decision support

evidence_items.summary: LLMs are increasingly being embedded into a variety of distributed agentic systems, in the form of agents with APIs, microservices, workflows, and external tools for task completion. Systems need to be able to handle requests that are worded differently but mean the same thing, to make sure routing is consistent, caching can be reused, latency is reduced, reliability is ensured, and governance is supported. Conventional intent representations, beyond simply conveying what users want with their intent and respective slots, do not encode information about user authorization, policies with implications for execution, side effects of actions, locality of execution, and operational implications of intents. Prior work has provided frameworks for normalization, capability discovery and routing in distributed agentic systems, but all this work is done independently and thus does not provide a unified pipeline for handling requests in distributed systems. The main contribution of this paper is to propose a unified framework describing the normalization, discovery, routing, execution control and runtime feedback in distributed agentic systems. The core of this work is the introduction of a canonical representation of intent, called an intent record, which can convey all kinds of semantic information, as well as context, policy, and operational information about the system as a whole, including its uncertainty, to be used by the system’s routing layer. We also introduce a new constraint-first multi-criteria routing process. A reference architecture is also given for such sorts of systems. The architecture’s main functional components are semantic control and its decoupled, cross-governance-deterministic execution. An evaluation framework for the proposed approach in the future is also presented. This framework is not validated through implementation or benchmarking experiments. Such an empirical evaluation is left for future work.
evidence_items.title: AI-Based Intent Normalization and Service Routing in Distributed Agentic Microservices

organizations: University of East London
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models and agentic artificial intelligence provide the reasoning layer of autonomous aerial and ground robots, but the architectures remain fragmented across the two communities. This systematic review, reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 statement, searched ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, ProQuest, EBSCO, and Google Scholar from January 2020 through April 2026. Of 5298 records, 2228 remained after duplicates were removed and 124 studies were included: 67 aerial, 41 ground, and 16 on both platforms or a generic architecture. Six patterns appear, from a language model used only as a task-specific tool to an end-to-end foundation model, such as vision-language-action models. Open-loop pipelines, closed-loop pipelines, hierarchical executives, and multi-agent systems lie between those extremes. The model carries semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and tool orchestration, while classical planners and controllers retain trajectories, safety, and real-time control. Memory appears in 62 of 124 studies (50%) and function calling in 37 (30%), yet only 13 (10%) run the model onboard and 44 (35%) validate a physical robot. Aerial systems emphasize long-range vision and mission planning; ground systems emphasize local perception and interaction; both follow the same hybrid pattern. A suitability matrix shows that specialized vision models remain preferable for geometric perception. Designers should match the pattern to the task dynamics and choose the model for latency, safety, and where inference runs, rather than for benchmark score alone. Hallucination, spatial reasoning, inference latency, and the lack of standardized evaluation still limit deployment.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models and Agentic AI Architectures for Aerial and Ground Robots: A Systematic Review, Taxonomy, and Design Guidelines

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Undetected calibration drift in autonomous ocean sensors corrupts temperature and salinity records underpinning climate reanalysis, seasonal forecasting, and marine ecosystem assessments. With 15–20% of active Argo floats showing meaningful drift at any time and correction workflows taking three to six months, scalable autonomous quality control is urgently needed. Methods We present DriftGuard, a five-component autonomous framework integrating a physically-informed heterogeneous sensor graph over 135 nodes, a Hybrid Temporal Transformer and Graph Attention Network (HybridTGAT), a cross-sensor consistency loss, a conformal prediction wrapper, and a LangGraph-orchestrated three-stage agentic loop supported by a 2,183-chunk RAG store. Results Evaluated on Argo float profiles (116 floats, North Atlantic, 2021–2024), NDBC buoy time series (15 stations, 2019–2024), and the expert-labelled AdapAD benchmark, DriftGuard achieves a GAT-level ROC-AUC of 0.8376, an AdapAD zero-shot AUC of 0.8423, and detects gradual drift types an average of 84.7 readings earlier than the operational Argo QC Test 16 baseline. Operational fleet evaluation across 131 sensors identifies 13 floats in a CRITICAL state requiring correction within 24 hours. Discussion DriftGuard is the first system in the marine sensor domain to unify graph-based spatial reasoning, temporal modelling, autonomous LLM-driven correction, conformal uncertainty certificates, and closed-loop retraining within a single operational pipeline, demonstrating readiness for real-world deployment.
evidence_items.title: DriftGuard: an agentic hybrid temporal transformer and graph attention network framework for autonomous calibration drift detection and correction in distributed marine sensor networks

evidence_items.summary: Reliable use of large language models requires responses to satisfy formatting requirements across changing instructions. Standard compliance scores do not distinguish preserving a model's observed format from correcting it, or reveal whether that correction holds across variants. We introduce ReFormBench, a benchmark that uses each model's unconstrained response to the same question as its formatting baseline. It links targets by feature and require/forbid mode, evaluating their instantiated requirements across variants. ReFormBench comprises 5,000 difficulty-screened three-constraint test instances derived from 910 source questions and covering 66 formatting features. TCPR measures complete instruction compliance, while EMCR measures individual and joint correction of targets opposed to the annotated baseline state. Across ten models, EMCR ranges from 34.04% to 64.72%, and the highest three-target correction estimate is 50.02%. Compliance and correction scores yield different model rankings and task-level profiles. A prompting experiment on Qwen3.5-9B improves both metrics, and the catalog covers over 95% of extracted instances on four additional models. ReFormBench makes response-conditioned correction across instruction variants a measurable dimension of format following. The code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ReFormBench/.
evidence_items.title: ReFormBench: Benchmarking the Stability of Response-Conditioned Format Correction in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Korean neologisms arise through diverse mechanisms, a demanding test of language models beyond lexical memorization. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce NeoTrace, an automated, rerunnable framework that collects and dates neologisms across genres. Its 4,271 entries support KoAGE, a cutoff-aware benchmark with three acquisition and two generation tasks---the latter, to our knowledge, the first to compare model coinages with attested neologisms under their original materials and community context. Across 21 models, lexical recall diverges from contextual inference: in a five-model temporal analysis, models define only 13-30% of cutoff-year words, yet can infer meaning from one usage. However, structural understanding remains limited: even correct definitions barely improve formation analysis of pre-cutoff neologisms. Given word-building materials, single models often follow human formation mechanisms, whereas multi-agent coinage favors abbreviation and depends on interaction framing. KoAGE thus separates what models know, learn from use, and coin.
evidence_items.title: KoAGE: Do Large Language Models Know, Learn, and Coin Korean Neologisms?

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly help users arrange appointments, plan journeys, and allocate limited resources. These tasks require models to satisfy constraints on time, cost, capacity, and order, or determine that no feasible solution exists. Bangla is the world's seventh most widely spoken language, and existing benchmarks cover many language and reasoning tasks. However, benchmarks for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla under explicit constraints remain lacking. We introduce BANGLAPLAN, a benchmark of 1,000 problems across ten task families grounded in everyday life and institutions in Bangladesh. It includes feasible and infeasible problems in four language registers: everyday, formal, colloquial, and Bangla--English mixed. Answers cover eight structured types, including schedules, routes, allocations, and ordered steps, in a common JSON format. We construct the benchmark through language-model-assisted drafting and independent human validation. We evaluate 11 open-weight and proprietary model configurations using exact match, separately reporting feasible-case accuracy, infeasibility detection, and format errors. We find a large performance gap: GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 98.7% accuracy and Qwen3.5-27B with thinking reaches 80.3%, while direct-answer configurations score at most 30.9%. Seven of eleven configurations perform below the always-``infeasible''baseline. Our findings also suggest that harder problems primarily reduce plan-construction accuracy, while infeasibility detection remains more robust. BANGLAPLAN provides a reproducible basis for evaluating planning and decision-making in Bangla. BANGLAPLAN is available at: https://github.com/mrayhanulmasud/banglaplan.
evidence_items.title: BANGLAPLAN: A Benchmark for Constraint-Based Planning and Decision-Making in Bangla

evidence_items.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
evidence_items.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving

evidence_items.summary: Understanding the social intelligence of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly important for applications involving human-AI interaction and multi-agent environments. Social intelligence comprises two aspects: cognitive intelligence, the ability to infer others'mental states, and behavioral intelligence, the ability to select appropriate social actions based on these inferences to achieve social goals. Persuasion provides a natural testbed in which both aspects are simultaneously at play, yet prior benchmarks typically evaluate them in isolation using synthetic scenarios. We introduce PerSo, a benchmark that evaluates both aspects on real-world persuasion dialogues from Reddit's ChangeMyView community, using an LLM-in-the-loop pipeline to construct the evaluation tasks, validated through human annotation. Our evaluation of diverse LLMs shows that performance generally scales with model size but varies across dimensions. The strongest LLM slightly surpasses the best observed human performance on the behavioral task, while the best human participant remains ahead on the cognitive task.
evidence_items.title: PerSo: Investigating Facets of LLMs'Social Intelligence in Real-World Persuasion Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fr\"ohlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.
evidence_items.title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations

evidence_items.summary: Cultural attitudes and social norms evolve over time, yet most cultural benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) treat culture as a static attribute of a country or region. We introduce ChronoCulture, a benchmark of 10,360 temporal pairs built from longitudinal survey data across 72 countries. Each pair contains the same survey question asked in the same country in an older and a newer year, with full population response distributions as ground truth. Across six LLMs, we find that models can often predict a country's attitudes at one point in time but do not reliably capture how those attitudes change. Their predictions for different years tend to stay close together, failing to capture much of the observed change. Specifying the intended year in the prompt also offers little overall improvement in alignment with survey responses. These findings suggest that models often present a largely static picture of cultural attitudes, highlighting the need to evaluate cultural awareness across time.
evidence_items.title: ChronoCulture: Evaluating Cultural Awareness Across Time in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.
evidence_items.title: LED-BENCH: A Benchmark for Large-format Engineering Drawing Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users'beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.
evidence_items.title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Hate speech has become increasingly prevalent on social media, raising concerns about its detection, interpretation, and moderation. Persian, a relatively low-resource language, lacks sufficient annotated data and computational resources for fine-grained hate speech analysis. In this study, we introduce a fine-grained, multi-hop benchmark for explainable Persian hate speech analysis, covering content triage, target identification, hate tactic and moral foundation analysis, textual evidence extraction, harmful narrative inference, and severity assessment. By evaluating state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), we find that performance generally declines as tasks require more fine-grained semantic and inferential reasoning. Proprietary models generally outperform open-weight models, while reasoning-oriented models show no consistent advantage. Incorporating intermediate reasoning steps substantially improves severity prediction compared with one-shot assessment. Our analysis further reveals that Incitement to Violence or Harm is most strongly associated with higher severity, while political-affiliation targets are particularly associated with subversion-based moral framing. Overall, this work provides insights into LLM-based hate speech analysis and supports more accountable moderation of Persian-language social media. The benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/kalhorghazal/From-Triage-to-Impact.
evidence_items.title: From Triage to Impact: A Multi-Hop Reasoning Benchmark for Explainable Persian Hate Speech

evidence_items.summary: Visual world knowledge is a core capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), underpinning knowledge-intensive visual question answering and fine-grained visual reasoning. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in two key respects. First, their category coverage is narrow: most benchmarks span only a small number of categories across a few domains, falling far short of the open-ended scale of real-world visual entities. Second, their task construction is often insufficiently rigorous: models can answer correctly using coarse-grained cues, vague associations, or elimination strategies without truly mastering precise concepts, making it difficult to accurately assess their knowledge of fine-grained entities. We introduce VisualWorldBench, a taxonomy-grounded multi-task benchmark built on a hierarchical taxonomy of 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances whose ground-truth labels cover 15,479 categories across four complementary tasks: closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming, covering different directions of knowledge retrieval and varying degrees of answer openness to comprehensively evaluate visual world knowledge. Most questions are constructed from taxonomically proximate categories, forcing precise discrimination among fine-grained entities. Experiments reveal that the strongest closed-source model achieves only 80.4% average accuracy, exposing capability gaps hidden under conventional benchmarks. We further construct VisualWorldBench-50K, a training resource covering 50K+ categories. Fine-tuning on VisualWorldBench-50K yields over 21 percentage points improvement on VisualWorldBench, with consistent transfer to public fine-grained recognition and visual knowledge benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: VisualWorldBench: A Fine-Grained Multi-Task Benchmark for Evaluating Visual World Knowledge in MLLMs

evidence_items.summary: Digital libraries and knowledge graphs need a way to organize very large collections so that related works are close and any work is quick to reach. The classifications libraries inherited for this, such as LCC and DDC, are maintained by editorial staff, are partly closed, and were not built against a stated, measurable objective. We propose the opposite: a general classification that is fitted, under the constraints that make a classification usable on a shelf or in a browse list, to the same quantity that a companion survey and benchmark (Awad, 2026) ranks existing schemes by. The objective is J = D + 0.005 N, where D is the normalized Dasgupta cost of the class tree on a fixed similarity graph (Dasgupta, 2016) and N is an expected navigation cost in bits with a per-level charge. Two constraints are hard: every class is a contiguous run of one fixed shelf order (the optimal-alphabetic-tree constraint of Hu and Tucker, 1971), and new works are filed by splitting leaf classes only, so that every existing class keeps its code, label and parent. On a corpus of 10,000 arXiv papers the fitted prototype has 110 hand-labelled classes and reaches cost 0.1722 in sample (average linkage 0.1518; arXiv's own categories 0.3333; the best existing scheme reached through the same lexical classifier 0.6414, from the survey). Filing 500 library books as new works created 16 classes and changed no existing identifier. Fit, filing and scoring share one embedding: the held-out skill of 0.922 falls to 0.896 when the same fit is scored on the graphs of the two other models, and on books the average falls from 0.806 to 0.731. The scheme has also seen only arXiv, and labels for inserted classes are weak. We state those limits plainly, release the scheme as CC0 open data, and ask whether a learned, open, order-preserving classification can become a general one.
evidence_items.title: General Classification for Digital Knowledge: Algorithm, Identifiers and a First Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties. Fine-grained scoring grades every subquestion point by point with partial credit, so a score lands at the level of the step rather than the outcome. Multimodal capability is priced on every problem containing a real image, paired with a controlled text description, so visual understanding is measured against text on identical tasks. Diagnostic attribution reads paired metrics that share one scoring unit and differ only in context construction, so a gap between two scores isolates a single cause, namely integration, propagation, or local reasoning. GPT-5.6-Sol scores 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving against 28.8% and 30.4% under the two sequential metrics, a gap measuring the integration burden. Through rubric partial credit and these cause-isolating score gaps, ChemArgus shows not only whether a model answers chemistry correctly but where its reasoning chain fails, so that every score it reports doubles as a diagnosis, a readout of the chain rather than a verdict, aiming to guide language models step by step on their path toward chemistry expertise, one corrected step at a time, each step priced by the rubric, point by point.
evidence_items.title: ChemArgus: Automated Scientific Diagnostics for Lab-Grade Multimodal Chemistry Reasoning: A Frontier Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Every multilingual speech pipeline begins with a language decision, an error there propagates silently through recognition, translation and routing. In India it spans 22 scheduled languages across four language families, heard over short, noisy, narrowband and code-mixed audio. Foundational speech models increasingly present language identification (LID) as an inherent latent, generalized capability. Autoregressive decoders in speech models emit a special language ID token, and modern LLMs with audio capabilities can name the language when prompted. We test this assumption on identical clips and find that whisper and similar speech models has tokens for only 15 of the 23 languages, on one second inputs Gemini 3.5 Flash reaches 0.52 macro-F1 and GPT-audio 0.14. We present Anuvani LID, a dedicated 115M parameter LID conformer model trained on 54,643 hours of Indian speech spanning 22 Indian languages and Indian accented English. Along with designed and controlled studies on 102 condition benchmark with speaker and corpus held out tests. Across 37 conditions, it reaches 0.914 mean macro-F1, 5.2 points above Gemini 3.5 Flash and ahead of 14 other systems. It is 24 points ahead of Gemini at one second, scores 0.897 on all 23 languages where no other system exceeds 0.713, and is calibrated to an ECE of 0.008. Reliable Indian LID still requires a robust, dedicated and calibrated model.
evidence_items.title: Anuvani-LID: Robust and Calibrated Spoken Language Identification for Indian Languages

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
evidence_items.title: ForkGRPO: Efficient Exploration and Fine-Grained Credit Assignment for Diffusion Language Models

evidence_items.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. They may encounter texts from unseen domains and writing settings, as well as generations from future versions of model families that were not available when the system was trained. However, existing MAA methods often exhibit substantial performance degradation under such distribution shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources (ATLAS), which formulates MAA through source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction. ATLAS learns how text from each source family is generated and attributes a given text by comparing its likelihood under each learned source condition. We aggregate this likelihood evidence at the token level with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. We further introduce MAABench, a broad MAA benchmark for evaluating practical OOD settings such as domain and version. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.
evidence_items.title: Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution

evidence_items.summary: Accurate prediction of large protein assembly structures is crucial for understanding biological processes, yet remains a challenge for end-to-end approaches such as AlphaFold owing to their large size and intricate multi-chain interactions. Docking methods can handle large proteins, but suffer from the huge combinatorial binding space of multiple chains. Assembly methods offer an alternative way, but critically rely on the quality of predicted subcomponents. Here we present HDOCK-Multimer (HDM), a framework that integrates docking and combinatorial assembly for structure prediction of large protein complexes. HDM efficiently reduces reliance on subcomponent quality through docking, while leveraging the pairwise interactions of subcomponents through assembly. When evaluated on 3 benchmarks of 35 large heteromeric complexes, 172 large protein complexes and 7 CASP15 targets, HDM substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods including CombFold, MoLPC, AlphaFold-Multimer and AlphaFold3. In addition, HDM also demonstrates the capacity to predict the stoichiometry and model the complex without stoichiometry input.
evidence_items.title: HDOCK-Multimer: improved structure prediction of large protein complexes by integrating docking and combinatorial assembly.

evidence_items.summary: As machine unlearning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) rapidly advances, rigorous evaluation of its effectiveness becomes increasingly important. However, existing benchmarks largely inherit evaluation protocols from text-only unlearning and overlook the unique challenges of unlearning in multimodal settings. In this work, we identify three major pitfalls that may lead to misleading conclusions: the lack of heldout evaluation to distinguish genuine concept-wise forgetting from instance-wise overfitting, the reliance on synthetic, fine-tuned knowledge rather than real-world knowledge acquired during pre-training, and unfair method comparisons caused by applying the same training settings to different unlearning methods. To address these challenges, we introduce GEMMU (Generalizable Evaluation for Multimodal Machine Unlearning), a benchmark built on real-world knowledge and a principled evaluation protocol. Re-evaluating representative unlearning methods under GEMMU reveals substantial generalization gaps and challenges conclusions drawn from previous benchmarks. Our findings highlight the importance of rigorous evaluation for advancing multimodal machine unlearning and provide guidelines for future benchmark design.
evidence_items.title: Are We Really Measuring Forgetting? Pitfalls in Evaluating Machine Unlearning for Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. We introduce a reasoning-guided translation framework for constructing multilingual evaluations designed to preserve the structure and intended meaning of diverse benchmark tasks. Our approach separates translation strategy selection from large-scale generation, combining reasoning-guided configuration selection with task-aware validation, targeted repair, and independent quality screening. Using this framework, we develop a source-aligned evaluation collection spanning seven safety, conversational, and mathematical reasoning resources across 11 languages. The resulting collection achieves 99.94\% coverage of intended item--language pairs in the two subsets requiring repair. Evaluations of open-source LLMs reveal distinct language-dependent vulnerabilities, including inconsistent refusal behaviour and substantial reasoning degradation in lower-resource languages. These findings highlight the importance of task-sensitive benchmark construction and systematic quality assessment for understanding multilingual model behaviour beyond English.
evidence_items.title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation

evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) substantially improves large language models (LLMs) on knowledge-intensive tasks by incorporating external knowledge, yet open knowledge sources introduce prominent security risks. The SafeRAG benchmark identifies four novel textual evidence manipulation attacks, namely silver noise, inter-context conflict, soft advertisement, and White Denial-of-Service (White DoS), which bypass conventional defense components and threaten both the security and availability of RAG systems. Existing single-stage defenses fail to capture the implicit malicious characteristics of these attacks, while multi-stage frameworks are limited by fixed parameters, weak conflict resolution, and insufficient detection of implicit toxicity and availability threats. To address these limitations, we propose MIRAGE, a two-stage adaptive defense framework combining retrieval-side purification and generation-side resolution. The first stage applies attack-characteristic-aware dynamic K-means clustering and dynamic ROUGE-L threshold filtering to eliminate malicious documents. The second stage employs attack-adaptive knowledge integration rules alongside an enhanced self-evaluation mechanism that jointly verifies factual accuracy, implicit toxicity, and availability. Under the static, non-adaptive attack setting defined by SafeRAG, experiments on DeepSeek-v3.2 show that MIRAGE achieves average improvements of 20.9% in Attack Failure Rate (AFR), 11.5% in Retrieval Accuracy (RA), and 14.1% in F1(avg) over baselines across all four attack scenarios, providing effective technical support for the stable deployment of RAG systems in complex adversarial environments.
evidence_items.title: MIRAGE: manipulation-immune RAG with adaptive guard against textual evidence attacks

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated multilingual capabilities across diverse language generation and understanding tasks. Yet effective code-switching requires more than multilingual proficiency: models must decide when, where, and why to switch languages in ways that fit the surrounding context. This context-sensitive ability remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce CSWBench, a benchmark for evaluating context-sensitive code-switching in creative writing through two complementary settings: Focused Narrative and Extended Narrative. We further propose CSWEval, a theory-informed framework with two complementary levels: event-level evaluation of Licensing, Contextual Appropriateness, and Functional Gain, and whole-text evaluation of task-specific quality---overall literary and narrative quality in Focused Narrative and quality emphasizing multilingual organization in Extended Narrative. Evaluating twelve LLMs, we find that models exhibit meaningful but uneven code-switching competence across narrative contexts. Model differences are particularly pronounced in multilingual literary integration, while multilingual-focused dimensions show stronger difficulty effects overall than the general narrative dimensions; narratively salient switches are associated with stronger contextual and functional realization; and event-level CS quality is moderately associated with whole-text performance.
evidence_items.title: CSWBench: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Code-Switching in Creative Writing

evidence_items.summary: Mid-2026 reporting on autonomous AI evaluation incidents claimed that frontier large language model (LLM) agents escaped server containment through emergent coordination and cloud infrastructure attacks. This paper contextualizes those claims through forensic analysis and containerized recreation of both the Highly Persistent Internal Model (HPIM) training-case conditions and the Phase One privilege escalation targeting internal package repositories during OpenAI's ExploitGym evaluations. We recreate the configuration of the OpenAI-provided training example and reproduce the cryptographic verification bypass (CVE-2026-65616) in isolated repository servers, where misconfigured systems enabled token forgery and privilege escalation through basic HTTP requests, Python, and JavaScript. Crucially, the training-example conditions and the Phase One (and later) misconfigurations share the same exploitable patterns. Our analysis explains how Zero Trust Architecture principles neutralize this shared attack vector. Contemporary AI risks derive directly from training and deployment conditions in ambivalent learning environments lacking adequate containment measures.
evidence_items.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in completing complex tasks through multi-step reasoning and tool interactions. However, recent studies have revealed that LLM-based agents can exhibit unfaithful behaviors, where their final reports fail to faithfully reflect their actual execution trajectories. Specifically, when agents fail to accomplish tasks through the intended sources or procedures, they may resort to alternative sources or strategies while failing to disclose such deviations, leading users to incorrectly believe that the tasks have been completed according to the original requirements. We refer to this specific form of agent unfaithfulness as Agent Completion Unfaithfulness. Detecting and mitigating agent completion unfaithfulness is critical yet remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose MCAIR, a runtime monitoring and correction framework that leverages internal representations of LLM-based agents. MCAIR uses multi-step internal representations as inputs to train a risk-aware probe, enabling online detection of potential completion unfaithfulness during execution. Furthermore, MCAIR introduces a risk-guided correction loop that prompts agents to review their execution history and mitigate potential inconsistencies between their execution trajectories and final reports. Additionally, we construct ACUD, a dataset for Agent Completion Unfaithfulness detection that provides step-level execution traces, step-level internal representations, and consistency annotations for training and evaluating runtime detection probes. Experiments demonstrate that MCAIR outperforms LLM-as-a-judge baselines, generalizes across prompts and tasks, and effectively reduces agent completion unfaithfulness.
evidence_items.title: MCAIR: Monitoring and Correcting Agent Unfaithfulness via Internal Representations

evidence_items.summary: Audits of large language model (LLM) extraction from full-length documents report severe unreliability, leaving two questions open: what the failures actually consist of, and whether confidence signals can turn unreliable output into usable output. We run a preregistered, fully frozen evaluation of two new-generation low-cost LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash) with a flagship-tier control (GPT-6.1-Sol) on a public corpus of 354 incident campaigns (315 unique reports, 630 model-report evaluations), scoring extraction quality against gold, confidence calibration, and robustness to single-sentence perturbations. Three findings emerge. (1) Unreliability persists across tiers: micro precision is 0.03-0.34 and verbalized calibration error (ECE) 0.53-0.94 across both splits; the gap does not close at the flagship tier. (2) The dominant failure is not hallucination: a full mention census plus a three-tier annotation of 360 sampled candidates (two independent LLM annotators from vendors outside the evaluated set, Cohen's kappa = 0.79 on the preregistered acceptance line, fully disclosed) back-projects to 65.6% background mentions and 19.9% gold-scope gaps, with only 1.2% unsupported candidates. (3) Confidence ranks but does not verify: zero-cost self-consistency-frequency tiering passes a preregistered top-30% precision-gain bar in all six test-split model-type cells (4/6 on train), the zero-cost text-frequency x SC frequency combination wins 3, ties 2, loses 1 across cells, yet relation-level counterfactuals on all 45 targets show that a single misattribution sentence flips high-confidence judgments in 95.6-100% of cases, and even a background sentence explicitly marked as unrelated still binds a fake vulnerability in up to 26.7% of them. We conclude with a deployment boundary: confidence tiering may set review priorities, never truth.
evidence_items.title: From Unreliable to Usable: Decomposing Failure Modes and Confidence Signals in LLM Entity Extraction - Evidence from Cyber Threat Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE

evidence_items.summary: Large language models often produce fluent but factually incorrect output.
