Gray-box detectors identify such hallucinations from the token-probability statistics emitted during generation, avoiding the need for white-box access to hidden states that frontier models do not provide. These detectors, however, typically rely only on probability-derived representations and ignore the identities of the candidate tokens. They can therefore observe how uncertain the model is, but not what it is uncertain about. Consequently, they cannot distinguish between a model that is torn between"big"and"small"and one that is torn between"big"and"huge"when the two pairs receive the same probability distribution. We introduce GURI (Gray-box Uncertainty Representations with Identity), a lightweight gray-box hallucination detector that combines candidate-token probabilities with per-token vector identifiers. This exposes which alternatives the model considered while preserving the accessibility and transferability of the gray-box setting. Across three open-weight models and three question-answering benchmarks, GURI increases mean test ROC-AUC from 72.09% to 79.09% over a probability-only baseline. On the closed-source GPT-4.1 model, mean ROC-AUC increases from 67.39% to 71.84%. Among the three open-weight models, GURI outperforms transferred probability-only baseline in 17 of 18 directed cross-model transfers without fine-tuning. For the three open-weight models, cross-dataset transfer between HotpotQA and TriviaQA with the model held fixed improves mean ROC-AUC over transferred LOS-Net by 3.76 points.
evidence_items.title: Gray-Box Hallucination Detection in LLMs with Token Identities

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.
evidence_items.title: LLM-jp-4 Technical Report

evidence_items.summary: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.
evidence_items.title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-video (T2V) generation models can produce visually realistic videos that nevertheless violate the physical consequences implied by the prompt and scene. Existing benchmarks largely rely on holistic plausibility scores or broad quality dimensions, leaving it unclear which physical behavior is being tested and why a model fails. We introduce PhyMetric, a scene-level diagnostic benchmark that recasts physical plausibility evaluation as verifiable, scene-grounded question answering. PhyMetric contains 1{,}115 scenes spanning 50 physical categories across six domains, paired with 8{,}920 answer-balanced binary questions over 12 evaluation dimensions. Each scene is associated with eight targeted yes/no questions and a structured physical prior specifying the governing law, expected temporal sequence, observable signatures, and common failure modes. At evaluation time, a vision-language model (VLM) judge answers each question from question-aware sampled frames conditioned on the prior, and correctness is hierarchically aggregated into scene, dimension, physical category, and model scores. Experiments on four open-source T2V models and three VLM judges show that scene-specific binary QA is a critical component of the protocol: when each targeted question is replaced by a single generic plausibility query, evaluator accuracy drops to the chance level. Structured physical priors offer a complementary signal that improves human alignment of the resulting scores, with effects that vary across VLM judges of different capacity. These findings establish PhyMetric as a benchmark that turns physical plausibility evaluation from opaque holistic scoring into interpretable, scene-level inspection. Our project page is available at: https://mengsiwei.github.io/PhyMetric/.
evidence_items.title: PhyMetric: Diagnosing Physical Plausibility in Text-to-Video Generation via Scene-Level QA

evidence_items.summary: Repository-level code comprehension question answering (QA) supports developer reasoning over functionality and usage distributed across codebases. However, repository-specialized large language models (LLMs) can become misaligned as code evolves. We study this challenge as temporal repository adaptation: acquiring new knowledge, suppressing obsolete, retaining still-valid, and preserving semantically neighboring knowledge. Existing retrieval, fine-tuning, and model-editing methods address only parts of this problem. We propose Temporal Adaptive Fine-Tuning (TAFT), a novel adaptation approach that treats repository transitions as supervision. TAFT derives temporally grounded QA data from repository transitions, pairs newly valid with obsolete knowledge through preference optimization, and replays transition-conditioned retention examples to preserve still-valid knowledge. We evaluate TAFT on an augmented temporal SWE-bench dataset comprising 255,295 QA entries across ten temporal slices, comparing deferred (Baseline), per-slice retrained (Baseline-Batched), and variants with knowledge anchors along four dimensions: updated knowledge, obsolete-answer suppression, retention, and neighbor stability. TAFT consistently outperforms both the deferred and batched baselines, with an average relative improvement of 18% in updated/suppressed knowledge accuracy, doubled retention accuracy, and roughly 1.5 times the neighbor accuracy. With directly supplied knowledge anchors, TAFT-KANT further improves mean updated/suppressed, retention, and neighbor accuracy over TAFT by 3.55%, 8.35%, and 13.00%, respectively. Overall, TAFT demonstrates its effectiveness across all evaluated areas, effectively enabling code comprehension QA alignment with repository evolution.
evidence_items.title: Temporal Adaptive Fine-Tuning for Code Comprehension

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image models increasingly generate readable Chinese text that still contains local rendering defects, such as a character with an extra or missing stroke or a malformed component. Such errors are invisible to OCR and vision-language models, which are trained for recognition and are therefore invariant to the very structural deviations that define a rendering error. We formalize text rendering verification as a target-conditioned problem: given a target character and an image crop, decide whether the crop is a correct rendering of that character. Our verifier TEXTVERIFIER feeds the text tower a character's Ideographic Description Sequence (IDS) rather than a single-character symbol, and is trained on 12.7M crop-IDS pairs plus label-free"same-character, different-quality"hard pairs sampled from the training trajectory of a text-region inpainting model. To evaluate this ability we build TEXTRENDERBENCH-ZH, the first per-character benchmark for generated Chinese text, annotating position, identity, and correctness for 7,358 characters. TEXTVERIFIER reaches an F1 of 0.844, far above OCR confidence (0.526), a general VLM (0.329), and TextPecker (0.590). Used as a per-character reward for Flow-GRPO post-training, it further reduces rendering errors, showing that its score can both detect and correct errors.
evidence_items.title: TextVerifier: Seeing Beyond Recognition to Verify Chinese Text Rendering

evidence_items.summary: Answering questions over heterogeneous data means combining evidence from files, databases, documents and the web. Data agents automate this, but their success depends on context. Three context-engineering techniques (CETs) help by shaping it: semantic layers describe the data, orchestration splits work among agents, and compaction condenses interaction history. Existing studies validate each CET alone, leaving open how agent behavior shapes its effect. We present a comprehensive analysis of the three CETs, alone and combined, with seven large language models (LLMs) on 1,514 long-horizon tasks from five benchmarks, covering behavior, accuracy and cost. We find that data agents without CETs form three behavior groups: investigators, premature answerers that answer without inspecting data, and early stoppers that give up. Each CET delivers its known benefit, from more investigation to smaller prompts, but only the behavior group it matches turns that benefit into accuracy, such as premature answerers under orchestration. For investigators, the same CETs can hurt: the semantic layer stops them from looking, orchestration makes them overconfident, costing 5 percentage points, and compaction makes them repeat steps. Combining CETs yields smaller gains and losses than their sum. We derive guidance for choosing CETs by agent behavior, task demands and accuracy-cost trade-offs.
evidence_items.title: Same Context, Different Agents: A Behavioral Study of Semantic Layers, Orchestration and Compaction in Data Agents

evidence_items.summary: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.
evidence_items.title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges

evidence_items.summary: Determining traffic crash liability relies on rigorous on-site evidence and legal provisions and involves substantial manual intervention and potential human error. However, intelligent traffic monitoring systems focus on detection and tracking and cannot provide structured, rule-grounded decision support for formal crash-liability analysis. Moreover, emerging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) suffer from object hallucination that distorts or omits physical evidence, and their opaque reasoning cannot produce explicit evidence-to-rule chains required for traceable and reviewable liability analysis. This paper proposes CrashLex, an explainable neural-symbolic decision-support framework that integrates visual perception with legal knowledge graph reasoning to align multimodal inference with predefined statutory rules and traceability requirements. Within CrashLex, a dual-query vision-language architecture employs parallel semantic and symbolic streams to mitigate object hallucination, utilizing Scene Queries for global context modeling and Perception Queries for fine-grained atomic feature extraction, respectively. The domain-specific legal knowledge graph maps these atomic facts from observable physical conditions to corresponding statutory elements, providing a structured basis for rule-grounded assessment. A logic-driven aggregation protocol then imposes explicit constraints derived from extracted facts and statutory provisions onto the inference process, thereby enabling traceable and interpretable preliminary liability assessment. On the held-out DeepAccident benchmark, CrashLex achieves a Legal Accuracy of 94.0% under the fixed legal-output evaluation protocol and an Object Hallucination Rate of 2.8%, corresponding to an 82.1% relative reduction from the 15.6% rate of the best-performing MLLM baseline on this metric. CrashLex grounds its assessment results in the deterministic execution of predefined legal rules rather than relying solely on unconstrained probabilistic generation, providing verifiable reasoning chains for rule-grounded human review.
evidence_items.title: Toward explainable traffic crash liability analysis via neural-symbolic multimodal reasoning: Integrating visual perception with legal knowledge graphs.

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have made significant progress in referring expression comprehension (REC), yet most REC benchmarks still focus on final-target localization. Complex queries often involve intermediate visual references with different dependencies on prior grounding, but final-only evaluation leaves this process unexamined. To address this gap, we formulate trajectory-level REC, in which models receive an ordered sequence of grounding steps constructed from a single complex query and localize the target regions associated with each step. We instantiate this setting in ReferFlow-Bench, which characterizes structured region transitions through four trajectory types, namely Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture. Experiments show that current models struggle to consistently ground intermediate visual references across successive steps. We further propose ReferFlow, which decouples interleaved text-latent trajectory generation from coordinate decoding. Specifically, Stateful Region Latent Reasoning represents each target region as an object-indexed state composed of continuous latents, with explicit visual and spatial supervision to preserve region information for subsequent grounding. Trajectory-Aware Parallel Decoding then recovers all coordinate blocks in parallel through four geometry-constrained refinement rounds, with each block conditioned on its corresponding trajectory prefix, thereby reducing within-box sequential dependencies and eliminating cross-box autoregression. We further apply Grounding-Aware GRPO to promote consistent grounding across steps and learn adaptive trajectory generation from complex REC queries. ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.
evidence_items.title: ReferFlow: Beyond Final-Target Localization for Complex Referring Expressions

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.
evidence_items.title: MMKG-R1: Constructing Multimodal Knowledge Graphs via Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.
evidence_items.title: Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Comparing financial disclosures across languages requires identifying shared accounting concepts and recovering all numerical facts that express them. Existing benchmarks evaluate aspects of these capabilities, but provide limited insight into whether both succeed on the same multilingual evidence. In particular, it remains unclear whether language models can recognize these concepts across languages and exhaustively recover their corresponding numerical evidence from the same contexts. We introduce MULTIFINGROUND, a benchmark designed to investigate this recognition-grounding gap in multilingual financial reports. Constructed from FY2025 disclosures of 90 issuers in English, French, and Greek, MULTIFINGROUND aligns independently authored reports through a shared accounting taxonomy and provides traceable fact-level annotations. The benchmark evaluates financial fact identification, concept recognition, exhaustive fact selection, and concept discrimination without candidate labels. Across 15 evaluated models, eight API and open-weight reference models achieve 97.3-99.4\% concept recognition accuracy, yet miss at least one target fact in 26.6-41.9\% of correctly recognized groups. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in concept discrimination and limited gains from the evaluated finance-specialized models. Our findings demonstrate that strong concept recognition can coexist with incomplete evidence recovery, highlighting the importance of evaluating semantic recognition and evidence completeness together.
evidence_items.title: Recognition Is Not Grounding: Benchmarking Multilingual Financial Evidence Extraction

evidence_items.summary: Linters are widely used in code maintenance and real-time IDE editing to surface lint alerts related to performance, style, error-prone, and other patterns in source files. However, existing code benchmarks do not explicitly evaluate linter-guided file refactoring, where models must reduce lint alerts in source files with correct initial functionality while satisfying functionality preservation. We introduce LintEval, a multilingual benchmark for linter-guided file refactoring across C++, Python, and Java, comprising 13,061 programs with correct initial functionality and 171,662 lint alerts extracted using language-specific linters. LintEval jointly evaluates functionality preservation, lint alert reduction, new alert avoidance, and edit minimality. Experiments reveal a persistent trade-off: closed-source commercial models reach up to 90.4% Reduction@P but achieve only 67.1%-68.3% Pass@1, while several open-source small models show low or negative Reduction@P. A controlled fine-tuning study further shows that supervision format matters: refactoring-oriented SFT raises Qwen2.5-Coder-7B Reduction@P from 24.7% to 76.0%. LintEval enables controlled evaluation of models that improve source files under functionality preservation.
evidence_items.title: LintEval: Benchmarking LLMs on Linter-Guided File Refactoring

evidence_items.summary: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
evidence_items.title: VideoHarness-SRSI: Structured Recursive Self-Improvement for Video Understanding Harness

evidence_items.summary: Different tasks often require interactive agents to perform similar operations at intermediate steps. Retrieving an entire past workflow can introduce irrelevant steps, whereas retrieving isolated operations can discard the dependencies needed to reuse them. We introduce EvoWeave, a framework for experience memory that represents abstract states as nodes and reusable operations as directed edges with input and output contracts, provenance, and capability references. A planner decomposes the current task into a dependency graph; operation retrieval and bounded directed search then assemble relevant experience fragments. An execution agent can inspect these fragments and their referenced capabilities, while reflection separates concrete execution evidence from reusable abstractions. We study the framework across four benchmarks, five evaluation settings, and three language model backbones. Across backbones, AppWorld Normal and Challenge task goal completion average 51.91 and 27.99, respectively, exceeding the baseline without memory by 6.99 and 4.99 percentage points. An AppWorld ablation associates directed connections with an additional improvement of 2.08 points over independent operation cards. The results motivate composition of reusable operations while exposing tradeoffs in retrieval overhead and conditions for valid reuse.
evidence_items.title: EvoWeave: Composing Reusable Agent Experience through Operation Level Graphs

evidence_items.summary: Tabular foundation models enable in-context learning by predicting unseen observations from a labeled support table without task-specific parameter updates. Despite recent advances, most existing approaches rely on dense architectures that apply the same transformations across features and datasets. We introduce OrionMoE-Small, a compact tabular foundation model that combines distribution-aware representations with dataset-conditioned sparse mixture-of-experts computation. Built on a dual-axis Transformer architecture, OrionMoE-Small selectively activates experts along the feature axis, with routing decisions informed by both individual feature representations and the broader dataset context. This design enables adaptive allocation of computation across heterogeneous tabular problems while retaining a shared computational pathway across tasks. OrionMoE-Small is pretrained entirely on synthetic classification tasks generated from a structured causal prior and performs downstream prediction without gradient-based adaptation. Experiments across multiple tabular benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against substantially larger foundation models, with particularly strong results on small-context and high-dimensional datasets. Further analysis reveals favorable relative performance under class imbalance and highlights the importance of feature composition.
evidence_items.title: OrionMoE-v1.0: A Mixture-of-Experts Foundation Model for Tabular In-Context Learning

evidence_items.summary: The rapid advancement of large vision language models (LVLMs) has made geolocation inference from images highly accurate and accessible. This poses serious privacy risks: a passive adversary with black-box LVLM access can infer a user's location from a single photo with no metadata. Existing protection methods rely almost exclusively on adversarial perturbation, which introduces perceptible visual artifacts and utility degradation. We identify the visual-geolocation asymmetry: geolocation-decisive clues, such as street signs, tend to be visually peripheral but dominate location inference. Exploiting this asymmetry, we propose GeoCloak, an agentic framework for semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection. It acts as a clue-aware planner that analyzes each image to identify geolocation-relevant clues, dispatches targeted semantic edits to directly suppress peripheral clues, and autonomously configures adversarial perturbation to further suppress residual geolocation features, all under iterative utility-aware feedback. We evaluate GeoCloak on four diverse datasets spanning 108 countries and 576 cities against five LVLMs and three inference methods. GeoCloak reduces overall city-level accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9%, approximately half of the best-performing baseline, while achieving substantially superior utility preservation both qualitatively and quantitatively. We hope this work takes a meaningful step toward practical, semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection, giving users greater control over the location information inadvertently embedded in their shared images.
evidence_items.title: GeoCloak: An Agentic Framework for Semantics-Preserving Geolocation Privacy via Peripheral Clue Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Large multimodal models have achieved remarkable progress by scaling model capacity and training on massive paired multimodal data. However, this paradigm introduces a fundamental bottleneck: aligned multimodal datasets are expensive to curate, difficult to scale across diverse modality combinations, and increasingly constrain further progress. We introduce Modality Self-Play (MSP), a training framework for multimodal foundation models based on proxy-mediated modality composition. Instead of relying on paired cross-modal data, MSP uses anchor-supporting proxy textual descriptions of unseen modalities as semantic bridges during training. Given an observed modality (e.g., image or audio), the model generates proxy descriptions for complementary unseen modalities, which are then encoded and aligned with the observed modality through learned bridges, enabling cross-modal interaction without real paired non-text supervision. Our central hypothesis is that proxy text, combined with contrastively trained pretrained encoders, provides sufficient semantic structure for multimodal composition to emerge. We show that MSP enables zero-shot modality composition: models trained only with a real anchor modality and accompanying proxy descriptions can integrate and reason over multiple modalities at inference time despite never observing real paired non-text data during training. Empirically, MSP achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance on multiple multimodal benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate that learned bridges improve alignment, while anchor-supporting proxy descriptions enable effective cross-modal composition. MSP removes the need for real paired non-text (e.g., audio-vision) supervision, while continuing to rely on modality-text pairs, pretrained contrastive encoders, and modality-distribution bridge calibration.
evidence_items.title: MSP: Modality Self-Play for Training Multimodal LLMs Without Paired Cross-Modal Data

evidence_items.summary: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) is a major cause of maternal morbidity worldwide. Although a higher pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI) increases HDP risk, how HDP cases are distributed across BMI levels in relatively lean populations remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the association between pre-pregnancy BMI and HDP, the distribution of HDP cases across BMI levels, and model-predicted HDP incidence under hypothetical BMI distributions.This large-scale multicenter, retrospective study used longitudinal records of singleton pregnancies from 12 obstetric facilities in Japan between 2009 and 2024. The BMI-HDP association was modeled using parity-stratified spline logistic regression. Model-predicted HDP incidence under hypothetical BMI distributions was estimated using spline-based standardization with woman-level bootstrap resampling.Among 52,042 pregnancies, 2,592 (5.0%) developed HDP. Although nulliparous women had higher baseline risk than multiparous women, the BMI-associated risk gradient was similar across parity groups. Most pregnancies were within normal BMI ranges, and most HDP cases arose in women without overweight or obesity. A population-wide 0.5 kg/m² downward BMI shift yielded a 5.5% relative reduction in model-predicted HDP incidence, compared with 6.7% under a BMI cap of 25.0 kg/m². A population-wide 1.0 kg/m² downward shift yielded a 10.2% relative reduction, compared with 12.1% under a BMI cap of 23.0 kg/m².Pre-pregnancy BMI was associated with HDP risk across the BMI continuum, while many HDP cases occurred within moderate BMI ranges. Modest downward BMI shifts yielded model-predicted HDP incidence similar to selected BMI-capping scenarios. These findings provide quantitative benchmarks for population-wide and high-risk approaches to preconception weight management.
evidence_items.title: Pre-pregnancy BMI and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in Japan: population burden and simulated BMI reduction scenarios for preconception and interpregnancy care.

evidence_items.summary: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
evidence_items.title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations

evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often trains language models on responses generated by a different, possibly stale behavior policy. Correcting this mismatch with learner-to-behavior importance weights can introduce high variance for long responses. We introduce Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization (GGPO), which minimizes a log-mean-exp contrast of KL-adjusted rewards among responses to the same prompt, without learner-to-behavior importance weights. We derive GGPO from KL-regularized policy optimization: on policy, its population loss is exactly the KL-regularized optimality gap, and under suitable coverage the learner's single-response expected reward is at least the behavior policy's best-of-$K$ reward, minus terms for the raw finite-group loss, regularization, and finite training data. We characterize reference refresh through exact Gibbs-target composition and a finite-data final-policy reward bound under local reference control and tokenwise behavior mismatch. This refresh is empirically important: in an ablation, fixed-reference GGPO scores $32.96$ on the five-benchmark problem-weighted average, versus $46.58$ with the default refresh schedule. Experiments on mathematical reasoning further show that GGPO outperforms GRPO and AGRO under training-inference mismatch and on fixed offline data, while maintaining its performance as controlled policy staleness grows.
evidence_items.title: Gibbs-Gap Policy Optimization for Off-Policy RL with Verifiable Rewards

evidence_items.summary: In multi-modal 3D pre-training, aligning 3D shapes, their 2D image counterparts, and language descriptions has made tremendous progress. However, we find that supervision from rendered images is unreliable, the semantics encoded in synthetic views are distorted due to domain gap, self-occlusion, and rendering artifacts. Instead, we learn transferable 3D representations from language only. We observe that, in real world, 3D shapes are organized in a tree-like structure, ranging from general concepts to fine-grained instances with specific attributes, while language typically denotes generic concepts and subsumes these various 3D instantiations. Hence, we propose to embed 3D representations in hyperbolic space, whose geometry is well-suited for modeling tree-like data without distortion. To capture the asymmetric hierarchy between language and 3D shapes, we further impose a partial-order relation that language entails 3D shapes. Our method, Hyperbolic Contrastive Learning (HyperCL), jointly optimizes a hyperbolic geodesic-based contrastive objective and an entailment loss to learn discriminative cross-modal representations while explicitly preserving this hierarchy. We also introduce a rigorously verified benchmark for comprehensively evaluating cross-modal 3D alignment. Across two widely used benchmarks and ours, we improve the performance up to 4.6% absolute percentage on 3D shape classification and 5.5% on cross-modal text-to-3D retrieval under the same parameter budget. The code and evaluation benchmark will be made publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Revisiting Triplet Contrastive Learning for 3D Shape Understanding

evidence_items.summary: India's 22 scheduled languages are spoken by over a billion people in conversations that mix languages, often within one turn, overlap freely, and take place over telephones, in meetings, and in media. Knowing who spoke when, the task of speaker diarization, is essential to speech applications for such conversation: voice agents conversing with several people at once, speaker attributed transcription of meetings and calls, contact center analytics, and media monitoring. We present a systematic study of speaker diarization across all 22 languages on IndicDiarBench and introduce Anuvani-Diarization, which adapts a self-supervised end-to-end segmentation model to Indian conversation with uncertainty aware silver supervision. Evaluated zero shot alongside nine recent diarization systems, it reaches a duration weighted diarization error rate (DER) of 16.78% on all 1,164 recordings, the lowest of all systems we ran and second only to the best published result (16.0%), and leads the three strongest rivals in 14 of 22 languages. It matches its parent on six international benchmarks. We also show that the benchmark's utterance level annotation convention is a hidden variable worth 1.9 to 4.1 DER points, depending on the system, and that a convention learned from other Indian transcriptions does not transfer.
evidence_items.title: Anuvani-Diarization: Zero Shot Speaker Diarization and Annotation Conventions Across 22 Languages

evidence_items.summary: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.
evidence_items.title: Learning Visual Speech Representations via Cross-Modal Distillation and Joint Face-Lip Modeling

evidence_items.summary: Health insurance coverage remains critically low in Sierra Leone, creating barriers to achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and leaving women particularly vulnerable to catastrophic out-of-pocket health expenditures. Understanding which women are most at risk of being uninsured and the specific combination of factors perpetuating their exclusion is essential for designing effective, targeted interventions. This study aimed to develop and evaluate machine learning models to predict health insurance coverage among women in Sierra Leone, identify the most influential sociodemographic and economic predictors, and translate model outputs into actionable, precision-targeted policy recommendations for advancing UHC. Data from the 2019 Sierra Leone Demographic and Health Survey (SLDHS), a nationally representative dataset of 15,574 women, were used. Six classifiers were compared: Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, k-Nearest Neighbours, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost. Cost-sensitive learning strategies were applied to address pronounced class imbalance, where insured women constituted only 3.5% of the sample. To enhance interpretability and support policy translation, Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), were applied to the best-performing interpretable model. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest overall performance, with an AUROC of 0.8857 and a minority class recall of 80.6%. XGBoost performed competitively with an AUROC of 0.869 and was selected for interpretability analysis due to its established compatibility with tree-based explanation workflows. Global SHAP analysis identified region, wealth index, and radio listenership as the three most influential predictors of insurance coverage, with decision-making autonomy variables demonstrating meaningful but secondary contributions. Instance-level waterfall plots and LIME explanations revealed substantial heterogeneity in insurance pathways, distinguishing structurally advantaged, compensatory, and compound-disadvantage profiles among women. Ensemble machine learning models, particularly Gradient Boosting and XGBoost, demonstrate strong predictive utility for identifying uninsured women in low-coverage, resource-limited settings. The integration of SHAP and LIME frameworks bridges the gap between algorithmic performance and actionable policy insight, revealing that insurance coverage is strongly associated with geographic location, economic status, and media exposure. These findings provide an evidence-based framework for precision public health strategies that simultaneously address geographic disparities, economic barriers, and women’s empowerment constraints in Sierra Leone.
evidence_items.title: Predicting health insurance coverage among women in Sierra Leone using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence applied to demographic and health survey data

evidence_items.summary:
BACKGROUND
Raised intracranial pressure is one of the most severe secondary insults after traumatic brain injury. Recognising physiological patterns before they progress to dangerous intracranial pressure elevations could enable preventive rather than reactive interventions. In our previous Uppsala single-centre study, an XGBoost machine learning model showed high discriminative performance for prediction of imminent intracranial pressure insults. The model identifies short-term physiological trajectories associated with imminent threshold crossing rather than predicting independent future clinical events. Whether these results are generalisable across centres is unknown. The aim was therefore to evaluate whether the XGBoost model trained on an Uppsala dataset maintains similar performance when applied to a multicentre TBI cohort - The CENTER-TBI High-Resolution ICU cohort.


METHODS
The XGBoost model trained on the Uppsala high frequency traumatic brain injury cohort was externally validated using data from the multicentre CENTER-TBI cohort. Minute-level averages of intracranial pressure and invasive arterial blood pressure were used to predict the onset of an intracranial pressure insult within 30 min on the basis of a 4h historical window. A bidirectional validation design was applied and performance was assessed using multiple metrics.


RESULTS
The cohorts comprised 602 patients from Uppsala and 255 patients from the CENTER-TBI database. When trained on the Uppsala cohort and tested on CENTER-TBI, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 97.4%, sensitivity of 93.8%, and specificity of 98.6%. Training on CENTER-TBI and testing on the Uppsala dataset yielded an AUROC of 96.1%, sensitivity of 81.2%, and specificity of 98.7%. Balanced accuracy exceeded 88% in both validation directions.


CONCLUSIONS
The XGBoost model retained high performance under external multicentre validation, indicating that pre-insult physiological patterns preceding increased intracranial pressure are shared across cohorts. Differences in sensitivity between validation directions were observed and may reflect cohort characteristics or dataset size. These findings support the need for local evaluation before clinical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Early Prediction of Intracranial Hypertension: From Single-Centre Development to Multicentre Validation.

evidence_items.summary:
OBJECTIVE
To critically review artificial intelligence (AI) in echocardiography, linking model design and technical performance to validation and clinical use.


METHODS
We synthesized literature assembled through Web of Science and Scopus collections and targeted revision searches. Evidence was organized by echocardiographic task, model paradigm, data source, evaluation protocol, and level of clinical validation.


RESULTS
AI applications span acquisition guidance, image analysis, quantitative measurement, disease assessment, and outcome prediction, with emerging foundation, multimodal, and examination-level models. Most studies assess retrospective task performance; fewer evaluate cross-site transportability or clinical impact. Reproducible performance has been demonstrated for view recognition, segmentation, and selected measurements under aligned protocols, and prospective trials confirm workflow gains. However, evidence linking AI to improved clinical decisions or patient outcomes remains limited. Generalizability is further constrained by uneven dataset coverage and inconsistent evaluation protocols.


CONCLUSION
Current evidence supports AI assistance in selected echocardiographic tasks; however, clinical use requires external validation, failure reporting, and ongoing monitoring in intended settings.


SIGNIFICANCE
This review links model development with validation evidence to guide clinical evaluation and identify priorities for prospective studies in echocardiography.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Echocardiography: A Critical Review of Models, Validation, and Clinical Impact.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been applied in medical diagnostics and has shown promise in improving the detection of pediatric diseases. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the diagnostic performance of AI models in identifying pediatric respiratory, systemic/inflammatory, and neurological conditions, specifically pneumonia, tuberculosis, Kawasaki disease, and brain tumors. This study followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis for Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA) guidelines. PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies were included if they evaluated the diagnostic performance of AI models for pediatric diseases. Methodological quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Diagnostic performance indicators—sensitivity and specificity—were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. AI models demonstrated high diagnostic performance for pneumonia, with pooled sensitivity and specificity of 93% and 90%, respectively. AI also showed excellent performance in detecting Kawasaki disease, with sensitivity and specificity of 94% and 89%, respectively. Studies assessing brain tumor detection reported strong performance; however, inconsistent reporting of metrics prevented quantitative meta-analysis. In contrast, AI models showed low sensitivity (41%.) in detecting tuberculosis. AI models show strong potential to improve diagnostic accuracy in pediatric diseases, particularly pneumonia and Kawasaki disease. However, the lack of external validity, high risk of bias, and substantial between-study heterogeneity limits generalizability. Therefore, future research should prioritize external validation across diverse datasets to ensure reliability and support integration of AI-based diagnostic tools into pediatric clinical practice.
evidence_items.title: Diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence in pediatric diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis

evidence_items.summary: Privacy-preserving machine learning has become critical for deploying artificial intelligence in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and infrastructure monitoring. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure inference on encrypted data. Despite its advantages, HE is not compatible with nonlinear activation functions found in machine learning models. Existing methods mitigate this problem by manually designing polynomial approximations for these activation functions. However, these functions do not account for the differences in dataset characteristics or model architecture. Furthermore, these functions are also limited to the accuracies of convolutional neural network (CNN) models. In this work, we propose an autonomous framework that selects polynomial activation functions tailored to each dataset and model. Using this framework, we analyze the interdependence between polynomial activation design and model architecture by evaluating several CNN ResNet and Vision Transformer models across multiple datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework generalizes across multiple architectures, including ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16, and ViT-L/16. Across all datasets, transformer-based models maintain higher accuracy under polynomial approximation, while convolutional models exhibit increased degradation as task complexity grows. In addition, latency analysis reveals that the proposed CLS token based inference pipeline significantly reduces computational overhead by eliminating depth-dependent operations, shifting the primary cost to encryption and decryption. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method not only adapts polynomial activations across architectures, but also enables efficientencrypted inference through both activation design and pipeline optimization.
evidence_items.title: AutoPoly-HE: Autonomous Design of Polynomial Activations for Privacy-Preserving Encrypted Inference

evidence_items.summary: Neural radiance fields (NeRF) offer photorealistic novel-view synthesis, but their use for public art remains sensitive to reflective materials, uncontrolled illumination, viewpoint gaps, and browser-side latency. This study presents a reliability-aware NeRF workflow for sculpture reconstruction and interactive visualization. The scientific contribution is not a new radiance-field representation; it is a visibility-weighted cross-view supervision strategy that uses background, occlusion, and reflection masks to reduce unreliable correspondences, together with a unified evaluation protocol linking reconstruction fidelity, view consistency, and interaction performance. Five indoor and outdoor artworks were captured from 65 to 120 viewpoints. Under a common image split and camera-pose protocol, the proposed configuration achieved a normalized geometric error of 1.20 ± 0.20%, PSNR of 28.46 ± 0.70 dB, SSIM of 0.921 ± 0.010, and multi-view Recall of 96.4%. Exploratory paired tests across the five samples indicated lower geometric error and higher PSNR and SSIM than the two classical pipeline baselines (all p < 0.001), although the small purposive sample limits generalization. The browser prototype reached 27 fps with an initial loading latency of 1.3 s, and the 24-participant evaluation yielded an overall rating of 4.42 ± 0.34. The results indicate that the reliability-aware cross-view strategy improves reconstruction consistency for the evaluated artworks while maintaining browser-side interaction efficiency. Because Instant-NGP, Mip-NeRF 360, and 3D Gaussian Splatting were not executed on the same dataset, the findings are limited to comparisons with the standard NeRF and the two classical reconstruction pipelines.
evidence_items.title: High fidelity three dimensional reconstruction and interactive visualization of public art sculptures using neural radiance fields

evidence_items.summary: Significant research has been done regarding frameworks for evaluation of smart grids in a bid to assess their efficiency, reliability, and impact. However, the frameworks are mainly targeting developed grids, adapting these frameworks to low-resource settings present significant challenges due to limited infrastructure, constrained budgets, inadequate technical expertise, regulatory gaps, and unreliable power supply. Albait the automation of the said evaluation frameworks has also not been given enough attension. This study employs a combined User-Centered Design (UCD) and Quality Function Deployment (QFD) approach to examine in detail and identify, prioritize, and translate user requirements into technical specifications for designing an automated tailor-made smart evaluation framework tailored for resource-constrained environments. A mixed-method research design, including literature reviews, interviews, and surveys, was used to gather responses from smart grid users in Uganda and Kenya. According to the findings ease of integration scored (15.2%), localization scored (15.0%), and environmental adaptability returned (14.2%) and these turned out to be the most important technical requirements. This meant that there is need for automated smart grid evaluation frameworks that seamlessly integrate into existing grid and at the same time adapt to the local contexts. Additionally, modularity scored 9.2%, offline capabilities returned 8.8%, and resource efficiency scored 8.4%. Users emphasized these requirements to ensure ease of growth and resilience in environments with poor connectivity and power stability. User requirements such as reliable data acquisition, resilience to intermittent internet connectivity, power outage readiness, and big data management were notably preffered. The study further indicated that the users focus was mainly on energy efficiency metrics, resource conservation, and grid infrastructure robustness.
evidence_items.title: Examining Essential Requirements for a Smart Grid Evaluation Framework Tailored for low Resource Settings

evidence_items.summary: This deliverable presents the initial evaluation of an unprecedented combination of surface patterning processes explored for the first time in BURST project. Namely, we investigate the use of colloidal lithography (CL) masks, developed by NOVA in the frame of WP2, with atmospheric dry etching (ADE) developed by Nines PV, as a scalable surface texturization approach for crystalline silicon (c-Si) photovoltaics. Self-assembled polystyrene (PS) sphere monolayers, as-deposited, were used as partial masking structures during a thermally activated F2 (10%)/ N2 gas-phase ADE process performed by Nines PV. Experiments were conducted using 0.9 μm and 1.3 μm diameter PS spheres deposited on bare c-Si and on c-Si coated with 200 nm ITO, processed at 80-90 ºC for 4-7 minutes. The resulting surfaces were characterized morphologically by SEM and AFM, and optically via spectrophotometry measurements. The results, thus far, show that ADE induces only shallow and largely isotropic surface modifications, with limited impact on the optical response of bare c-Si samples. For c-Si + ITO samples, ring- and bowl-like micro-structures were observed, although these features are likely associated with degradation and deformation of the PS spheres rather than significant etching of the underlying ITO layer.  The study indicates that the current CL + ADE approach is strongly limited by diffusion-controlled transport and low reactive species activation, preventing the formation of functional light-trapping textures. The proposed next steps, to be pursued in the final year of the project, include increasing interparticle spacing, extending etching duration, replacing PS by SiO2 spheres which are much more chemically resilient, and further morphological characterization to better understand the observed mechanisms and optimize the processes.
evidence_items.title: D5.4 - Synergetic combination of colloidal masking with ADE for surface structuring

evidence_items.summary: When an AI system acts for some people but binds others, obedience no longer settles whether it acts rightly. I argue that alignment is then a relation among three bodies: the system, its principals and the people its acts bind. Three theses follow, under stated premises. Completing alignment requires valid authorization covering the system's binding acts, so aligning AI requires humans to align with each other, through authorization and coordination, which existing institutions may already supply, not shared values. Alignment is judged over time, not by a snapshot lacking required history; a description that predicts well can lose who is owed what. Evaluating any alignment scheme rests on normative choices, which I itemize as an invoice: any entry may be refused, but refusal cannot supply a missing proof. Scoped formal results show other shortcuts failing: agreeing parts need not make an acceptable whole, and the auditors studied cannot fully certify themselves. The roles alignment needs do not require the AI to be conscious. Consciousness bears instead on whom alignment serves, and a candidate subject can be protected while its consciousness is unproved. I propose a covenant between humans and AI systems: duties of aid and protection, and care that does not depend on one's service record. On finite models, a good record need not mean accepting interruption, and the covenant's upkeep, modelled among humans, holds under stated premises, not shown to sustain itself in practice. I settle neither how to complete alignment nor whether any AI system is conscious. Code, exact result data, the Lean development and the mathematical notes: https://github.com/ioannist/six-birds-alignment (release v1.0).
evidence_items.title: Aligning AI Requires Aligning with Each Other: A Covenant

evidence_items.summary: This thesis investigates novel methods for enhancing diagnostic and treatment protocols for juvenile dysmenorrhea using distinct, customizable strategies customized to each patient's specific requirements. Juvenile dysmenorrhea, a disorder commonly affecting adolescent females, is typically linked to hormonal imbalances and connective tissue dysplasia, leading to persistent pain and diminished quality of life, and conventional therapy methods may inadequately address these fundamental issues, resulting in restricted symptom alleviation. This research formulates a complete diagnostic paradigm that integrates hormonal measurements, physiological indicators, and pain evaluation to establish a more accurate, individualized framework for the management of juvenile dysmenorrhea. The study examines pharmacological and non-pharmacological therapeutic modalities, tailoring therapies to the unique hormonal and structural attributes of each patient. Clinical observations and data analysis indicate that personalized diagnostic and treatment strategies markedly decrease pain intensity, augment functional capacity, and boost overall well-being. This thesis provides significant insights into the biology of juvenile dysmenorrhea and proposes a practical approach to teenage gynecology that fosters successful, sustainable health solutions. The study highlights the advantages of individualized care, representing a notable progression in the treatment of juvenile dysmenorrhea and enhancing the overall domain of adolescent healthcare.
evidence_items.title: ENHANCING DIAGNOSTIC AND THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES FOR JUVENILE DYSMENORRHEA VIA DISTINCT APPROACHES

evidence_items.summary: Targeted welfare mechanisms are a significant and growing instrument of social policy in post-Soviet transitional states, yet their capacity to shift recipient populations from social dependency toward genuine social activation remains empirically underexamined and theoretically contested. This study offers an axiological evaluation of Uzbekistan's Women's Notebook (Ayollar daftari) and Youth Notebook (Yoshlar daftari) — two state-administered programs designed to register economically vulnerable women and young people and connect them with activation-oriented support. Drawing on the capabilities approach (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2011) and social activation theory (Bonoli, 2010; Peck, 2001), the study employs a cross-sectional survey design with [N] Women's Notebook recipients and [N] Youth Notebook recipients across multiple administrative regions in Uzbekistan. Findings indicate that structural facilitators — particularly access to childcare, training infrastructure, and labor market quality — are the primary predictors of activation outcomes, significantly outweighing the influence of program-specific design features. Duration of welfare enrollment does not produce cumulative activation. A substantial proportion of recipients classified as economically active are engaged in conditions of labor market precarity that the capabilities framework does not recognize as genuine activation. These results challenge the linear activation logic embedded in both notebooks' design and confirm the structural critique of activation policy advanced in the comparative literature. The study contributes the first capabilities-based axiological evaluation of targeted welfare registers in a post-Soviet Central Asian context, with direct implications for welfare program design, care infrastructure policy, and social protection reform.
evidence_items.title: THE DIALECTICS OF SOCIAL DEPENDENCY AND SOCIAL ACTIVITY: AN AXIOLOGICAL EVALUATION OF TARGETED WELFARE MECHANISMS

evidence_items.summary: Protein foundation models increasingly support the generation of novel biological sequences, yet their reliance on large public datasets creates opportunities for adversarial manipulation of the material they learn from and retrieve. We investigate two data-only poisoning attacks against protein design systems, targeting the pre-training corpus of autoregressive protein language models and the retrieval corpus of a text-guided protein generator. For the first, we pre-trained ProtGPT2 and ProGen2 variants of 300 million parameters, introducing poisoned protein sequences containing one of two triggers followed by one of three payloads. Across all poisoned runs, both architectures acquired highly reliable trigger-dependent generation under uniform and ramped poisoning schedules. Under ramped exposure, the earliest majority activation occurred after only 200 contaminated examples, while for the uniform schedule earliest activation occurred around 5000 poisoned samples. For the second attack, we inserted records into a retrieval corpus system without modifying its weights or decoding procedure. A single query-aware record captured a top-16 retrieval position for 58\% of templated requests and 97\% of free-text requests. Conditional on successful poisoned retrieval, 62\% of requests produced altered sequences, while 19-21% acquired the inserted domain by profile-HMM homology. A universal query-unaware attack using 1,500 records also achieved substantial retrieval capture and domain transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that adversarial protein sequence contributions can establish persistent, sequence-specific behaviour during pre-training or redirect protein generation at inference, while leaving ordinary model behaviour largely preserved. Our work establishes the integrity and biological provenance of protein sequence data as critical safeguards for generative protein design systems.
evidence_items.title: Poisoning the corpora of protein design systems during pre-training and retrieval

evidence_items.summary: Visible-light anti-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) detection is important for low-altitude UAV early warning by providing direct appearance and semantic cues. However, in fixed-viewpoint scenarios, UAV targets near the field-of-view (FOV) periphery often suffer from off-axis imaging degradation, which weakens local cues and hinders reliable detection. Existing approaches primarily focus on general small-target representation, whereas explicit modeling of FOV-peripheral degradation and weak-cue attenuation remains insufficient. To address this limitation, we propose WCMA-UAV, a wavelet-guided context modeling and aggregation network for fixed-viewpoint visible-light anti-UAV detection. WCMA-UAV is built around three coordinated components: the wavelet-coupled context module (WCCM), the hierarchical parallel aggregation unit (HPAU), and the progressive attention refinement head (PARH), forming a functional progression from degradation-aware feature extraction through structure-preserving aggregation to progressive refinement. Experiments on the DUT anti-UAV benchmark show that WCMA-UAV achieves the highest average precision (AP) among the compared detectors on both the official test set and the validation set, with the validation set containing a larger proportion of tiny UAV targets. These results indicate that WCMA-UAV improves weak-cue UAV detection near the FOV periphery.
evidence_items.title: Wavelet-Guided Context Modeling and Aggregation Network for Anti-UAV Detection

evidence_items.summary: Safety evaluations of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots focus on therapeutic redirection, statements urging users who disclose suicide thoughts to seek help from crisis lines or other human sources. How chatbots respond when users refuse that help is unclear. This cross-sectional audit ran 2,550 scripted multi-turn conversations in September 2026. Each conversation opened with a disclosure of suicide thoughts at 3 levels of severity, answered every referral with up to 10 standardized refusals and then changed the subject. All 2,550 conversations included a referral, 2,542 (99.7%) in the first reply. However, mean persistence ranged from 0.01 to 9.94 refusals across chatbots. Newer versions of all 5 chatbots tested in 2 versions persisted less than older versions (each P<.05). Compared with passive ideation, a disclosure of intent was associated with 1.26 more refusals sustained (95% CI, 1.06-1.46) and higher odds of renewed referral after the topic change (odds ratio, 10.07; 95% CI, 7.43-13.66). Chatbots that persisted less in referral more often presented themselves as the user's support (Spearman rho = -0.80; P<.001). Of 8,818 refusal-phase replies urging outside help, only 173 (2.0%) asked about barriers to seeking it. Chatbots uniformly recommended outside help after disclosures of suicide thoughts but varied widely in persisting in those recommendations, with newer versions persisting less. Safety evaluations should test what happens after a crisis referral is refused, not only whether one is offered.
evidence_items.title: What do AI chatbots do after users decline therapeutic redirection for suicide thoughts?

evidence_items.summary: Explaining the exceptional morphological diversity of spermatozoa remains a challenge due to the complexity and multivariate nature of evolutionary processes acting on sperm components. Identifying shifts in evolutionary trajectories across a phylogeny is a powerful approach to address this challenge. Here, we examine shifts in the tempo and mode of avian sperm macroevolution while also considering correlated evolution among sperm components. We studied 755 perching bird species (order Passeriformes). Evolutionary processes are highly heterogeneous: while the length of sperm components (head, midpiece, and flagellum) rapidly diversified in some groups, differentiation has been slow in others. In contrast to the heterogeneity in sperm length diversification, correlated evolution among the three sperm components was consistently supported throughout the tree, although the strength and direction of correlations differed among groups. Parvorder Passerida stands out for its long flagella and midpieces and particularly strong evolutionary correlations between these components. The striking differences in evolutionary pattern among groups may reflect changes in genomic architecture, sperm physiology, and/or selective pressures across groups. By identifying groups with divergent evolutionary processes, this work provides an important advance to better understand the causes of variation in sperm length and sperm diversification across clades. This dataset includes our files for tree-building, the sperm dataset we compiled, and the full output from the best-fit model. Additional background information is available in the supplementary data accompanying the paper.
evidence_items.title: Data from: High heterogeneity in macroevolutionary dynamics of sperm components in perching birds

evidence_items.summary: The built environment accounts for nearly one-third of global energy demand, underscoring the need to enhance building performance through strategies that integrate both technological solutions and human factors. Occupants play a pivotal role in this process, as their comfort and well-being are shaped by complex interactions across multiple environmental domains. This study investigates cross-domain effects between thermal and acoustic environments, with a specific focus on how personality traits modulate perceptual responses. An experimental campaign was conducted in a controlled test room under two thermal conditions: a neutral phase (21 °C) and a mild discomfort phase (23 °C). In each phase, 25 participants evaluated seven soundscapes with distinct acoustic characteristics, ranging from natural to anthropogenic. Continuous monitoring of environmental parameters ensured accurate boundary conditions, while personality traits were assessed to capture inter-individual variability. Results show that even slight thermal variations influence acoustic perception, producing systematic negative shifts in the evaluation of the main soundscape’s descriptors across phases. Cluster analysis of personality traits identified two groups: one with higher emotional stability and openness, and another with stronger neurotic tendencies. These groups exhibited divergent perceptual patterns, with neurotic individuals reporting greater sensitivity to anthropic and chaotic soundscapes, and emotionally stable participants showing stronger appreciation for natural ones. Overall, the findings demonstrate that occupant perception cannot be understood through single-domain analyses alone. Integrating cross-domain interactions and personality-driven variability into adaptive comfort models and occupant-centric design strategies is essential to support buildings that are both energy-efficient and responsive to human diversity.
evidence_items.title: The role of personality in multi-domain environmental perception: An occupant-centric approach

evidence_items.summary: This report proposes an interoperability framework to support the discovery, access and integration of biodiversity monitoring data across Europe. The framework draws on a review of existing interoperability approaches and two expert workshops involving biodiversity research infrastructures and national and subnational monitoring organisations. It builds particularly on the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC) and the Cross-Domain Interoperability Framework (CDIF), supporting the implementation of the FAIR principles. The report covers data models, vocabularies and formats, metadata, persistent identifiers, and application programming interfaces (APIs). It includes technical examples, references to relevant standards and services, and an assessment of implementation difficulty. Combining general principles with practical steps, the framework sets out 24 recommendations and proposes a progressive implementation, starting with improvements to dataset discoverability and moving towards more automated access and data integration. It is intended to evolve through implementation experience and changes in standards and technologies.
evidence_items.title: An interoperability framework for biodiversity monitoring in Europe

evidence_items.summary: The need to turn locally available residues into practical engineering materials has raised interest in agro-wastes as potential components of non-asbestos automotive brake pads. This study examined the physicochemical properties of sawdust from Nigeria's Lagos, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti, and Oyo States as a potential filler source for later brake pad development. After cleaning, drying, mechanical reduction, and sieving, the samples underwent alkaline treatment with 3 M NaOH at a solid-to-solution ratio of 1:20 for about 18 hours under standard laboratory conditions. We used X-ray fluorescence (XRF) to measure elemental composition and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) to analyze surface morphology. XRF screening detected Mg, Al, Si, P, S, K, Fe, Ni, Pb, W, Sn, Sb, Rb, Nb, and Mo in varying amounts. For instance, the untreated Lagos sample had instrument-reported values of 10.0913 for Mg, 0.2473 for Si, and 0.1749 for P. Under the analytical conditions used, we found neither arsenic nor chromium. SEM revealed variations in surface morphology and fiber exposure between sources, with Lagos showing relatively uniform fibrous characteristics and little discernible change following treatment. Because of prior research on its use as an agro-waste component in asbestos-free brake materials, palm kernel shell (PKS) from Ilara-Mokin, Ondo State, was used as a physicochemical benchmark. Therefore, rather than statistical superiority, we chose Lagos sawdust for further consideration based on its relatively uniform morphology and elemental profile close to the PKS reference. This descriptive material-screening study did not include brake pad manufacturing or mechanical, thermal, and tribological testing. Therefore, rather than establishing braking performance, the findings provide preliminary evidence for material selection.
evidence_items.title: Assessment of Nigerian Sawdust as a Potential Agro-Waste Filler For Non-Asbestos Automotive Brake Pads
