evidence_items.summary: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are persistent contaminants detected in groundwater at closed municipal landfills in rural Minnesota, where legacy waste continues to release PFASs decades after closure. In this setting, contaminated groundwater used for irrigation creates a direct pathway for PFAS transfer into the food supply. This study evaluates remediation at the groundwater–irrigation interface through a unified techno-economic assessment comparing granular activated carbon (GAC) adsorption and phytoremediation with Festuca rubra (F. rubra). Design influent concentrations were set at the 90th percentile (P90) of five representative PFASs measured in rural Minnesota landfill groundwater. Adsorption was simulated using a pore and surface diffusion model for single-bed and lead–lag configurations under fouling and non-fouling conditions. Phytoremediation was modeled using three complementary scenarios: a greenhouse-derived upper bound, a bioconcentration factor (BCF)-derived mechanistic case, and a decomposed scaling formulation. Unit costs were anchored to Minnesota Pollution Control Agency 2023 guidance and University of Minnesota (UMN) Extension data. Adsorption achieved compliance within weeks at $5.24–$8.00 m−3; phytoremediation showed lower per-volume cost ($0.43 m−3) but required centuries to multi-millennial timescales for long-chain PFASs. Cumulative cost was dominated by treatment duration rather than per-volume intensity, with adsorption more cost-effective when compliance timeframes are constrained. These findings highlight that remediation feasibility depends on alignment between treatment timescale and risk-management objectives rather than levelized cost alone.
evidence_items.title: Techno-Economic Assessment of Treatment Methods to Remediate PFAS Contamination in Leachate of Closed Landfills in Rural Minnesota

evidence_items.summary: Virtual reality enables studying active visual search and gaze behavior under naturalistic, free-viewing conditions while preserving experimental control. However, free head-eye coordination, extended 3D space, dynamic target trajectories, and headset-specific field of view and eye-tracking constraints mean that findings from traditional 2D paradigms cannot be assumed to generalize to immersive environments. Interpreting gaze-based outcomes in VR requires bench-marks that establish how basic target properties influence detection. We used target eccentricity, size, and speed as benchmark predictors of visual detection in an immersive VR coin-foraging task. Using in-headset eye-tracking, participants guided a gaze-controlled avatar to collect coins that varied in gaze-relative eccentricity, size, and speed. We modeled gaze-based observation probability, observation latency, dwell time, gaze-coin angular distance, and saccade dynamics. Observation probability was analyzed using mixed-effects logistic regression, whereas latency was analyzed with a censoring-aware Cox framework that retained never-detected coins. Eccen-tricity and size showed the clearest benchmark effects. Peripheral and small coins were less like-ly to be detected. Speed’s role was more nuanced. Although slow coins were detected more of-ten in a binary model, this advantage did not persist in a censoring-aware survival analysis, suggesting that speed influenced the opportunity for observation more than momentary salience. Consistent with this interpretation, slow coins produced longer dwell times, and gaze-coin an-gular distance and saccade measures indicated that target properties shaped both the geometry and effort for acquisition. These findings establish a feature-based benchmark for gaze-based de-tection in immersive visual search and demonstrate the importance of modeling missed targets as censored detection opportunities.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark for Gaze-Based Target Detection in Immersive Virtual Reality: Effects of Eccentricity, Size, and Speed on Observation and Detection Dynamics

organizations: SEIHWAN Inc.
evidence_items.summary: ReaxFF reactive molecular dynamics (MD) is increasingly used to study organic peroxide decomposition, although the parameter sets supplied with common MD codes were developed for other chemistries. We benchmarked the six C/H/O ReaxFF parameter sets distributed with LAMMPS against CBS-APNO O–O bond dissociation enthalpies (BDEs) of 13 peroxides and tested whether the static error carries over to the kinetics. All six sets underestimate the O–O BDE (mean signed errors of −11.9 to −30.5 kcal mol-1) and correlate only weakly with the references (r = 0.14–0.50). The newer CHO-2016 set (not distributed with LAMMPS) gives −19.5 kcal mol-1, whereas the same protocol yields 85–90 kcal mol-1 for the ethane C–C bond (experiment, about 90 kcal mol-1). The errors increase with alkyl and acyl substitution. For di-tert-butyl peroxide (DTBP), the sets predict 0.4–16.7 instead of 42.4 kcal mol-1, four of them stretch the O–O bond to 1.68–1.76 Å, and a fifth breaks it. Isothermal MD of DTBP at 575–1480 K with three sets gave activation energies of 45.0–76.5 kJ mol-1, consistent with each set’s static BDE (48.7–69.9 kJ mol-1) but 2.0–3.4 times lower than the experimental 153 kJ mol-1. At 121 °C, the extrapolated rate constants exceed manufacturer data by factors of 3.4 × 108 to 5.0 × 1012, and the predicted 10 h half-life temperatures (−147 to −59 °C) lie 180–270 °C below the measured 121 °C. Calculating the O–O BDE of the target peroxide is therefore a simple but necessary check before using a ReaxFF parameter set for hazard assessment.
evidence_items.title: Off-the-Shelf ReaxFF Parameter Sets Underestimate O–O Bond Strengths in Organic Peroxides: A Static and Kinetic Benchmark for Thermal-Hazard Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Visual generation is becoming a general component of AI infrastructure, supporting content creation across design, entertainment, education, science, and industry. Generative and multimodal models have substantially improved single-pass synthesis. At the same time, multi-step visual creation requires spatial precision, identity persistence, temporal coherence, editable structure, factual fidelity, and physical plausibility throughout the creation process. Errors in intermediate artifacts can propagate across subsequent steps, making creation control a central requirement. Model scaling, prompt refinement, additional conditioning, and repeated sampling improve individual outputs; coordinating these capabilities across a task requires runtime evidence to influence subsequent creation decisions. Within AI-generated content (AIGC), we use Agentic AIGC to describe goal-driven content creation organized through a multi-step control loop. This survey focuses on visual generation agents: systems that use runtime evidence from evolving visual artifacts, task environments, and interaction histories to change later creation-relevant action selection or parameterization, including generation, editing, verification, recovery, replanning, and stopping. The defining behavioral property is therefore an observation--action dependency: runtime observations change later action selection. Whether those decisions improve task or constraint outcomes is evaluated separately with matched tools and resource budgets. We organize this emerging field around the control mechanisms and behavioral evidence that connect generative capabilities to autonomous visual creation. Specifically, we formalize this boundary and characterize autonomy through five cumulative levels (L1--L5).
evidence_items.title: Agentic AIGC: A Survey of Visual Generation Agents

evidence_items.summary: On-screen text can describe what a video shows, or it can frame what the video is supposed to mean. Current benchmarks treat both alike, testing whether a model can read the text rather than whether it should trust it. We study claim deference, multimodal large language models'tendency to let an on-screen claim override conflicting visual evidence. We introduce VisualTrust, a counterfactual benchmark with 5,063 cases across 14 claim-fact classes. Each case pairs a question with three versions of the same video: one with no claim, one with an accurate claim, and one with a misleading claim that alters a single grounded fact. The option the misleading claim supports is the trap answer. Across seven open-weight and four proprietary models, mean accuracy falls from 90.1% without a claim to 51.9% with a misleading claim. Among initially correct responses, 42.8% flip to the trap answer and only 0.6% become other errors. Strong no-claim accuracy does not ensure resistance. We also introduce DEAR (Decoupled Evidence Arbitration and Reading), a training-free agent for video question answering that separates evidence arbitration from reading. An independent check reports conflicting evidence, a selector weighs it without a fixed modality priority and blinds what it withholds, and the reader answers from the resulting video in a fresh context. On 500 videos across three proprietary models, DEAR raises accuracy under misleading claims from 47.2--64.0% to 81.8--85.2% and reduces trap-answer selection from 34.4--50.8% to 11.6--15.0%, while preserving no-claim accuracy.
evidence_items.title: VisualTrust: Video Reasoning under On-Screen Claim Framing

evidence_items.summary: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.
evidence_items.title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Language models are often asked to make judgments: whether a proposed answer is correct, whether one statement follows logically from another, or whether a response is safe. Yet changing the instructions that specify how the judgment should be expressed can make the final answer less reliable, even for the same input. We ask whether this reflects a change in internal judgment or a failure to express it. Comparing hidden-state vectors for the same input under different instructions, we find that their differences concentrate in a low-dimensional expression subspace. We identify this subspace without benchmark labels and remove its contribution from a linear predictor to obtain an isolated judgment. Across correctness, entailment, and safety, the isolated judgment remains reliable under instructions not used to identify the subspace, even when the model's final answer and the original predictor degrade. When the judgment question is negated, isolation raises the predictor's AUROC from 0.504 to 0.825 for entailment and from 0.480 to 0.891 for safety. We also find that judgment is readable in earlier layers, before the expression subspace begins to disrupt the predictor. Together, these results provide a way to separate judgment from expression and recover internal judgments even when the model's final answers are unreliable.
evidence_items.title: Isolating a Language Model's Judgment with a Label-Free Subspace

evidence_items.summary: This study examines the use of machine learning for predicting default risk within the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) 7(a) loan program using publicly available loan-level data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). Using 488,772 resolved loans originated over fifteen fiscal years from FY2010 through FY2024, the study compares a traditional logistic regression benchmark with Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and an ensemble model. Gradient Boosting produces the strongest out-of-time predictive performance, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.9178 compared with 0.7641 for the logistic regression benchmark, representing a 20.1% relative improvement. The model also reduces the Brier Score by 44.5%, indicating substantially more accurate probability forecasts. Loan term, initial interest rate, and the SBA guarantee ratio emerge as important predictors of default. Default outcomes also vary considerably across industries, with Transportation (9.84%), Arts and Entertainment (9.70%), and Wholesale Trade (8.52%) exhibiting the highest default rates, while Agriculture (4.09%), Finance and Insurance (4.60%), and Healthcare (4.81%) exhibit the lowest. Across the study period, among the resolved-loan sample has an overall default rate of 7.47%, with annual rates ranging from 5.48% in FY2013 to 16.27% in FY2023. The findings demonstrate the potential value of machine learning for credit risk prediction in government-guaranteed small business lending while highlighting the importance of out-of-time model validation. More broadly, the study provides evidence relevant to SBA policymakers, participating lenders, and the responsible development of AI-assisted credit risk assessment tools for small business lending.
evidence_items.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Credit Decisions? Evidence from Large-Scale Lending Data

evidence_items.summary: An ensemble of language models is a jury, not an electorate. The answers are testimony from witnesses of unknown reliability, and the question is not what the majority said but who is credible. Most ensemble methods assign each expert a fixed reputation, often learned from labels. We ask whether it can instead be inferred from the pattern of agreement and disagreement among the experts. We model the experts as a jury: each question has a latent true answer, each expert reports it with unknown reliability, and those reliabilities are estimated by Expectation Maximisation (EM) from unlabelled answer configurations alone. We show that its decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts'answer distributions. What changes is not how the jury votes, but how it learns whom to trust. On a 1560-question benchmark, the jury, with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. Instead, it outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark.
evidence_items.title: A Jury, Not an Electorate: Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Ensembles of Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.
evidence_items.title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an empirical study of a multi-persona large language model (LLM) consensus architecture deployed in a live retail FinTech platform for equity and options trade signal generation. Grounded in a prior quantitative trading framework (Anton, 2025) and building upon academic antecedents in multi-agent LLM systems (Xiao et al., 2024), the Edge Stack Trading platform deploys a six-persona AI analyst panel producing structured, constrained verdicts across a real-time multi-signal scoring architecture. Analysis of nine live trade reports generated between April and May 2026 reports a preliminary 87.5% directional accuracy rate across eight assessable signals in an exploratory proof-of-concept evaluation, with unanimous panel consensus strongly correlated with system confidence extremes. Inter-model disagreement functions as an auditable risk signal, and model API failures produce identifiable, recoverable degradation patterns consistent with graceful degradation requirements for financial AI systems. The architecture addresses the 2026 conference theme of Reliable and Deterministic AI for Financial Systems through structured verdict formats, role-constrained persona prompting, and explicit multi-signal deterministic scoring as mechanisms for AI governance in retail financial decision support. One incorrect signal (Palantir) reveals a boundary condition in which extreme valuation risk overrides technical alignment, informing a specific architectural recommendation. Implications for HBCU financial technology education, democratized institutional-grade AI analysis, and regulatory auditability are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Ensemble LLM Consensus Architectures for Deterministic Trade Signal Generation: An Empirical Study of Multi-Persona AI Panels in Retail FinTech Applications

evidence_items.summary: Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to assess large language model (LLM) outputs by decomposing quality into multiple criteria and assigning each a binary judgment from an LLM verifier. However, judgment certainty varies substantially across criteria. Existing methods uniformly aggregate these judgments into a final score, implicitly treating every criterion as equally certain and overlooking this heterogeneity. As a result, uncertain judgments remain incorporated into reward estimation without distinction, potentially yielding misleading training signals for downstream reinforcement learning (RL). To address this limitation, we propose Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level judgment uncertainty via conformal calibration. Specifically, URW elicits a soft uncertainty signal from a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates and converts it into a per-criterion weight using split-conformal $p$-values with provable coverage guarantees. Extensive experiments demonstrate that URW consistently improves pairwise preference accuracy and delivers stronger downstream RL alignment.
evidence_items.title: Rubric Judgments Lack Uncertainty: Conformal Weighting for LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Agent memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to reuse past experiences without updating their parameters. However, semantic similarity alone does not guarantee memory usefulness: downstream performance depends on how memories are selected and presented to the agent. We propose MemComposer, a memory composer that jointly examines the current query and retrieved candidates to decide which experiences to include, how many to select, and how to order them. We train the composer using Experience Policy Optimization (ExPO), a GRPO-based framework that evaluates assembled memory contexts through complete agent interactions and uses task-success feedback to optimize the assembly policy. Across three $\tau^2$-bench domains with two frozen executors, MemComposer outperforms the strongest baseline for each executor while reducing average memory-token usage by 16.9% and 4.9%, respectively. The learned policy also transfers to unseen domains, executors, and memory banks, and benefits from memories generated by stronger models without further training. These results demonstrate the value of learning query-specific memory assembly using downstream task feedback.
evidence_items.title: MemComposer: Learning to Assemble Memories for LLM Agents via Reinforcement Learning

evidence_items.summary: Contribution guidelines help newcomers participate in open-source software projects, yet often contain incomplete or outdated information. Existing studies characterize newcomers'information needs and documentation gaps, but revising these guidelines requires recovering and validating project-specific knowledge from scattered sources. We present ContribAlign, a framework for automatically revising CONTRIBUTING files through category-guided evidence integration. A qualitative analysis yields a taxonomy of 30 fine-grained guidance types across six contribution categories. ContribAlign uses a classifier to diagnose coverage of the six categories in the original guidance, then uses the taxonomy to collect and organize project-specific evidence. It filters detected conflicts and uses a large language model to generate category-level revisions. The classifier achieves a weighted F1 score of 0.764, improving on the existing classifier by 0.156, while the verifier detects factual conflicts with 97.3% precision and 91.5% estimated recall. Human evaluation shows that ContribAlign achieves the highest overall quality among the original guidelines and three baselines, with significant improvements in usefulness, beginner-friendliness, and completeness. These results suggest that ContribAlign can help maintain more accurate and useful contribution guidelines.
evidence_items.title: When CONTRIBUTING Files Fall Short: Revising OSS Contribution Guidelines with Repository Evidence

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-guided Bayesian optimization (BO) uses past observations to guide search, but proposed directions and their revision can remain implicit. We propose Feedback-Guided Search State (FGSS), a structured hypothesis-management interface connecting language-based guidance to observed evidence, executable parameter interventions, and comparative support updates. An LLM reflector proposes and revises hypotheses; a deterministic curator validates them and maintains identities and test records. The evolving state guides candidate construction and priorities. Instantiated on LLAMBO, FGSS-BO retains its surrogate and default expected improvement selection, with a bounded testing policy. On two retrospective protocol/media tasks with nearest-neighbor response oracles, it attains higher sample mean final best and search AUC than the matched LLAMBO baseline and evaluated non-LLM baselines. Prose-reflection and EI-only controls show mixed component effects. Six direct-training hyperparameter-optimization tasks show task-dependent transfer, strongest on diabetes SVM; exact-grid and reaction controls examine other settings. FGSS exposes hypotheses, their execution, and cross-round revisions for inspection while supporting search gains in selected settings.
evidence_items.title: FGSS-BO: Feedback-Guided Hypothesis Management for LLM-Based Bayesian Optimization
An evaluation guided multiagent framework for generating floor plans that comply with municipal building regulations

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-turn interactions that require maintaining latent conversational states, not only explicit facts. We study affective state as an implicit state inferred from sparse contextual cues that remain relevant after topic shifts, and ask whether LLMs expose internal attention signals for routing such evidence at inference time. Prior attention interventions rely on labeled in-domain head profiles and externally specified target spans, limiting transfer across affective-evidence distributions. We propose Self-targeted Internal Attention Boosting (SIAB), which localizes sparse affective heads via causal localization (in detail activation patching) on synthetic minimal pairs and boosts, at the answer position, the content tokens these heads already attend to; both edited heads and target tokens are derived from the model's own behavior, enabling the same head set to be reused across tasks.We evaluate on ECC and GoEmotions across three LLMs and multiple prompting settings. Across settings, SIAB improves prompt-matched baselines by up to +10.3 macro-F1 on ECC and +5.5 on GoEmotions. Combined with PASTA-style external supervision, it achieves up to +13.84 accuracy points and +12.51 macro-F1 points, while mechanistic analyses trace the gains to sparse, emotion-enriched heads and show that layer proximity affects additivity.
evidence_items.title: Emotion Is Not External Knowledge: Internal Attention Signals for Affective State Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent reasoning with large language models (LLMs) raises a central question for collective decision-making: when agents disagree, whose decision should be trusted? Resolving such disagreements is difficult because agents'decisions are susceptible to non-semantic biases such as majority pressure and response-style preferences, which can obscure the quality of the underlying reasoning. Our analysis shows how bias can be both mitigated and exploited: bias control improves initial answer selection, while bias injection elicits decision instability that serves as a reliability signal. Building on these findings, we introduce a test-time aggregation framework that requires neither validation data nor prior knowledge of relative model strength. The framework implements bias control by presenting one style-normalized reasoning trace per distinct answer, and bias injection by placing each aggregating agent's initially selected answer in the minority. Overall, our framework achieves higher average accuracy and better token efficiency than competing non-oracle aggregation methods across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and four heterogeneous LLM combinations. It also improves final-answer accuracy when applied to multi-agent debate and Mixture-of-Agents, without modifying their interaction or synthesis processes.
evidence_items.title: Bias Control and Injection for Multi-Agent Aggregation

evidence_items.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but prompt transformations designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them. A feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur, and even a recurring change need not affect a downstream computation. We introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), which identifies large feature responses that recur in a consistent direction, and evaluate the resulting supports on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, the tested prompt transformations produce a reproducible redistribution profile on these excluded variants. We then separate recurring representation change from signed readout contribution and decision failure. For a fixed linear readout, an exact decomposition shows how response magnitude, readout coefficients, directional alignment, and the clean margin determine downstream consequences. In two frozen safety readouts, combining RSS support erosion with the full clean margin yields recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958 using median supports of 20 and 19 features, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion. RSS therefore provides a way to identify recurring sparse representation changes and quantify their contribution to a downstream readout without equating representation change with failure. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score
evidence_items.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders

evidence_items.summary:
This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and implementation outcomes of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted screening tools for depression and anxiety in primary care settings, with a focus on literature published since the advent of advanced large language models. A systematic search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Cochrane Central from January 2020 to September 2025. Ten studies met the inclusion criteria, comprising randomized controlled trials, pragmatic trials, and validation studies. Included studies demonstrated that AI-assisted tools (including conversational chatbots, machine learning models using voice and behavioral data, and digital decision-support systems) can achieve high diagnostic accuracy, with balanced accuracy up to 88.2% and Area Under the Curve (AUC) up to 0.82. Clinically, AI-assisted interventions were associated with higher depression remission (e.g., 27.3% vs. 12.0%) and better anxiety outcomes than treatment-as-usual in individual trials. Feasibility and acceptability were generally favorable, with completion rates often exceeding 60-70% and user satisfaction reaching 79%, even among older adults. Key challenges included limited external validation, demographic homogeneity, and insufficient reporting on ethical safeguards.
AI-assisted screening tools show potential to improve the detection and management of depression and anxiety in primary care, with encouraging accuracy, clinical effectiveness, and user engagement in the available studies. However, the evidence base is small and heterogeneous, and future research needs to address gaps in generalizability, long-term efficacy, ethical oversight, and seamless workflow integration to ensure equitable and responsible implementation.
evidence_items.title: Effectiveness of AI-Assisted Screening Tools for Depression and Anxiety in Primary Care: A Systematic Review

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used upstream of decision-making to clean data, detect label errors, and reconstruct missing values. Yet LLM-assisted data curation creates a new operational tradeoff: higher-fidelity models and richer prompts can be substantially more expensive, while the value of this additional fidelity depends on the downstream optimization accuracy. This raises the central question of this work: when should one pay for a better LLM, given a specific downstream task at hand? We study this question through stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, which can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance. We develop two cost-aware algorithmic frameworks that allow adaptive switching between stochastic oracles. With known bias, the first meta-algorithm applies a restarted, cost-aware policy that adaptively selects oracle fidelity across optimization stages. Its cumulative cost is no larger than that of the best fixed oracle in hindsight and can be substantially smaller. With unknown bias, we develop a budgeted certification scheme that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to certify the optimization progress and eliminate unsuccessful oracle sources, and show an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources. We provide concrete realizations of these meta-algorithms by applying biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments illustrate the qualitative switching behavior predicted by the theory: the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy.
evidence_items.title: When is a better LLM worth paying for? Stochastic Optimization with Switching Mixed-Fidelity Oracles

evidence_items.summary: As large language models become increasingly capable of generating, and assisting with, scientific writing, there is a need for greater transparency and disclosure around the use of AI in research. Consequently, a veritable subfield of research and a number of commercial services aim to flag AI-generated content automatically. However, existing detectors which rely only on text extracted from PDFs fail to benefit from the rich visual information contained in the formatting of math-heavy scientific content. To study this, we select human-written proof and prose passages from pre-2022 arXiv LaTeX sources and re-generate them using 15 modern LLMs within the context of the same paper. This leaves us with coupled human and AI outputs in three different representations: the LaTeX source, a rendered image of the PDF, and the text extracted from the PDF. We find that the accuracy of the state-of-the-art Pangram 4 drops significantly as the mathematical content in a passage increases, especially when evaluated on text as opposed to LaTeX. However, this is not an inherent limitation of detecting AI-generated math: finetuning Qwen-3.5-27B based detectors on this domain recovers the gap, with LaTeX inputs performing significantly better than text since they preserve more formatting information. Since LaTeX sources are rarely available in practice, we also train SnapJudge: an image-based detector operating on screenshots of both prose and proofs from papers. At 0.1% false positive rate, SnapJudge achieves a detection rate of 92% on proofs and 93% on prose generated by frontier models, substantially outperforming both Pangram 4 and our text-based detector. We release our data, models and code at https://nlplab.cs.duke.edu/snapjudge.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal AI Detection for Math-Heavy Scientific Text

evidence_items.summary: A coding agent works on repositories that can be far larger than its context window can hold. Prompt compressors and retrievers offer solutions to this problem, but patching an issue needs two things at once: the files that must change, and their code exactly as written, since the model must reproduce the lines it edits. Retrievers rank code by its similarity to the issue rather than by whether it must change, and compressors delete text to fit the budget. We show that at an equal token budget, an agent resolves more issues when the budget goes to choosing which files to show verbatim, as our simple selector CQ2-CARE does, than when it goes to pruning tokens or retrieving chunks. We fit every context to the same per-issue budget on 300 recent SWE-rebench issues and grade each patch with the benchmark's tests. With GPT-5.6 and Claude Opus 5, CQ2-CARE resolves 43.7% and 46.7% of the issues, 6.3 points more than the best of three compressors with either model, and 9.3 and 12.7 points more than the best of three retrievers. CQ2-CARE even resolves more issues than two methods trained for issue resolution, SweRank (by 0.7 and 1.7 points) and SWE-Pruner (by 2.0 and 7.3). Our analysis shows the defects of the baseline methods: retrievers often miss the files to edit, and compressors keep them but alter their text, so fewer patches apply. Exact-file selection needs no compression model and shows every line as the repository has it, so the model can quote the code it edits.
evidence_items.title: Skip the Compressor: Coding Agents Fix More Issues When They Pick Whole Files

evidence_items.summary: Cybersecurity interviews uncover critical security experiences, behaviors, and privacy concerns often not fully captured by conventional technical assessments. Consequently, identifying genuine self-disclosures is challenging because statements are context-dependent, categories overlap, and automated interpretations may introduce unsupported claims. Locally deployed Small Language Models (SLMs) protect sensitive participant data by keeping processing within controlled environments, but their limited reasoning capabilities make simple prompting insufficient for context-aware and factually reliable analysis. This study developed CARE-SD (Context-Adaptive Reasoning and Explanation for Self-Disclosure), a novel four-module architecture integrating context-adaptive processing, hierarchical disclosure reasoning, explanation-consistency verification, and cross-batch reconciliation. We evaluated three local SLMs, including Llama 1B, Qwen 1.5B, and Llama 3B, using 82 independently annotated cybersecurity interviews across five organizational sectors. Comparisons included conventional classifiers, three prompting strategies, larger 8B--32B models, and architectural ablations. Two independent reviewers assessed disclosure labels, factual claims, and explanation correctness. CARE-SD improved the accuracy and evidence reliability of SLMs, increasing Llama 3B Macro-F1 from 0.80 to 0.88 while reducing unsupported claims by 60\%. Remarkably, the 3B model matched the 20B reference model in category Macro-F1, demonstrating the effectiveness of the architecture without requiring a larger model.
evidence_items.title: CARE-SD: Explainable Reasoning Architecture for Local SLM Self-Disclosure Analysis in Textual Data

evidence_items.summary: The convergence of blockchain, financial technology, digital assets, and generative artificial intelligence creates important opportunities and challenges for undergraduate education, especially at Historically Black Colleges and Universities. Students preparing for careers in business, computing, analytics, cybersecurity, and financial services need more than exposure to emerging technologies; they also need confidence, collaboration skills, ethical awareness, computational fluency, and experience applying tools to realistic problems. This paper proposes a human-centered pedagogical framework to engage HBCU students in active learning about blockchain, FinTech, and generative AI. The framework synthesizes classroom-tested strategies from computer information systems, business analytics, programming, mathematics, and interdisciplinary student research. It emphasizes structured collaboration, low-stakes practice, role rotation, peer evaluation, reflective learning, responsible use of generative AI, reproducible computational notebooks, and applied problem contexts such as credit risk, fraud detection, investment analysis, digital trust, and smart financial systems. The paper presents an evidence-informed model that instructors can adapt across introductory and advanced undergraduate courses. The framework suggests that active, collaborative, and AI-supported pedagogy can increase student participation, reduce anxiety around technical topics, support inclusive learning, and strengthen workforce readiness for emerging blockchain and FinTech ecosystems.
evidence_items.title: Engaging HBCU Students in Active Learning for Blockchain, FinTech, and Generative AI: A Human-Centered Pedagogical Framework

evidence_items.summary: The rapid expansion of blockchain technology and digital asset markets has increased the demand for intelligent tools capable of evaluating cryptocurrency performance using real-time financial data. As cryptocurrency markets become more dynamic and interconnected, investors, researchers, and financial technology practitioners require timely, data-driven insights to support informed investment decisions (Lazea et al., 2026). While numerous market platforms provide real-time price information, relatively few integrate live market data, technical analysis, artificial intelligence (AI), and comparative analytics within a unified decision-support environment. The study demonstrates how integrating live market data, technical analysis, and AI-driven analytics within a browser-based platform enables transparent and efficient comparative evaluation of leading cryptocurrency assets. The proposed framework provides a practical approach for assessing digital asset performance and supports investment decision-making while offering a scalable foundation for future research involving alternative cryptocurrencies, sector-specific digital assets, and extended market periods.
evidence_items.title: AI-Powered Comparative Analysis of the Top Five Cryptocurrency Assets Using Real-Time Market Data

evidence_items.summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into financial technology (FinTech) has transformed the delivery of banking, lending, and financial management services across the global economy. For underserved communities, including low-income and historically marginalized populations, AI-powered financial systems present both significant opportunities and emerging risks. This paper examines how AI-driven FinTech applications can expand financial inclusion by increasing access to digital banking, personalized financial education, automated credit assessment, fraud detection, and alternative lending solutions. The study also explores how data analytics and machine learning models are reshaping financial decision- making processes within decentralized and technology-driven financial ecosystems. Despite these advancements, concerns remain regarding algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital literacy gaps, and unequal access to technological infrastructure. AI systems trained on historically biased financial data may unintentionally reinforce discriminatory lending patterns and economic disparities, particularly among underserved populations. Additionally, the increasing dependence on automated financial systems raises questions surrounding transparency, accountability, and regulatory oversight within emerging financial technologies. Using a qualitative analysis of existing literature, industry reports, and current FinTech case studies, this paper evaluates both the benefits and challenges of AI adoption in financial services. The findings suggest that while AI has the potential to promote greater economic participation and financial accessibility, ethical implementation, deterministic AI frameworks, and inclusive regulatory policies are necessary to ensure equitable outcomes. This research contributes to ongoing discussions regarding the societal implications of AI-driven financial innovation and the future of inclusive digital finance.
evidence_items.title: Financial Inclusion in the Age of AI: Opportunities and Risks for Underserved Communities

evidence_items.summary: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.
evidence_items.title: Frame Evidence:A Benchmark for Reference Frames and Visual Evidence in Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.
evidence_items.title: TacClaw-Infinity: A Large-Scale Vision-Tactile-Language-Action Dataset for Dexterous Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.
evidence_items.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling

evidence_items.summary: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.
evidence_items.title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization

evidence_items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) struggle to parse paralinguistics (e.g., emotion, pace, pitch) in speech that combines intense emotion with complex acoustic environments. Strengthening this ability calls for training data that reflects such conditions. However, existing corpora rely heavily on studio-recorded speech, offering limited emotional and acoustic diversity. To address this gap, we introduce TVPara, a paralinguistic captioning dataset built from TV series. Speech in TV series often carries diverse emotional expression and co-occurs with scene-specific background sound, providing expressive emotion and complex acoustic environments at scale. Constructed via LALM pre-annotation and human correction, TVPara includes two tasks: Single-Utterance (~492h) and Multi-Utterance (~213h) Paralinguistic Captioning. Fine-tuning open-source LALMs on TVPara yields an average relative improvement of 31.26% in paralinguistic understanding under complex acoustic environments. The gains further generalize to an unseen TV series and to cleaner, cross-domain speech.
evidence_items.title: TVPara: Paralinguistic Captioning of Expressive TV-Series Speech in Complex Acoustic Environments
