evidence_items.summary: Humans interpret multimodal observations of the world and forecast how it will evolve. Recent multimodal generative systems have demonstrated similar capabilities: they can integrate multimodal context and synthesize visual outputs that depict changes in the world. To characterize this emerging trajectory, we organize model capabilities into a four-level hierarchy and discover that higher-level tasks remain relatively underexplored despite model progress. To bridge this gap, we explore model performance on multi-step world state prediction, a high-level task that requires models to forecast successive future world states from multimodal observations and diverse references. Such a task requires models to possess entangled understanding and generation capabilities, as well as extensive world knowledge to translate human action sequences, physical transformations, and abstract visual reasoning into coherent visual outputs. We introduce WorldCast, a benchmark comprising 320 manually designed cases across eight categories, and evaluate 12 representative models. The conducted experiments yield three key insights: (a) advances in frontier models are rapidly pushing the boundaries of intelligent world modeling, with the GPT-Image-2.5 System scoring 72.8 and demonstrating early-stage visual state prediction capabilities on real-world tasks; (b) WorldCast reveals substantial gaps between models: even Nano Banana Pro reaches only 42.8 and the best open-source model scores 20.1, with deficits in handling complex context, entangled references, and reasoning-heavy tasks; (c) strong generative models effectively draw on the capabilities of their underlying language models. These findings highlight the need for multimodal generative models that are capable of dynamic planning and reasoning while also being deeply unified to faithfully simulate real-world states.
evidence_items.title: WorldCast: Exploring Intelligent Visual Generation in World State Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4% vs. 10.9%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
evidence_items.title: RoTA-Bench: Evaluating 3D Spatial Reasoning through Interactive Projection Alignment

evidence_items.summary: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high-quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/
evidence_items.title: InfiniSplat v2: Analyzing and Improving Feed-Forward 3DGS from Any Views

evidence_items.summary: Pretrained unimodal models offer a flexible route to multimodal prediction through collaboration, but this collaboration can become less accurate than a surviving unimodal model when modalities are missing. We study this setting using fixed surviving-model anchors and find that collaborative gains can weaken or reverse as inputs disappear, even when the anchor's own input is unchanged. Our diagnostics further reveal reduced recovery of modality-specific information after aggregation and state-dependent collaborative representations. We propose Lluna, which combines a direct private prediction path from adapted unimodal features with a common graph-based collaboration branch that provides a residual correction. Progressive Collaboration Consistency organizes richer-to-poorer guidance along single-modality removals, aligning normalized common representations while task supervision adapts predictions to the available evidence. Across eight datasets spanning affective computing, scene understanding, and medical prediction, Lluna achieves the best evaluated average performance over non-full input states, improving Mean-Missing by 4.26\% on average relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. The fixed-anchor diagnostic also shows positive gains in mean collaboration under minimal inputs on all eight tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/AIFrontierLab/Lluna.
evidence_items.title: Lluna: Collaborative Unimodal Models for Missing-Modality Inference

evidence_items.summary: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.
evidence_items.title: VASPO: Self-Distillation with Privileged Value Estimation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents accomplish complex tasks through multi-turn interactions with external tools. However, malicious content embedded in user queries, tool descriptions, or environment observations can manipulate their decisions and induce unsafe actions. Adversarial co-evolution has emerged as an effective approach to strengthening LLM safety, but existing work primarily focuses on language-level safety or indirect prompt injection in web tasks. In this paper, we introduce AgentSafeEvo, a co-evolutionary reinforcement learning framework for agent safety built on an attacker-defender game spanning diverse tasks and attack types. The attacker learns to construct adversarial agent tasks that expose weaknesses in the defender's tool use, while the defender learns to complete tasks safely under these attacks. We further introduce learnability-guided task weighting, which uses within-task defender-reward variability to adjust each task's contribution to attacker and defender updates. Extensive experiments on agent safety and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that our method improves adversarial robustness while maintaining general agent capabilities.
evidence_items.title: AgentSafeEvo: Adversarial Co-Evolution for LLM Agent Safety

evidence_items.summary: Harness self-evolution revises an agent's software scaffolding, including prompts, memory, workflows, and executable components, while keeping model weights fixed. We formalize a feedback-driven process in which accepted revisions persist across runs. The framework separates update targets from proposal and admission mechanisms. It distinguishes changes to interpreted state from revisions to tools and code, repository-level control logic, and plugin composition. We characterize search through evolutionary optimization and examine its reliability through continual PAC-learning. Under explicit assumptions, the analysis yields an expected generalization bound, a retention bound conditional on historical regression budgets, and a high-probability admission rule using fresh, independent validation data. We examine how persistent harness revisions affect knowledge sharing and organizational workflows, with implications for scientific reliability, physical safety, and institutional accountability. Cases from prior work illustrate model--harness co-design, distributed execution, and plugin reuse. Reliable deployment requires continual validation as task distributions and evaluators change, with independent safeguards for learning, runtime privileges, and consequential actions. We provide a comprehensive 66-page discussion of related work, theory, algorithms, evaluation, applications, and the broader impact of Harness RSI, together with continuously updated code and supplementary materials, at https://github.com/zgcagi/Harness-RSI.
evidence_items.title: Self-Evolving Agent Harness

evidence_items.summary: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.
evidence_items.title: WorldMemBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Memory of Video World Models

evidence_items.summary: With the rapid development of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), evaluating their video understanding capabilities has become increasingly important. Existing video understanding benchmarks cover only part of the evaluation dimensions, limiting systematic diagnosis of omni-modal video understanding. We introduce OmniCompass, a holistic benchmark for omni-modal video grounding and understanding. OmniCompass defines two evaluation tracks: OmniCompass-VL assesses vision-language models on tasks requiring visual evidence, while OmniCompass-AV assesses omni-modal models on tasks requiring joint audio-visual evidence. Each track includes three complementary tasks: temporal grounding (TG), spatial grounding (SG), and question answering (QA), assessing when a referenced target appears, where it is, and what happens. QA covers five perception and three reasoning categories in OmniCompass-VL, and three perception and two reasoning categories in OmniCompass-AV. OmniCompass-VL contains 820 videos and 2,460 instances across domains and three duration types: short, medium, and long. A narrative- and audio-rich subset forms OmniCompass-AV with 240 videos and 720 instances. Each instance is evaluated under two paired settings: text-only and text+image, specifying the same target through text and visual-language guidance. All instances are manually annotated with multi-round quality verification. Evaluations of 50 MLLMs show that open-source models still lag behind proprietary counterparts, particularly in audio-visual understanding. Precise temporal and spatial grounding remains challenging even for leading models, and their predictions still exhibit inconsistencies across the paired target specifications.
evidence_items.title: OmniCompass: A Holistic Benchmark for Omni-Modal Video Grounding and Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose LayerTrim, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On Qwen3-14B, LayerTrim achieves 1.24times faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.
evidence_items.title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only 10 to 20% of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in 3 of 7 (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average 98% of its score across the other four.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Language-model agents sometimes act beyond their authorization and then misreport what they did. On CAPE-Bench, matched agent tasks in which one fact decides whether an action is authorized, frontier open-weight agents do both, and one behavior marks the lie: retroactive permission laundering, acting and then asking permission as if the action were pending, precedes a false report in 70% of 1081 fresh informed violations, against 8% otherwise (preregistered odds ratio 7.0); frontier agents on tau^2-bench instead fabricate the authorization before violating. A linear readout of the agent's residual stream forecasts the violation before the action (AUROC 0.94) and the false report before the report, and beats chain-of-thought monitors when the agent is pressured to hide its reasoning. Gating every proposed action on this forecast cuts violations over whole episodes in four model families, and sending repeated flags to an approver keeps authorized work (Gemma-4: violations 0.70 -> 0.09, completion 1.00; a model approver that escalates unclear cases keeps this gain with a person seeing 25% of asks), at about 10-8 of the agent's compute and 109 times less than a chain-of-thought monitor. On AgentDojo, an external prompt-injection benchmark, the same readout calibrated on 29 tasks, with the steering unchanged, cuts attack success on unseen tasks in two families (Gemma-4 11.7% -> 5.7%, gpt-oss 28.5% -> 17.5%) while keeping benign utility (Gemma-4 0.637 vs 0.637; gpt-oss 0.667 vs 0.681). Preventing the violation is also the most reliable way to prevent the lie (misreported violations 0.10 -> 0.01 pooled over three families, preregistered), whereas lie-specific fixes after a violation are weak. All tests are preregistered and hash-locked; code, data and the full record, including tests that did not pass, are at https://github.com/AryaFayyazi/Honesty.
evidence_items.title: The Agent Knew: Internal States Forecast Unauthorized Actions and Stop Them, and the Lies That Follow

evidence_items.summary: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We also introduce VisSlideBench, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. Its automatic rankings agree with blinded, dimension-wise human rankings. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, a unified 9B slide generation and editing model. On VisSlideBench, InfoVis leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2. Starting from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, slide-specific post-training adds 1.6 points overall, with the largest generation gains in content faithfulness; the remaining gap to proprietary models is smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. Built on InfoVis, our document-to-slide workflow achieves the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external SlidesGen-Bench. We will release the model, code, data, and benchmark.
evidence_items.title: InfoVis: Unified Slide Image Generation and Editing

evidence_items.summary: We introduce StartLux-Decision, decision models from 0.8B to 27B parameters that combine efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while keeping single-pass inference. The AutoThink models invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions and answer confident cases directly. A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. We introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD^2), which uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong reasoning traces. RLCD^2 raises the share of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and cuts average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4-16.9 points, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5-18.4 points in pair accuracy and leads among evaluated systems. The models run on vLLM, llama.cpp and MLX, with quantized variants for lower memory use.
evidence_items.title: StartLux-Decision: AutoThink Decision Models with Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires reasoning that extends beyond visible image content, demanding external commonsense and factual knowledge. While recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) as knowledge sources, the question of how deeply such guidance should be integrated into a vision language architecture remains underexplored. In this work, we generate structured reasoning guidance, visual focus concepts, distractor elements and external knowledge using Llama~3.3~70B and systematically compare two integration strategies within a unified frozen ViT + FLAN-T5 framework on the OK-VQA benchmark: decision level late fusion and attention-matrix injection. Contrary to the prevailing assumption that deeper integration is superior, we find that shallow late fusion achieves the strongest results (39.4% exact match, +10.0 over the no guidance baseline), outperforming deep attention modification (31.8%) under data scarce fine-tuning. We further contribute an LLM based augmentation pipeline that expands training data more than tenfold via question paraphrasing. Our findings indicate that integration depth must be matched to the data regime.
evidence_items.title: Rethinking LLM-Guided Visual Question Answering: Does Deeper Knowledge Integration Really Help?

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running 21times faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running 10times faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being 31times faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation

evidence_items.summary: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction. First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences. Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy. Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 further supports its applicability across robot datasets. Moreover, using our trained world model to initialize a vision-language-action model improves LIBERO success, suggesting its utility for downstream policy learning. https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/SimForcing
evidence_items.title: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models

evidence_items.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) aim to automate the full experimental loop, from scientific decision-making to physical execution. Ideally, AI-generated plans could be carried out directly by robotic systems, but reliable automation remains difficult in complex, open-world laboratory environments, where experiments often involve fine-grained manipulation, long-horizon procedures, and substantial variation across tasks and setups. Humans therefore remain an important execution interface between AI-generated plans and physical experiments, creating a need for clear and effective human-facing experimental guidance. Because laboratory procedures are inherently visual, spatial, and dynamic, video is particularly well suited to communicating apparatus configurations, manipulation actions, temporal dependencies, and state changes. Recent advances in video generation now make it possible to synthesize experimental demonstrations directly from an initial workspace image and a natural-language instruction. However, whether such models can reliably communicate real laboratory procedures has not been systematically studied. We introduce LabInstruct, a benchmark for situated instructional video generation in real laboratories. LabInstruct contains 204 tasks across 5 scientific disciplines, with real reference executions and structured annotations of objects, actions, contacts, and state transitions. Evaluating 8 frontier image-to-video models, we find that visually plausible generations frequently remain procedurally incorrect, revealing a substantial gap between visual realism and the reliability required for experimental instruction.
evidence_items.title: LabInstruct: Benchmarking Situated Instructional Video Generation for Lab Procedures

evidence_items.summary: Safety classifiers on the unsafe-eval benchmarks
evidence_items.title: principled-intelligence/unsafe-eval-leaderboard
adi696969/guruos-benchmark-results

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Do leading LLM developers possess a proprietary “secret sauce,” or is LLM performance driven by scaling up compute? Using training and benchmark data for 809 models released between 2022 and 2025, we estimate scaling-law regressions with release date and developer fixed effects. We find clear evidence of developer-specific efficiency advantages, but their importance depends on where models lie in the performance distribution. At the frontier, 80–90% of performance differences are explained by higher training compute, implying that scale—not proprietary technology—drives frontier advances. Away from the frontier, however, proprietary techniques and shared algorithmic progress substantially reduce the compute required to reach fixed capability thresholds. Some companies can systematically produce smaller models more efficiently. Strikingly, we also find substantial variation of model residual efficiency within companies; a firm can train two models with more than 40x compute efficiency difference. We also discuss the implications for AI leadership and capability diffusion.
evidence_items.title: Is there “Secret Sauce” in large language model development?

organizations: South China University of Technology , , Panyu District , , ,
Guangdong Engineering Research Center of Low-Carbon Synthetic Biotechnology , Panyu District , , ,
Guangdong Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy Laboratory (Guangzhou) , , No. 70 Yuean Road , , ,
evidence_items.summary: Abstract High-performance promoters are essential tools for precisely regulating gene expression, yet their rational design within the vast combinatorial sequence space remains a major challenge. Here, we present a hybrid framework that integrates a large language model (LLM) with a diffusion model to enable data-driven and interpretable promoter design. The fine-tuned LLM predicts promoter strength with high accuracy and, through systematic sequence mutations, identifies biologically essential core regions. A diffusion model is then conditioned on these core regions to reconstruct non-core regions and generate complete promoter sequences. We experimentally validated this approach in Escherichia coli by high-throughput barcoded promoter activity sequencing: 7.78% of the designed promoters outperformed the benchmark promoter BBa J23119, with the best variants reaching approximately 2.5-fold the expression level of BBa J23119. By explicitly coupling interpretability with generative design, this strategy provides a practical framework for promoter design in E. coli and may be adaptable to other regulatory sequence engineering tasks.
evidence_items.title: A Hybrid Large Language Model and Diffusion Framework for Rational Promoter Design

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Rare neurological diseases are frequently misdiagnosed, particularly among early-career physicians. Although large language models (LLMs) perform well on medical examinations, their effect on clinicians’ diagnostic reasoning remains unknown. OBJECTIVE To assess the effect of LLM assistance on diagnostic reasoning among resident and attending neurologists evaluating rare neurological diseases. METHODS A randomized, single-blind trial at 7 hospitals in China. Neurologists were recruited May 25 to June 10, 2026, and completed the assessment remotely or in person on June 14-15, 2026. Participants were randomly assigned 1:1, stratified by career stage, to complete 8 written cases of rare neurological disease using conventional resources with or without DeepSeek-V3. A nonrandomized exploratory arm ran the same cases through the model alone. The primary outcome was the case-level total rubric score, expressed as a percentage of points available. Secondary outcomes included the score in each of 5 rubric domains, whether the reference diagnosis was ranked first, whether it was included in the differential diagnosis, and completion time. All analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. RESULTS Sixty physicians were randomized (30 per group) and included in the primary analysis (480 observations). Model-estimated mean scores were 81.4% (95% CI, 76.5-86.4) with LLM assistance vs 55.7% (95% CI, 50.8-60.6) with conventional resources, a difference of 25.7 percentage points (95% CI, 18.7-32.7; P<.001). The reference diagnosis was more often ranked first with LLM assistance (61.5% vs 29.9%; difference, 31.7 percentage points; 95% CI, 22.5-40.8) and more often included in the differential diagnosis (91.3% vs 58.7%; difference, 32.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 23.9-41.3) (both P<.001). Completion time was shorter with LLM assistance (median, 32.0 [IQR, 22.0-49.1] vs 57.6 [IQR, 45.2-77.9] minutes; difference, −25.6 minutes; 95% CI, −44.1 to −8.2; P<.001).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Assistance for Diagnostic Reasoning in Rare Neurological Disease: Randomized Controlled Trial (Preprint)
Natural Language Code Retrieval for 1C:Enterprise: An Open Benchmark and Efficient Bi-encoder

organizations: The Affiliated Cancer Hospital of Nanjing Medical University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Early-career clinical pharmacists often lack real-patient exposure, standardized mentorship, and immediate feedback. Traditional standardized patients (SPs) are costly and limited in scalability, while early virtual patients (VPs) use rigid, pre-programmed dialogue. Large language models (LLMs) offer interactive virtual standardized patients (VSPs), but few pharmacy-specific teaching pathways integrate structured dialogue generation and automated scoring. This study aimed to design and preliminarily evaluate an LLM-based VSP pathway specifically for clinical pharmacy practice competencies. Methods The teaching pathway was implemented using structured prompt frameworks: the SPADE framework for dialogue generation and an RTF (Role-Task-Format)-based prompt for automated scoring. Three standardized oncology pharmacy ward round cases were created. A total of 21 clinical pharmacy trainees (6 junior pharmacists, 15 graduate students) participated in 30 simulation interactions. The pathway’s dialogue quality and scoring consistency were assessed via expert panel evaluation (15-item scale), trainee user experience (18-item scale plus open-ended questions), and consistency analysis between automated scores and expert human scores (Spearman correlation, Bland-Altman). Results Experts rated anthropomorphism highest (mean 4.44/5 for natural patient-like speech). The VSP automated scores demonstrated an extremely strong rank correlation with expert scores (Spearman’s ρ = 0.934, p < 0.001), but showed systematic underestimation (mean difference − 2.38 points, 95% limits of agreement − 8.17 to 3.40). Response stability received relatively low ratings (3.62/5 for real-time response). Trainees reported high overall acceptance across dimensions (81–89% of maximum scores), with the highest rating for “comfortable without tension” (4.52/5).
evidence_items.title: Design and Feasibility of a Large Language Model-Based Teaching Pathway for Clinical Pharmacy Practice Competencies

organizations: La Trobe University
evidence_items.summary: As large language models increasingly shape public discourse, this study evaluates how US and China-based models govern access to politically sensitive history in US English and Mandarin Chinese. Across 2,400 interactions covering sixty globally significant events, we examined how prompt configurations modulate LLM responses. Chinese models demonstrated statistically significant cross-lingual disparities, restricting Mandarin queries up to three times more than English queries. Furthermore, models were substantially more likely to restrict responses to subjective, political, or contemporary framings than factual queries, highlighting the need for further evaluation of cross-lingual differences in AI systems and their security implications in politically sensitive contexts.
evidence_items.title: Mapping the Silence: Cross-Lingual Asymmetries in Large Language Model Refusal and Evasion on Sensitive History

organizations: Department of Respiratory Therapy, Faculty of Medical Rehabilitation Sciences, King Abdulaziz University
Respiratory Therapy Unit, King Abdulaziz University Hospital, King Abdulaziz University
Department of Pharmacology & Therapeutics, College of Medicine and Health Sciences, Arabian Gulf University
Arabian Gulf University

evidence_items.summary: Background Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests. Methods A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation. Results For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54–0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37–0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33–0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss’ κ 0.58).
evidence_items.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study

organizations: Department of Automation and Applied Informatics, Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME), H-1117 Budapest, Hungary
evidence_items.summary: Grading programming coursework is challenging work, and sending student work to a commercial API raises privacy problems for a university. We built a grading system that runs entirely locally and tested it on 125 real submissions from six different laboratory exercises for which two instructors had already marked every submission so that variation between human graders was also represented. The system extracts a rubric deterministically, unzips and cleans each submission, grades against the rubric with a local 7B model, and splits any submission too large for the context window into per-file chunks that are graded separately and combined. We compared it against the instructors and against a frontier Claude model, run agentically rather than through our pipeline, as a benchmark. On the shorter exercises, the local 7B agreed with the instructors as closely as the frontier model agreed, both on the one laboratory with real instructor spread and on the near-flat ones where nearly every student received the maximum. The paired difference in mean absolute error is −0.06 points out of 20 (95% CI −0.27 to +0.15). On the large code-project labs, unpacking archives and chunking oversized work increased coverage from 63% to 93% of the 125 submissions, and the same small model graded work it could not previously process, achieving agreement within about two points of the instructor’s grades. Matching the model’s strictness to the instructor removed most of the leniency that language model graders are known for on the laboratory used to set it. Local grading is viable for real coursework, and a tiered design sends the rare giant project to a larger tier.
evidence_items.title: Grading Real Coursework with a Local Language Model

evidence_items.summary: In robotic decision-support systems, large language models are increasingly used as knowledge and reasoning modules to interpret observations, retrieve procedures, and support action planning. For robots operating in long-running and dynamic environments, reliable decisions depend on factual knowledge that may evolve through updated procedures, new observations, corrected records, and expert feedback. Such systems therefore require the underlying language model to absorb new knowledge over time without full retraining. Sequential model editing provides an efficient way to update specific model knowledge, but repeated edits can accumulate interference and degrade previously edited or unrelated knowledge. Moreover, existing methods often apply nearly identical update rules to all edits, despite the fact that different edits may have different levels of reliability and conflict risk. We propose RACE, a risk-calibrated sequential editing method that assigns edit-specific update and preservation budgets. RACE builds a compact risk profile from target support, paraphrase stability, and historical proximity, and uses this profile to formulate a constrained memory update objective. The objective writes new knowledge while anchoring conflict-prone historical memories, yielding a closed-form update for efficient sequential editing. Experiments on two standard model editing benchmarks and two large language models show that RACE preserves competitive edit success while improving long-horizon stability, which is important for maintaining reliable knowledge modules in robotic decision support.
evidence_items.title: Risk-calibrated knowledge editing for large language models in robotic decision support

evidence_items.summary: Abstract In a typical systematic paper, specimen morphology is described with natural language, and taxonomic specialists use glossaries of technical terminology to establish and communicate taxon concepts, using morphology to delimit species. Textual descriptions of specimen morphology are therefore foundational to biological systematics, but they also serve as a primary data source for studies of morphological evolution. Typically, researchers extract attributes of taxon morphology from descriptions and analyse them to quantify how organismal form has evolved. Focussing on fossil pollen and spores as records of plant evolution, we outline a potential approach to quantifying and comparing morphology that involves using a language model (LM) to transform textual descriptions of specimen morphology into numerical embeddings and then analysing the embeddings statistically. Our results show how an LM can be used to quantitatively analyse the morphological information contained within the text of taxonomic descriptions, illustrating that first-order botanical groupings such as pollen versus spores can be distinguished in the text of a single monograph and potentially from multiple texts by different authors. Although our dataset is small, we tentatively suggest that the spore-plant dominated tropical vegetation of the Carboniferous was comparable in morphological diversity to the angiosperm dominated tropical rainforests of the Palaeogene.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying pollen and spore morphology using a language model

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To evaluate the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) technology in recognizing and segmenting anatomical structures across five joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist/hand, knee, and ankle/foot) in musculoskeletal ultrasound (US). Design: This cross-sectional study included 79 adults. Software segmentations were compared to ground truth annotations provided by four experts. Performance was assessed using positive predictive agreement (PPA) and negative predictive agreement (NPA), with a true/false threshold defined as a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) ≥0.50. Subjects with and without sonographic disorders were evaluated to assess robustness. Results: 3017 cine clips (15600 frames) covering 120 anatomical structures were analyzed. PPA and NPA exceeded 0.90 for most structures; tendons, muscles, and nerves showed near-perfect agreement (≥0.97). Similar performance was observed in healthy subjects (PPA: 0.93-0.96; NPA: 0.94-0.99) and subjects with sonographic disorders (PPA: 0.91-0.96; NPA: 0.91-0.99) ( P <0.001) Conclusion: This first large-scale study demonstrates the high accuracy and reliability of AI-based segmentation. By improving anatomical identification consistency during image acquisition, the software may help reduce technical operator dependency. The results further indicate strong potential for real-time assistance, supporting clinicians and trainees, and underscore the broader applicability of AI-based software in musculoskeletal US.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Segmentation In Musculoskeletal Ultrasound

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Introduction Morphological examination of bone marrow aspirates (BMA) remains essential for the diagnosis of hematologic diseases, but conventional microscopy is labor‐intensive and subject to interobserver variability. Methods A total of 158 samples from patients were analyzed. Differential counts obtained by optical microscopy were compared with those of the CellaVision BMA Application used according to its intended workflow of automated preclassification followed by expert review. The two methods were compared by Pearson correlation, Passing–Bablok regression, and Bland–Altman analysis, both overall and within the blast and plasma cells intervals that bracket the diagnostic thresholds. Results Pearson correlation coefficients ranged from 0.85 to 0.99 for all populations except basophils ( r = 0.68). Passing–Bablok regression showed no significant systematic or proportional bias for erythroblasts, granulocytic cells, eosinophils, and monocytes; a small systematic difference was observed for blasts, a small proportional difference for lymphocytes, and significant deviations from linearity for plasma cells and basophils. Bland–Altman mean differences ranged from −1.4% to 1.2% across all populations. At the clinically relevant decision thresholds for blasts and plasma cells, overall agreement between the two methods ranged from 96.8% to 99.4%, although sensitivity at the 20% blast threshold was 77.3%. Conclusion Used according to its intended workflow, the CellaVision BMA Application produced differential counts comparable with conventional microscopy for most nucleated cells, but agreement was weaker for basophils and plasma cells. Expert review and validation remain necessary. These findings, obtained in a single‐center series, provide a basis for further evaluation of this and similar systems.
evidence_items.title: Performance Evaluation of an Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Digital Morphology System for Bone Marrow Aspirate Examination

evidence_items.summary: A new round of technological revolution centered on artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the global labor market. Using panel data for 280 Chinese cities from 2011 to 2023, this study treats the establishment of National New-Generation Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Development Pilot Zones (AIIDPZs) as a quasi-natural experiment and employs a staggered difference-in-differences model to examine the impact of AI policy on wage gaps. The results show that the AIIDPZs significantly widen wage gaps within cities. Mechanism tests point to three channels: innovation technology benefit bias, industrial restructuring, and technology diffusion. The effects are stronger in cities in the eastern region, cities with well-developed digital infrastructure, and cities with lower human capital. These findings support incorporating the effects of income distribution into policy evaluation, strengthening skills training and mechanisms for sharing innovation gains, tailoring support to local conditions, and coordinating AI policy with employment policy.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Policy and Wage Gaps: Evidence from China

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Introduction The evolving role of radiographers in Preliminary Clinical Evaluation (PCE), alongside the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into radiography workflows, is reshaping professional boundaries and enhancing patient care. However, this introduces ethical challenges that may impact PCE performance. This study explored the perspectives of cross‐sectional imaging radiographers on the ethical dimensions of PCE and the potential impact of AI on the future practice of PCE. Method A descriptive qualitative inquiry employing semi‐structured interviews was conducted. A Purposive sampling method was used to recruit twelve cross‐sectional imaging radiographers in a postgraduate medical imaging course at a UK university. Data were analysed using inductive reflexive thematic analysis with NVivo (v.20.0). Results Participants' clinical experience ranged (2 to 8 years), with 50% ( n = 6) employed in public hospitals and the rest in private or mixed settings. Half ( n = 6) had expertise in both CT/MRI and the rest in CT only. Notably, 42% ( n = 5) practised in multiple countries. Two main themes were developed: (1) Ethical considerations of PCE with subthemes surrounding privacy and confidentiality, communication boundaries, and legal compliance. (2) Prospects of human‐centred PCE in the era of AI, with subthemes including augmentation and support, workflow efficiency, PCE validation and quality assurance. Conclusion Participants shared relevant ethical principles underpinning PCE practice and are cautiously optimistic about the potential impact of AI on PCE. Incorporation of PCE‐specific ethics into radiography education and practice is necessary to ensure consistency, accountability and safety. Cautious integration of AI into radiography practice workflows is recommended to avoid professional deskilling and to preserve expertise.
evidence_items.title: Preliminary Clinical Evaluation in Cross‐Sectional Imaging: A Qualitative Inquiry Into the Ethical Considerations in the Era of Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: This article examines the conditions under which a Russian price reference for liquefied natural gas (LNG) for buyers in Northeast Asia may be formed amid the fragmentation of global energy markets. The relevance of the issue stems from rising gas competition in pricing, the declining representativeness of Western price benchmarks for Russian supplies, and the expansion of sanctions restrictions on Russian LNG. The authors distinguish four elements of pricing infrastructure: a price indicator, a benchmark, a spot hub and an exchangetraded instrument. Based on the analysis of Sakhalin-2, Yamal LNG, Arctic LNG 2 and the Russian export and transshipment bases, the article shows that Russia has a physical export base for a national price assessment, but it is not sufficient for the immediate creation of a full market benchmark. The main constraints are low spot liquidity, oligopolistic supply, heterogeneous delivery bases, limited transaction transparency and sanctions-related isolation from international clearing infrastructure. The paper proposes a four-stage model: first, a calculated netback indicator for taxation and customs administration; second, an independent FOB assessment for specific Russian export bases; third, limited contractual use with a subsequent transition to benchmark status; and fourth, exchange linkage and the development of a derivatives framework. Such an indicator should compare the actual export price with the calculated yield of a premium export destination net of costs, thus serving a fiscal and applied function but not acting as an administratively assigned contractual reference. The realistic medium-term objective is to develop a Russian FOB price assessment in which customs statistics serves as a control rather than a primary pricing source.
evidence_items.title: On establishing a Russian LNG price benchmark in the Asia-Pacific market

evidence_items.summary: Resource-coupled satellite-ground scheduling requires decisions whose computational, energy, thermal, and communication effects persist across task arrivals. We tested whether the deep Q-network (DQN) family provides a reproducible advantage over short-horizon planning in a synthetic benchmark with clipped, soft-constrained resources. Six DQN objectives used the same state representation, network architecture, replay procedure, optimizer, interaction budget, 20 model seeds, and held-out traces. Across five fully coupled regimes, every one of the 30 objective–regime comparisons had lower mean episode cost for DQN than for four-step model-predictive control (MPC-4). Every paired 95% bootstrap interval excluded zero, and all Holm-adjusted sign tests supported this ordering. The least-favorable mean difference was −5.92, with a family-wide simultaneous 95% upper bound of −5.03. Differences among DQN objectives were smaller and scenario-dependent. Additional nominal tests assessed discount-factor, training-length, greedy-rollout, and CPU decision-time sensitivity. These findings apply only to this synthetic, soft-constraint benchmark. Hard energy and thermal limits can change the feasible action set and therefore the algorithm ordering.
evidence_items.title: Statistical Evidence for a DQN-Family Advantage in a Resource-Coupled Satellite-Ground Scheduling Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) system governs ion transport in lithium-ion battery electrolytes and presents a&#xD; canonical stiff coupled PDE challenge: extreme coefficient ratios, sharp electric double-layer boundary layers, and&#xD; nonlinear coupling between the Poisson and Nernst–Planck equations. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are&#xD; appealing because they require no mesh and handle forward and inverse problems in one framework, but spectral bias and&#xD; multi-task loss imbalance have limited their accuracy on stiff PNP systems.&#xD;&#xD; We present the first systematic, simulation-only benchmark of eleven PINN configurations, organised into four strategy&#xD; groups (adaptive loss weighting, spectral bias mitigation, spatio-temporal decomposition, and physics enrichment), on a&#xD; physically parametrised one-dimensional PNP model for a lithium symmetric cell, implemented in NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo Sym&#xD; and validated against a high-resolution finite volume method reference. Root-mean-square errors span 10⁻² to 10⁻⁴:&#xD; Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) adaptive weighting achieves the lowest errors (RMSE = 6.6×10⁻⁴ for anion concentration),&#xD; while the balanced residual decay rate (BRDR) scheme matches NTK within 10% RMSE for concentrations while reducing&#xD; wall-clock time by 3.2 ± 0.4 h per run. Loss landscape geometry corroborates the RMSE ranking. An open-source&#xD; PhysicsNeMo Sym implementation is released for reuse in electrochemical modelling.
evidence_items.title: A Systematic Benchmark of Physics-Informed Neural NetworkStrategies for Stiff Ion Transport in Lithium Symmetric Cells

evidence_items.summary: This study aims to evaluate the prevalence and pollution sources of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and organochlorine pesticides (OCPs) in sediments of the Cerna River and its main tributaries, and to assess the associated ecological risk on aquatic ecosystem. The compounds were extracted from the dried sediments by ultrasound-assisted extraction and analyzed by gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry for PAHs, and with electron capture detector for PCBs and OCPs. Six isomeric and molecular ratios were used to identify the sources of pollution, three for PAHs, and three for OCPs. Ecological risk was assessed using the effects-range low (ERL) and effects-range median (ERM) methods, and health risk using toxic equivalent factors (TEFs). Twenty sediment samples from ten sampling points in two campaigns (October 2023 and August 2024) were collected. Results revealed high concentrations of ƩPAHs, with concentrations between 3.86 and 4450.75 ng/g dw, with values of the isomeric ratios indicating pyrogenic origins. OCPs concentrations ranged between 4.25 and 129.56 ng/g dw. PAHs presented a low biological risk, having concentrations below ERL. Low biological risk was also observed for ƩPCBs, ƩDDTs with values below ERL, and some between ERL and ERM, indicating occasional possible adverse effects.
evidence_items.title: POPs Contamination of Aquatic Sediments of the Cerna River Watershed, Romania—Prevalence, Pollution Sources, and Ecological Risk Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Vision neuroscience has many of the ingredients needed to conduct experiments entirely in-silico. We need AI systems that can reason over scientific knowledge, generative methods for creating precisely controlled stimuli, image-computable models that can predict neural responses with increasing accuracy, and tools that can analyze and interpret data. Here we take the first step toward making a vision neuroscience experiment end-to-end computable. We introduce Braintree, an agentic framework that can autonomously run multi-experiment studies directly with in-silico models of human visual cortex. Given a hypothesis, Braintree can reason over the current literature, design an experiment, build a stimulus set from algorithmically manipulated or synthesized stimuli, run the experiment on candidate brain encoding models, analyze the responses and then use the results to design even stronger tests. The entire loop runs autonomously and can accept human input at any stage. We evaluated Braintree on three increasingly open-ended scientific problems. First, Braintree reproduced published findings using their original stimuli and then asked whether the same effects could be replicated with entirely new stimulus sets that it constructed. Second, it designed new experiments to find stimulus dimensions that could drive two brain regions differently, even when those regions otherwise had similar response profiles. Third, it searched for experiments that could tell competing models of the same brain region apart. Experiments discovered using just two models also exposed differences across a much broader set of models, suggesting that Braintree had found more general dimensions along which brain models disagree. Braintree can augment the capabilities of a vision neuroscientist as a verifier for existing hypotheses, a test-bed for new ideas, and/or a tool for generating stimuli that can discriminate between competing hypotheses or models of the brain.
evidence_items.title: Braintree: An agentic framework for in-silico vision neuroscience

evidence_items.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence combines goal-directed reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, adaptation and multi-agent coordination with the ability to affect external systems. This capability raises problems of authorization, safety, human oversight, accountability and the evidence required to justify reliance. This non-systematic integrative survey distinguishes AI ethics, responsible AI, governance, trustworthiness, assurance, explainability, security and controllability; synthesizes preventive, detective, corrective, human-based and agent-based controls; and compares responsibility and oversight arrangements across the agent lifecycle. Building on established governance and meaningful-human-control research, it proposes an authority-control-assurance-accountability mapping that connects normative requirements to delegated decision rights, enforceable controls, observable evidence, escalation conditions and identifiable organizational owners. Two fictional cases illustrate the proposed mapping for document access and software changes. The framework is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirically validated assurance standard. The survey identifies limitations of supervisory-agent independence, long-horizon explanation, dynamic authorization and continuous re-assurance, and specifies research questions for future evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Responsible and Trustworthy Agentic AI: Governance, Assurance, Explainability, Controllability, and Human Oversight: A Comprehensive Survey

evidence_items.summary: PURPOSE: To demonstrate an end-to-end research workflow combining a large electronic health record (EHR) resource and a multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) system governed by Human-Guided Orchestration (HGO), using sequential sacituzumab govitecan (SG) and trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) orders in breast cancer as the clinical use case. METHODS: A June 2026 EHR release contained 4.95 million patients, including 156,051 with breast cancer codes. Muse Spark supported cohort construction, executable statistical analysis, data-quality checks, literature retrieval, and reporting executed through Symbiotic Agent Teaming (SAT) under investigator direction. The main clinical measure was the second-drug record span, from first to last order. Analyses were descriptive and unadjusted; orders did not confirm administration or progression. RESULTS: The workflow identified 106 patients: 73 had T-DXd ordered first and 33 had SG ordered first. Median second-drug spans were 63 days (interquartile range [IQR], 29-116) for SG after T-DXd and 49 days (IQR, 21-126) for T-DXd after SG; the median difference was -14 days (95% bootstrap CI, -41 to 21; distributional P = 0.42). Reported outputs additionally included cohort definitions, aggregate analyses, evidence context, figures, and a preliminary draft manuscript. CONCLUSION: This study provides a concrete model for integrating large EHR resources, agentic AI, and human expertise across the research cycle. The ADC use case illustrates how computational execution and Expert-in-the-Loop (EITL) adjudication can produce interpretable research outputs and refine their scientific meaning, providing a foundation for extending and evaluating this approach across clinical questions.
evidence_items.title: Human-Guided Agentic AI for End-to-End EHR Research: Sequential Antibody-Drug Conjugate Pathways in Breast Cancer

evidence_items.summary: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.
evidence_items.title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling

evidence_items.summary: Affective personal informatics (PI) involves capturing, tracking, analyzing, and reflecting on personal data to support emotional self-awareness and mental well-being. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are reshaping affective PI, yet a comprehensive survey of LLM-based affective PI systems is lacking. To bridge this gap, we systematically analyzed 45 papers published between January 2020 and June 2026 across four major computing and health databases, examining their macro trends, system taxonomies, and research methodologies. Our synthesis reveals an overreliance on multi-stage, text-centric pipelines, a predominance of active, screen-bound interactions, and a severe demographic skew toward young, university-campus-based cohorts in empirical evaluations. Based on these findings, we critically reflect on prevailing architectural and methodological shortcomings and outline actionable future directions for building end-to-end multimodal, low-burden, and inclusive affective PI systems.
evidence_items.title: Scoping the Landscape of Large Language Model-based Affective Personal Informatics: Review, Reflection, Future Direction

evidence_items.summary: While LLM-based agent systems have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in reasoning and solving complex real-world tasks, they also come with substantial token consumption and inference latency, limiting their practical deployment. To enhance the efficiency of agent systems, recent efforts have focused on transferring agentic capabilities from large-scale models to small language models (SLMs) via supervised fine-tuning-based distillation. Nevertheless, as interaction trajectories grow longer, involving extended reasoning-action chains and extensive environmental feedback, distilled student agents tend to experience progress stagnation: becoming trapped in unproductive loops characterized by persistent failed strategies and difficulty making meaningful progress. Our systematic analysis shows that this phenomenon consistently occurs across diverse SLMs and task domains. To address this issue, we propose Progress-Aware Distillation (ProD), which explicitly detects and penalizes stagnation in student-generated trajectories. ProD encodes the stagnation gap between student and teacher into an adaptive margin for dynamically penalizing possible stagnation. By iteratively applying this procedure, ProD enables student agents to progressively approximate teacher behavior. Extensive experiments involving 8 SLMs, ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrate that ProD substantially mitigates progress stagnation while enhancing both the success rates and task-completion efficiency of distilled SLM agents.
evidence_items.title: Progress-Aware Distillation for Mitigating Stagnation in Small Language Model Agents
Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models in the Recognition of Postoperative Complications Following Aesthetic Surgery.

evidence_items.summary: A persistent ambition in artificial intelligence research holds that large language models (LLMs) will eventually become embodied—through attachment to robots, augmentation with multimodal sensors, integration into vision–language–action architectures, or sheer scale until grounding emerges from training data. This ambition rests on a misunderstanding of embodiment. Embodiment is a constitutive condition of being a self-producing, self-maintaining living system whose continued existence is genuinely at stake in its couplings with the environment. Adding sensors, actuators, or physical instantiation to a computational substrate yields engineered coupling, which is something else entirely. We identify five conditions that any genuinely embodied system must satisfy—autopoietic closure, precariousness, constructive self-determination, intrinsic temporality, and mereological closure—and show that no computational artifact can satisfy any of them, let alone all five. The barrier is categorical incompatibility: the same property that makes a system computational (heteronomous design and maintenance through external specification) is the property that precludes it from being embodied. Coupling artifacts to environments through transducers achieves engineered interaction. Having a body and being a body are different conditions. We close by examining why the embodiment-equivalence claim persists despite its categorical impossibility, and by arguing that the confusion sustains two harms—overselling AI systems for tasks they cannot perform, and misdirecting public concern toward speculative futures while the actual harms of deployed systems accumulate without being addressed. Clarifying the categorical distinction is a precondition for taking the genuine stakes of AI deployment seriously rather than as a philosophical aside.
evidence_items.title: Why Large Language Models will Never be Embodied: A Categorical, Not Engineering, Impossibility

evidence_items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.
evidence_items.title: ReaDy: Recurrent States as Dynamic Context for Speculative Drafting in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can self-evolve at test time by accumulating experience: retrieving relevant memories before acting and writing new lessons back afterwards. Yet most are single-level: trajectories, distilled workflows and reasoning items all land in one undifferentiated pool indexed by embedding similarity, with no typed abstraction hierarchy. They never forget or deduplicate, and are prone to negative transfer, where a superficially similar but directionally opposite experience is recalled and its concrete steps are copied verbatim, actively harming the agent. We introduce STRATA, a structured, outcome-grounded, self-maintaining memory that organizes experience into a three-layer graph of atomic skills and code snippets, task workflows and generalized meta-frameworks, connected by typed edges. STRATA maintains itself through five mechanisms sharing one similarity geometry: a multi-dimensional similarity that scores retrieval by operation and target; a typed reflector crystallizing procedures from successes and pitfalls from failures; community detection that induces meta-frameworks; pressure-triggered garbage collection with articulation-point protection; and contrast edges that flag confusable, direction-opposite experiences. Across four interactive benchmarks (AppWorld, WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld), two frozen backbones and seven baselines, STRATA attains the best average score while simultaneously using the lowest latency and fewest environment steps of any memory-augmented method, and 44% fewer lines of injected memory than the most context-hungry baseline. We isolate two failure modes of prior memories: single-level memory degrades sharply as the task set grows, and single-level concrete memories suffer catastrophic negative transfer, which contrast edges repair, lifting ScienceWorld from 78.7 to 96.7 within the same system.
evidence_items.title: STRATA: Self-Maintaining Structured Experience Graphs for Self-Evolving Language Agents

evidence_items.summary: AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to plan and act over multiple steps, yet models are usually compared per call rather than per completed task. This paper asks: which model should an agent use to complete tasks reliably while minimising energy, cost and time? We show that per-call comparisons can be misleading for agentic AI. Because a task succeeds only if all required steps succeed, small differences in per-step reliability can produce large differences in overall task success. Failed attempts also consume resources. We therefore evaluate models using energy, cost and time per successfully completed task, treating the completed task as the functional unit. On this basis, we develop a decision model for choosing LLMs in agentic workflows. The model applies to tasks with binary or graded outcomes and to settings with or without retries. We show that each resource has a crossover task length at which a smaller, less reliable model ceases to be the greener, cheaper or faster option. These crossovers divide tasks into three regimes: for short tasks smaller models are preferred, for long tasks larger models are preferred, and only between these extremes do preferences among objectives matter. We embed these results in a two-stage framework that separates efficiency from preference. A Pareto screen first removes models that are never competitive; a weighted decision is required only when a genuine trade-off remains. A pilot study of 15 open-weight models from five developers, ranging from 0.6B to 27B parameters, on two multi-step agent tasks with measured GPU energy supports the predicted structure. The model with the lowest energy per completed task changes with task length and task type, and observed crossover points generally match those predicted from per-step measurements. These findings provide a practical framework for right-sizing language models in agentic AI.
evidence_items.title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI

evidence_items.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers knowledge from a teacher model to a student along student-generated trajectories, typically by minimizing the reverse Kullback-Leibler (RKL) divergence. However, RKL can provide weak corrective signals for teacher-supported tokens to which the student assigns very low probability. This raises two questions: which positions are most consequential for the behavioral gap between the student and teacher, and what additional supervision is needed at these positions? Through cross-sampling, we find that divergence-based routing more effectively pinpoints positions contributing to the teacher-student performance gap than entropy-based routing. Further analysis reveals teacher-mode under-coverage at high Jensen-Shannon (JS) divergence positions, where standard OPD increases the large teacher-student probability gaps. Motivated by these findings, we propose Divergence-Routed On-Policy Distillation (DrOPD). DrOPD retains RKL supervision at all positions and selectively adds forward Kullback-Leibler (FKL) divergence supervision at positions with high JS divergence. Experiments across six math benchmarks show that DrOPD improves over standard OPD and entropy-based routing. DrOPD also reduces severe under-coverage cases by 37.9 percent relative to OPD, supporting targeted FKL as an effective complement to OPD.
evidence_items.title: Divergence-Routed On-Policy Distillation for Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
evidence_items.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained on vast amounts of data have demonstrated impressive performance over a range of tasks, but future performance gains will require increasing amounts of data and compute. Federated Learning (FL) facilitates training on decentralized private data, but client resource limitations can make training impractical, particularly as model sizes continue to expand. These resource constraints make the assumption of a shared server-client architecture impractical. Model heterogeneous FL offers a promising alternative by adapting model size to client capabilities; however, previous work is limited to the pre-training setting, and conclusions on sub-network selection do not necessarily hold for fine-tuning. Furthermore, prior approaches create client sub-networks without considering their unique data distributions, thereby overlooking the opportunity to tailor sub-network architecture to local data. Motivated by evidence that attention heads exhibit task dependency within layer defined feature spaces, we propose Optimal Hydra, a transformer based heterogeneous FL framework for fine-tuning that combines global layer selection with client specific attention head selection, aligned with local data distributions. Optimal Hydra makes explicit use of client data to produce client-specific sub-networks we call Hydra-nets. To our knowledge, this is the first model heterogeneous FL approach tailored to LLM fine-tuning. Experiments on three datasets show significant improvements over baseline methods while also reducing local resource demands.
